<a id="letter-a"></a>

## A

<a id="a-stability"></a>**A-stability** — The property that a numerical integrator is stable for every decaying mode (Re hλ < 0) at any step size; backward Euler and the trapezoidal rule are A-stable, explicit methods never are. *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md). *See also:* [Stiff system](#stiff-system).

<a id="abcd-parameters"></a>**ABCD parameters** — Transmission parameters, V1 = A V2 − B I2 and I1 = C V2 − D I2, chosen so that cascaded two-ports multiply; a series impedance is [[1, Z], [0, 1]], a shunt admittance [[1, 0], [Y, 1]], and AD − BC = 1 for a reciprocal network. *First defined in* [07-10](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-10-two-port-networks.md). *See also:* [Two-port network](#two-port-network).

<a id="absolute-summability"></a>**Absolute summability** — The condition Σ|h[n]| < ∞ (or ∫|h(t)| dt < ∞) on an impulse response, necessary and sufficient for BIBO stability of an LTI system; the sum is also the system's worst-case gain for bounded inputs. *First defined in* [11-03](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-03-convolution.md). *See also:* [BIBO stability](#bibo-stability).

<a id="absorption-coefficient"></a>**Absorption coefficient** — The rate α at which light intensity decays with depth in a material, I ∝ e^(−αx); 1/α is the penetration depth, and direct-gap materials have large α just above the gap. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="abstraction"></a>**Abstraction** — A simplified description of a system level that exposes a contract (inputs, outputs, assumptions) and hides internal detail, so that the level above can be designed without the detail. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="ac-analysis"></a>**AC analysis** — A simulation of a circuit's small-signal sinusoidal response versus frequency, computed with phasors after linearizing around the operating point. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="ac-analysis-spice"></a>**AC analysis (SPICE)** — A simulator analysis that linearizes the circuit at its DC operating point and solves its complex nodal equations at each frequency of a sweep, giving phasors; it ignores nonlinearity, clipping and transients. *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="ac-bridge"></a>**AC bridge** — A four-arm bridge driven by a sinusoid whose detector nulls when Z₁Z₄ = Z₂Z₃; being one complex equation, balance gives two real conditions, such as an unknown inductance and its resistance (Maxwell bridge). *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="accelerated-life-test"></a>**Accelerated life test** — A test at elevated stress (temperature, voltage, humidity) that makes failures occur sooner, with an acceleration model used to translate results to use conditions. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="acceptor"></a>**Acceptor** — An impurity with one fewer valence electron than the atom it replaces (B, Al, Ga or In in silicon), which captures an electron from the valence band, leaving a mobile hole and making the material p-type. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md). *See also:* [Donor](#donor).

<a id="accumulation"></a>**Accumulation** — The MOS bias regime in which majority carriers crowd to the surface (gate below flat band for p-type), so the capacitor behaves like a simple parallel-plate capacitor, C ≈ C_ox. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="accumulation-function"></a>**Accumulation function** — A(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt, the running total of f from a fixed start; for a current it is the charge delivered so far. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="active-load"></a>**Active load** — A transistor current source used in place of a load resistor, giving a large small-signal resistance (its r_o) while consuming little DC headroom; a common-source stage with an active load approaches gain g_m(r_o1 ∥ r_o2). *First defined in* [10-06](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-06-mos-single-stage-amplifiers.md).

<a id="activity-factor"></a>**Activity factor** — α, the fraction of clock cycles in which a node makes a 0→1 transition; it scales the dynamic power αCV²f. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="adiabatic-charging"></a>**Adiabatic charging** — Charging a capacitor with a slowly ramped or stepped source so that the voltage across the series resistance stays small, reducing the loss below ½CV² (to CV²/2N for N equal steps). *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="admittance"></a>**Admittance** — Y = 1/Z = G + jB (siemens), the ratio of current phasor to voltage phasor; admittances in parallel add. Its real part, the conductance G = R/(R² + X²), is not 1/R unless the reactance is zero. *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md). *See also:* [Impedance](#impedance), [Susceptance](#susceptance).

<a id="agile-development"></a>**Agile development** — Iterative development in short cycles (sprints) that each deliver working software, with continuous customer feedback and adaptation to changing requirements (Agile Manifesto, 2001). *First defined in* [05-09](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-09-software-engineering-practices.md).

<a id="aliasing-predictor"></a>**Aliasing (predictor)** — Two branches sharing a predictor entry because their indexes coincide; usually destructive when their behaviour differs. *First defined in* [14-07](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md).

<a id="aliasing-programming"></a>**Aliasing (programming)** — Two or more names referring to the same object, so a change made through one is visible through the others; assignment in Python never copies. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="aliasing-sampling"></a>**Aliasing (sampling)** — The folding of frequencies above half the sample rate onto lower ones, because tones differing by a multiple of f_s give identical samples; a tone at f₀ appears at |f₀ − kf_s| ≤ f_s/2, and aliased signal or noise cannot be separated after sampling. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Anti-aliasing filter](#anti-aliasing-filter), [Sampling theorem](#sampling-theorem).

<a id="all-pass-filter"></a>**All-pass filter** — A circuit with |H(jω)| = 1 at all frequencies but a frequency-dependent phase, such as (1 − jωRC)/(1 + jωRC) with phase −2 arctan(ωRC); it changes a waveform's shape without changing its amplitude spectrum. *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="amdahls-law"></a>**Amdahl's law** — Speedup on N processors is 1/((1 − p) + p/N) when a fraction p of the work parallelizes; as N → ∞ it approaches 1/(1 − p), so the serial fraction caps scaling. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="amortized-cost"></a>**Amortized cost** — The average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, in which rare expensive steps are paid for by many cheap ones; a doubling array's append is O(1) amortized. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="amperes-law"></a>**Ampere's law** — (Ampère's law.) For steady currents, ∮ B · dl = µ₀ I_enc around any closed loop; with symmetry it gives the fields of wires, solenoids (µ₀nI), toroids and coaxial cables (zero outside). *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="ampere-hour"></a>**Ampere-hour** — A unit of charge, 1 Ah = 3600 C, used for battery capacity; 1 mAh = 3.6 C. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="amplitude-modulation-am"></a>**Amplitude modulation (AM)** — Carrying a message in a carrier's amplitude, A[1 + m x(t)] cos(2πf_c t); its spectrum is the carrier plus the message's spectrum shifted to ±f_c as two sidebands, occupying twice the message bandwidth. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [DSB-SC modulation](#dsb-sc-modulation), [Modulation index](#modulation-index), [Envelope detector](#envelope-detector).

<a id="and-inverter-graph-aig"></a>**And-inverter graph (AIG)** — A logic network of two-input AND nodes with optional inversions on the edges, able to express any function; the internal representation of modern synthesis and verification engines such as ABC. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md). *See also:* [Logic synthesis](#logic-synthesis).

<a id="and-or-invert-aoi-gate"></a>**AND-OR-INVERT (AOI) gate** — A single static CMOS compound gate computing the complement of a sum of products, such as AOI22 = NOT(AB + CD) with 8 transistors; its dual is the OR-AND-INVERT (OAI) gate. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md).

<a id="angle-argument"></a>**Angle (argument)** — The direction ∠z of a complex number's arrow, measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis; computed with the quadrant-aware atan2(y, x). This curriculum reports principal values in (−180°, 180°]. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="angle-condition"></a>**Angle condition** — The requirement that a point s lies on the root locus of 1 + KG(s) = 0 with K > 0, namely that the angle of G(s), the sum of angles from the zeros minus the sum from the poles, is an odd multiple of 180°. *First defined in* [15-06](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-06-root-locus.md). *See also:* [Root locus](#root-locus).

<a id="angle-deficiency"></a>**Angle deficiency** — In root-locus design, the phase a compensator must add at a desired closed-loop pole location so that the loop's total angle there is −180°; a lead compensator's zero and pole are placed to supply it. *First defined in* [15-09](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-09-lead-lag-compensation.md). *See also:* [Angle condition](#angle-condition), [Lead compensator](#lead-compensator).

<a id="angular-frequency"></a>**Angular frequency** — ω = 2πf, the rate of a sinusoid's phase advance in rad/s, where f is the frequency in hertz. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="antenna"></a>**Antenna** — A structure that converts guided electromagnetic energy into radiated waves and back; by reciprocity its pattern, gain and impedance are the same for transmitting and receiving. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Radiation pattern](#radiation-pattern), [Antenna gain](#antenna-gain).

<a id="antenna-gain"></a>**Antenna gain** — Directivity times radiation efficiency, G = e_r·D, usually quoted in dBi (relative to an isotropic radiator); EIRP = P_t·G_t. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Directivity](#directivity), [Effective aperture](#effective-aperture).

<a id="anti-aliasing-filter"></a>**Anti-aliasing filter** — The analog low-pass (or band-pass) filter before a sampler that attenuates everything that would fold into the band of interest; its requirement is set at the first alias frequency f_s − f_B, and oversampling relaxes it. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Aliasing (sampling)](#aliasing-sampling), [Oversampling](#oversampling).

<a id="anti-windup"></a>**Anti-windup** — A modification that stops integrator windup, either by clamping (pausing integration while saturated in the direction that would deepen saturation) or by back-calculation (feeding the difference between the limited and unlimited controller output back into the integrator). *First defined in* [15-08](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-08-pid-control.md). *See also:* [Integrator windup](#integrator-windup).

<a id="antiderivative"></a>**Antiderivative** — A function F with F' = f; any two differ by a constant, written ∫ f dx = F + C. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="aperture-jitter"></a>**Aperture jitter** — Random variation of a sampler's timing; it turns into noise proportional to the input's slope, limiting SNR to −20 log₁₀(2πf₀σ_t) for a sine at f₀ and RMS jitter σ_t, independent of the sample rate. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Jitter](#jitter).

<a id="apparent-power"></a>**Apparent power** — S = V_rms·I_rms, in volt-amperes; real power is S times the power factor. Wiring and transformers must be sized for S. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md). *See also:* [Power factor](#power-factor).

<a id="application-binary-interface-abi"></a>**Application binary interface (ABI)** — The binary-level contract that lets separately compiled code work together — calling convention, data type sizes and alignment, structure layout and object-file conventions; RISC-V's are ILP32 and LP64 families. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md). *See also:* [Calling convention](#calling-convention).

<a id="arc-length"></a>**Arc length** — The length of a curve, L = ∫√(1 + f'(x)²) dx, built from the element ds = √(dx² + dy²). *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="architecture-license"></a>**Architecture license** — A licence to design one's own processor cores that comply with a licensed ISA, as opposed to using the licensor's core designs; Arm's architecture licensees also pay a per-chip royalty. *First defined in* [14-02](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-02-isa-risc-v-arm-x86.md). *See also:* [Core license](#core-license).

<a id="arithmetic-intensity"></a>**Arithmetic intensity** — Operations performed per byte moved from memory. A workload whose intensity is below a machine's ridge point (peak operations per second ÷ memory bandwidth) is memory-bound; a matrix–vector product has about 1 flop per byte in 16-bit precision. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="arithmetic-logic-unit-alu"></a>**Arithmetic-logic unit (ALU)** — A block that performs one of several arithmetic and logical operations on two words, chosen by an operation code, and reports status flags; the computational core of a processor datapath. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md). *See also:* [Status flags](#status-flags).

<a id="array-factor"></a>**Array factor** — The pattern of an array of identical isotropic elements, set by their spacing and relative phases; the array's pattern is the element pattern times the array factor, and a progressive phase steers the beam. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Phased array](#phased-array).

<a id="arrhenius-model"></a>**Arrhenius model** — A thermally activated rate ∝ exp(−E_a/(kT)); the acceleration factor between temperatures is exp[(E_a/k)(1/T_use − 1/T_stress)], exponential in the often-uncertain activation energy. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="assembler"></a>**Assembler** — The tool that translates assembly language, instruction by instruction, into machine code in an object file, leaving addresses it cannot know as relocations for the linker. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md). *See also:* [Object file](#object-file), [Linker](#linker).

<a id="assertion"></a>**Assertion** — A statement (assert condition) that stops the program if a condition the code relies on is false; used for internal invariants and tests, not for validating input, because python -O removes assertions. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md).

<a id="assumed-state-method"></a>**Assumed-state method** — Analyzing a circuit with diodes by guessing which conduct, replacing each with its on or off model, solving the linear circuit, and checking every guess for consistency. *First defined in* [10-01](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-01-diodes-and-diode-circuits.md).

<a id="asymptote"></a>**Asymptote** — A line that a curve approaches in a limit, horizontal (x → ∞), vertical (f → ±∞ at a finite x) or slanted; Bode-plot straight lines are asymptotes of a frequency response. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="asymptote-centroid"></a>**Asymptote centroid** — The point (Σ poles − Σ zeros)/(n − m) on the real axis from which the n − m asymptotes of a root locus radiate, at angles (2k + 1)·180°/(n − m). *First defined in* [15-06](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-06-root-locus.md). *See also:* [Root locus](#root-locus).

<a id="asymptotic-gain-formula"></a>**Asymptotic-gain formula** — The exact closed-loop gain of a circuit with one controlled source, A_f = A∞·T/(1 + T) + A0/(1 + T), where A∞ is the gain with the controlling variable forced to zero, A0 the gain with the source set to zero, and T the return ratio. *First defined in* [12-05](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-05-feedback-topologies.md). *See also:* [Return ratio](#return-ratio).

<a id="asynchronous-fifo"></a>**Asynchronous FIFO** — A dual-port memory written in one clock domain and read in another, whose Gray-coded read and write pointers cross the domains through synchronizers and produce conservative full and empty flags. *First defined in* [08-10](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-10-timing-metastability-cdc.md). *See also:* [Clock-domain crossing (CDC)](#clock-domain-crossing-cdc).

<a id="asynchronous-reset"></a>**Asynchronous reset** — A reset that acts on a flip-flop immediately, without a clock; its release must meet a recovery time before the next clock edge, so it is usually asserted asynchronously and released through a reset synchronizer. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md). *See also:* [Recovery time](#recovery-time).

<a id="auger-recombination"></a>**Auger recombination** — Recombination in which the released energy goes to a third carrier, at rate (C_n n + C_p p)(np − n_i²); it dominates at high doping, limiting the lifetime of heavily doped regions and the efficiency of silicon solar cells. *First defined in* [09-04](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-04-generation-recombination-continuity.md).

<a id="autocorrelation-function"></a>**Autocorrelation function** — R_X(t₁, t₂) = E[X(t₁)X(t₂)]; for a stationary process R_X(τ), whose value at τ = 0 is the average power and whose decay measures how long the process remembers. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="auxiliary-polynomial"></a>**Auxiliary polynomial** — In a Routh array with a row of zeros, the even or odd polynomial formed from the row above; it divides the original polynomial, and its roots (symmetric about the origin, often an imaginary-axis pair) give the oscillation frequency at a stability boundary. *First defined in* [15-05](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-05-stability-routh-hurwitz.md). *See also:* [Routh array](#routh-array).

<a id="avalanche-breakdown"></a>**Avalanche breakdown** — Reverse breakdown in which the ionization integral reaches 1 and multiplication becomes self-sustaining; it dominates in silicon above a few volts, its voltage falls roughly as N^(−0.6) to N^(−0.75) and rises with temperature. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md). *See also:* [Critical field](#critical-field), [Tunneling breakdown](#tunneling-breakdown).

<a id="avalanche-multiplication"></a>**Avalanche multiplication** — The growth of a reverse current by repeated impact ionization in a depletion region, measured by the multiplication factor M, where 1 − 1/M equals the ionization integral; M diverges at breakdown. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="avalanche-photodiode"></a>**Avalanche photodiode** — A photodiode biased near breakdown so that photogenerated carriers are multiplied by impact ionization (APD), giving gain at the cost of extra noise. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="average-real-power"></a>**Average (real) power** — P = (V_m I_m/2) cos θ = V_rms I_rms cos θ (watts), the time average of p = vi for sinusoids; only resistance absorbs it, and it is the real part of complex power. *First defined in* [07-06](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-06-ac-power-and-power-factor.md).

<a id="average-memory-access-time-amat"></a>**Average memory access time (AMAT)** — Hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty, nested for each level of the hierarchy; the average latency a memory access sees. *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md). *See also:* [Miss rate](#miss-rate).

<a id="average-power"></a>**Average power** — The energy delivered over an interval divided by its length, (1/T)∫p dt; for varying signals it is the average of v·i, not the product of the averages. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="average-value"></a>**Average value** — (1/(b − a)) ∫_a^b f dx, the height of the rectangle with the same area; over one period it is a signal's DC value. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="axi"></a>**AXI** — Arm's AMBA Advanced eXtensible Interface, a royalty-free on-chip bus protocol with five independent valid/ready channels (write address, write data, write response, read address, read data), bursts and multiple outstanding transactions; AXI-Lite is its simple register-access subset. *First defined in* [14-11](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-11-io-buses-and-interconnect.md). *See also:* [Valid/ready handshake](#valid-ready-handshake).

<a id="axial-ratio"></a>**Axial ratio** — The ratio of the major to the minor axis of the ellipse traced by a wave's electric field; 1 for circular polarization and infinite for linear. A linear antenna on an axial-ratio-r wave captures between 1/(1 + r²) and r²/(1 + r²) of the power. *First defined in* [13-05](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-05-plane-waves.md). *See also:* [Polarization (light)](#polarization-light).

<a id="letter-b"></a>

## B

<a id="b10-life"></a>**B10 life** — The time by which 10% of a population has failed, α(−ln 0.9)^(1/γ) for a Weibull; percentile lives matter more than MTTF for wear-out. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="back-emf"></a>**Back-EMF** — The EMF a running motor's rotating coil generates against its supply, proportional to speed; it limits running current, so a stalled motor draws far more current than a spinning one. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="backside-power-delivery"></a>**Backside power delivery** — Routing a chip's power supply through thick wires on the back of the thinned wafer, freeing front-side wiring for signals and cutting IR drop; Intel ships it as PowerVia on 18A, and TSMC plans it for A16. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="baligas-figure-of-merit"></a>**Baliga's figure of merit** — The material figure εμE_c³ that sets the lowest specific on-resistance of a unipolar power device at a given blocking voltage; the cube on the critical field gives wide-bandgap materials their advantage. *First defined in* [09-13](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-13-compound-and-wide-bandgap-semiconductors.md). *See also:* [Specific on-resistance](#specific-on-resistance), [Critical field](#critical-field).

<a id="ballistic-transport"></a>**Ballistic transport** — Carrier motion across a region shorter than a few mean free paths, with few or no collisions, where mobility and velocity saturation lose their meaning; modern short-channel transistors are partly ballistic. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md).

<a id="band-gap"></a>**Band gap** — The range of energies with no allowed electron states between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band, E_g = E_c − E_v (1.12 eV in silicon); it sets intrinsic carrier density, absorption edge and breakdown strength. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="band-gap-narrowing"></a>**Band-gap narrowing** — The reduction of a semiconductor's band gap at high doping, tens of meV near 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ in silicon, which raises the effective n_i² of the region exponentially and affects bipolar emitters and solar cells. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md).

<a id="band-pass-sampling"></a>**Band-pass sampling** — Sampling a band f_L–f_H below twice its highest frequency by placing it inside one Nyquist zone: 2f_H/n ≤ f_s ≤ 2f_L/(n − 1); the band reappears between 0 and f_s/2, inverted when n is even. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Nyquist zone](#nyquist-zone), [Aliasing (sampling)](#aliasing-sampling).

<a id="bandgap-reference"></a>**Bandgap reference** — A circuit that adds a junction voltage (falling about 2 mV/K) to a voltage proportional to absolute temperature so that the temperature coefficients cancel; its output sits near the silicon bandgap, about 1.2 V. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="bandwidth"></a>**Bandwidth** — The frequency extent of a spectrum or a frequency response; it must be defined (−3 dB, null-to-null, fractional-energy such as 99%, or Nyquist frequency of a symbol stream), since the definitions can differ by large factors for one signal. *First defined in* [11-06](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-06-continuous-time-fourier-transform.md).

<a id="bandwidth-separation"></a>**Bandwidth separation** — Designing nested (cascade) loops so each outer loop is several times (typically 5 to 10) slower than the loop inside it, which lets the outer loop treat the inner one as an ideal actuator. *First defined in* [15-12](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-12-control-applications-pll-regulators-thermal.md).

<a id="bank-conflict"></a>**Bank conflict** — Several lanes of a warp accessing different words in the same shared-memory bank, which serializes the access; for a word stride s with 32 banks, the conflict degree is gcd(s, 32). *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [Shared memory (GPU)](#shared-memory-gpu).

<a id="barkhausen-criterion"></a>**Barkhausen criterion** — The condition for a sustained oscillation in a positive-feedback loop, loop gain exactly 1 with zero phase at the oscillation frequency; practical oscillators start with loop gain above 1 and rely on a nonlinearity to bring it to 1. *First defined in* [12-09](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-09-oscillators.md). *See also:* [Describing function](#describing-function), [Loop gain](#loop-gain).

<a id="barrel-shifter"></a>**Barrel shifter** — A shifter that shifts by any amount in one pass, built from log2 n stages of 2-to-1 multiplexers, stage k shifting by 2^k. *First defined in* [08-09](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md).

<a id="base-transport-factor"></a>**Base transport factor** — The fraction α_T of carriers injected into the base that reach the collector without recombining, 1 − W_B²/2L_B²; essentially 1 in modern thin-base transistors. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="base-rate-effect"></a>**Base-rate effect** — Even an accurate test produces mostly false positives when the condition it detects is rare, because its false-positive rate applies to the large unaffected majority. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="basis"></a>**Basis** — A set of independent vectors that spans a subspace; every vector in the subspace is then a unique combination of the basis vectors. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="bathtub-curve"></a>**Bathtub curve** — A curve shaped like a bathtub, used in two senses: bit error rate against sampling instant across the unit interval, and failure rate against age (infant mortality, flat mid-life, wear-out). *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="bayes-rule"></a>**Bayes' rule** — P(A | B) = P(A) P(B | A)/P(B), which turns the probability of an observation given a cause into the probability of the cause given the observation. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md). *See also:* [Base-rate effect](#base-rate-effect), [Maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection](#maximum-a-posteriori-map-detection).

<a id="beats"></a>**Beats** — The slow swelling and fading of a sum of two sinusoids of nearly equal frequency, or of an undamped system forced near its natural frequency; the envelope varies at half the difference frequency. *First defined in* [02-04](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-04-forced-response-and-resonance.md).

<a id="benchmark"></a>**Benchmark** — A fixed workload with rules for how it is run and reported, used to compare systems; its rules (fixed code, accuracy targets, mandatory baselines) are what make results comparable. *First defined in* [14-15](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-15-roofline-and-benchmarks.md). *See also:* [SPEC CPU](#spec-cpu), [MLPerf](#mlperf).

<a id="bernoulli-equation"></a>**Bernoulli equation** — y' + p(t)y = q(t)yⁿ, made linear by the substitution v = y^(1−n); the logistic equation is the case n = 2. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="bessel-filter"></a>**Bessel filter** — A filter whose poles are chosen for maximally flat group delay, preserving pulse shapes with almost no overshoot, at the cost of a gentle magnitude roll-off. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [Group delay](#group-delay), [Elliptic filter](#elliptic-filter).

<a id="beta-helper"></a>**Beta helper** — A transistor added to a bipolar current mirror to supply the mirror's base currents from the supply, cutting the reference's base-current loss by a factor of about β. *First defined in* [10-08](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-08-current-sources-and-mirrors.md).

<a id="bfloat16"></a>**bfloat16** — A 16-bit floating-point format with 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 fraction bits; it keeps FP32's range (about 3.4×10^38) at about 2.4 decimal digits of precision, and FP32 converts to it by rounding away the low 16 bits. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md). *See also:* [Floating-point number](#floating-point-number), [FP8](#fp8).

<a id="bias"></a>**Bias** — The difference between an estimator's expected value and the true parameter; mean square error equals bias squared plus variance. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="bibo-stability"></a>**BIBO stability** — Bounded-input, bounded-output stability; every bounded input produces a bounded output. An LTI system is BIBO-stable exactly when its impulse response is absolutely summable (integrable); accumulators, integrators and lossless resonators are not. *First defined in* [11-02](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-02-system-properties.md). *See also:* [Stability (of a circuit)](#stability-of-a-circuit).

<a id="bicmos"></a>**BiCMOS** — A process that integrates bipolar (often SiGe heterojunction) transistors with CMOS on one chip, for RF, mmWave and precision analog functions alongside digital logic, at the cost of extra process steps. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="big-o-notation"></a>**Big-O notation** — f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g for large n; it keeps an algorithm's growth rate (constant, log n, n, n log n, n squared) and drops constant factors. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="bilateral-laplace-transform"></a>**Bilateral Laplace transform** — X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^{−st} dt over all t, with s = σ + jω: the Fourier transform of x(t)e^{−σt}; it describes signals and systems for all time and is meaningful only together with its region of convergence. *First defined in* [11-08](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-08-laplace-transform-and-system-functions.md). *See also:* [Laplace transform](#laplace-transform), [Region of convergence (ROC)](#region-of-convergence-roc).

<a id="bilinear-transform"></a>**Bilinear transform** — The s-to-z map s = (2/T)(1 − z^{−1})/(1 + z^{−1}), from the trapezoidal rule: it maps the left half-plane into the unit disk and the whole jω axis onto the unit circle once, so stability is kept and there is no aliasing, at the cost of frequency warping. *First defined in* [11-09](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-09-z-transform.md). *See also:* [Frequency warping](#frequency-warping), [Impulse invariance](#impulse-invariance).

<a id="binary-heap"></a>**Binary heap** — A complete binary tree stored in an array (children of i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2) with every parent no larger than its children; supports a priority queue with O(log n) insertion and removal of the minimum. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="binary-search"></a>**Binary search** — Searching a sorted array by comparing with the middle element and discarding half each step; at most floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons (20 for a million items). *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="binary-search-tree"></a>**Binary search tree** — A tree whose nodes keep smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right, so search, insertion and deletion cost O(height); self-balancing variants (red-black, AVL, B-trees) keep the height O(log n). *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="binary-coded-decimal-bcd"></a>**Binary-coded decimal (BCD)** — Storing each decimal digit in its own 4-bit group (97 is 1001 0111); it wastes 6 of 16 patterns per digit, and binary addition of BCD digits needs a +6 correction when a digit sum exceeds 9. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md).

<a id="binomial-distribution"></a>**Binomial distribution** — The number of successes in n independent trials each succeeding with probability p, with PMF C(n,k) p^k (1 − p)^(n − k). *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="binomial-series"></a>**Binomial series** — (1 + x)^α = 1 + αx + α(α − 1)x²/2! + …, valid for |x| < 1 and any real α; the source of (1 + x)^n ≈ 1 + nx. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="biot-savart-law"></a>**Biot–Savart law** — The field of a current element, dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl × r̂ / r²; integrated, it gives µ₀I/(2πr) for a long wire and µ₀I/(2R) at the center of a loop. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="bipolar-junction-transistor"></a>**Bipolar junction transistor** — A transistor of two back-to-back PN junctions sharing a thin base, in which a forward-biased emitter injects minority carriers that diffuse across the base and are collected by a reverse-biased collector; I_C ≈ I_S e^(V_BE/V_T). *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md). *See also:* [Heterojunction bipolar transistor](#heterojunction-bipolar-transistor).

<a id="biquad"></a>**Biquad** — A second-order filter section with transfer-function denominator s² + (ω0/Q)s + ω0²; low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch and all-pass sections differ only in the numerator, and higher-order filters are cascades of biquads (plus a first-order section for odd order). *First defined in* [07-08](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-08-filters-and-resonance.md).

<a id="bisection-bandwidth"></a>**Bisection bandwidth** — The total bandwidth of the links crossing the narrowest cut that divides a network into two equal halves; for a k × k mesh it is k links in each direction. *First defined in* [14-11](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-11-io-buses-and-interconnect.md). *See also:* [Network-on-chip (NoC)](#network-on-chip-noc).

<a id="bisection-method"></a>**Bisection method** — Root finding by repeatedly halving a bracket that contains a sign change; after n steps the bracket width is (b − a)/2ⁿ, about 3.3 steps per decimal digit, and it cannot fail once a bracket is found. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="bistable-circuit"></a>**Bistable circuit** — A circuit with two stable states and an unstable balance point between them, such as two cross-coupled inverters; the rail states are stable because the loop gain there is below 1, the midpoint unstable because it is above 1. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md). *See also:* [SR latch](#sr-latch).

<a id="bit-error-rate-ber"></a>**Bit error rate (BER)** — The probability, or long-run fraction, that a transmitted bit is received in error; serial-link standards specify targets such as 1e-12. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="bit-field"></a>**Bit field** — A group of adjacent bits inside a register or word that holds one value (a 3-bit mode at bits 6:4); extracted with shift-and-mask and written by clearing the field and OR-ing in the shifted value. *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="bit-mask"></a>**Bit mask** — A bit pattern with 1s at the positions of interest, used with AND to test or keep bits, OR to set them, AND-NOT to clear them and XOR to toggle them. *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="bit-reversed-order"></a>**Bit-reversed order** — The order in which a radix-2 FFT reads its input (DIT) or produces its output (DIF): index n is placed at the position whose log₂N-bit binary representation is n's bits reversed. *First defined in* [16-04](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-04-the-fft.md). *See also:* [Decimation in time](#decimation-in-time).

<a id="bitstream"></a>**Bitstream** — The configuration data that sets every LUT, routing switch and mode bit of an FPGA; SRAM-based FPGAs load it at every power-up, usually from flash. *First defined in* [08-11](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-11-memories-and-programmable-logic.md). *See also:* [Field-programmable gate array (FPGA)](#field-programmable-gate-array-fpga).

<a id="blackmans-impedance-formula"></a>**Blackman's impedance formula** — The impedance at any port of a feedback circuit, Z = Z0(1 + T_sc)/(1 + T_oc), with Z0 the impedance when the controlled source is zero and T_sc, T_oc the return ratios with the port shorted and open. *First defined in* [12-05](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-05-feedback-topologies.md). *See also:* [Return ratio](#return-ratio), [Feedback topology](#feedback-topology).

<a id="blochs-theorem"></a>**Bloch's theorem** — In a periodic potential the electron eigenstates are plane waves times a function with the lattice period, ψ_k(x) = e^(ikx) u_k(x); such waves travel through a perfect crystal without scattering. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="block-diagram"></a>**Block diagram** — A drawing of a system as blocks (transfer functions) joined by signal arrows, summing junctions and pickoff points; series blocks multiply, parallel blocks add, and a feedback loop reduces to G/(1 + GH). *First defined in* [15-02](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-02-transfer-functions-and-block-diagrams.md). *See also:* [Signal-flow graph](#signal-flow-graph), [Loop gain](#loop-gain).

<a id="block-floating-point"></a>**Block floating point** — Storing a block of numbers with one shared scale (exponent) and a few bits per element, so each block gets its own range; the OCP MX formats share one 8-bit power-of-two scale per 32 elements. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md). *See also:* [FP8](#fp8), [Fixed-point arithmetic](#fixed-point-arithmetic).

<a id="block-processing"></a>**Block processing** — Processing samples in groups of L rather than one at a time, which lowers per-sample overhead on a processor but adds about 2L samples of latency with double buffering (one block filling while the previous one is processed and emitted). *First defined in* [16-01](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-01-discrete-time-systems-review.md).

<a id="block-ram"></a>**Block RAM** — A hard, synchronous memory block (typically a few to tens of kbit, often dual-ported) embedded in an FPGA's fabric; reads take one clock cycle. *First defined in* [08-11](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-11-memories-and-programmable-logic.md). *See also:* [Field-programmable gate array (FPGA)](#field-programmable-gate-array-fpga).

<a id="blocking-assignment"></a>**Blocking assignment** — The Verilog assignment a = b inside a procedural block, which updates a immediately so that later statements see the new value; correct for combinational logic, a source of races in clocked blocks. *First defined in* [08-05](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-05-verilog-and-testbenches.md). *See also:* [Non-blocking assignment](#non-blocking-assignment), [Race condition](#race-condition).

<a id="bode-plot"></a>**Bode plot** — A pair of plots of a frequency response, magnitude in dB and phase in degrees, against frequency on a logarithmic axis; each real pole or zero contributes a straight-line asymptote of ∓20 dB/decade from its corner, so responses can be sketched by adding factors. *First defined in* [07-07](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-07-frequency-response-and-bode-plots.md). *See also:* [Corner frequency](#corner-frequency), [Asymptote](#asymptote), [Frequency response](#frequency-response).

<a id="bodes-sensitivity-integral"></a>**Bode's sensitivity integral** — For a stable closed loop whose loop gain has relative degree of at least 2, the integral of ln|S(jω)| over all positive frequencies equals π times the sum of the real parts of the open-loop right-half-plane poles (zero for a stable plant), so sensitivity reduced in one band rises in another (the waterbed effect). *First defined in* [15-07](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-07-frequency-domain-design.md). *See also:* [Sensitivity function](#sensitivity-function), [Sensitivity peak](#sensitivity-peak).

<a id="bode-fano-limit"></a>**Bode–Fano limit** — The bound on matching a reactive load with any lossless network; for a parallel RC load, the integral of ln(1/|Γ|) over angular frequency cannot exceed π/(RC), so a better match is possible only over a narrower band. *First defined in* [13-09](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-09-smith-chart-and-matching.md). *See also:* [Impedance matching](#impedance-matching).

<a id="body-effect"></a>**Body effect** — The rise of a MOSFET's threshold with source-to-body reverse bias, V_TH = V_TH0 + γ(√(2φ_B + V_SB) − √(2φ_B)); the body acts as a weak second gate. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="body-transconductance"></a>**Body transconductance** — g_mb = ∂i_D/∂v_BS, the MOSFET's response to its body voltage through the body effect; g_mb = χg_m with χ = γ/(2√(2φ_F + V_SB)), typically 0.1–0.3. *First defined in* [10-04](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-04-small-signal-models.md). *See also:* [Body effect](#body-effect).

<a id="body-effect-parameter"></a>**Body-effect parameter** — The coefficient γ = √(2qN_Aε_s)/C_ox (V^1/2) that sets how strongly source-to-body bias shifts a MOSFET's threshold. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="boltzmann-approximation"></a>**Boltzmann approximation** — Replacing the Fermi–Dirac occupation by e^(−(E − E_F)/kT), valid to within 5% for states more than 3kT above E_F; it gives n = N_C e^(−(E_C − E_F)/kT) for non-degenerate semiconductors. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md). *See also:* [Degenerate semiconductor](#degenerate-semiconductor).

<a id="boolean-algebra"></a>**Boolean algebra** — The algebra of two values, 0 and 1, with AND, OR and NOT, defined by axioms such as Huntington's (identity, commutativity, both distributive laws, complement); it describes logic circuits exactly, and has no subtraction or division, so nothing may be cancelled. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md). *See also:* [Duality principle](#duality-principle), [De Morgan's theorem](#de-morgans-theorem).

<a id="boolean-mask"></a>**Boolean mask** — An array of True/False values from an elementwise comparison, used to select elements (x[mask]) or count them (mask.sum()); combine masks with &, | and ~. *First defined in* [05-02](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-02-numpy-and-vectorization.md).

<a id="booth-recoding"></a>**Booth recoding** — Rewriting a two's-complement multiplier in signed digits (radix 4 uses -2 to +2) from overlapping bit triplets, which halves the number of partial products. *First defined in* [08-09](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md). *See also:* [Partial product](#partial-product).

<a id="bootstrapping"></a>**Bootstrapping** — Driving the far end of an element with a copy of the voltage at its near end, so that little voltage appears across it and its effective impedance rises by 1/(1 − A_v); used to raise a follower's input resistance or to cancel cable capacitance with a driven guard. *First defined in* [12-05](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-05-feedback-topologies.md). *See also:* [Blackman's impedance formula](#blackmans-impedance-formula).

<a id="bounce-diagram"></a>**Bounce diagram** — (Lattice diagram.) A plot of position against time that tracks each wave launched on a transmission line and its reflections at both ends; the voltage at a point is the sum of all the waves that have passed it. *First defined in* [13-07](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-07-transmission-lines-time-domain.md). *See also:* [Reflection coefficient](#reflection-coefficient).

<a id="boundary-condition"></a>**Boundary condition** — A rule linking fields on the two sides of an interface, derived from the integral laws on vanishing loops and pillboxes; in electrostatics the tangential E is continuous and the normal D jumps by the surface charge, and at a conductor E is normal with D_n equal to the surface charge. *First defined in* [13-02](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-02-electrostatics-boundary-value-problems.md). *See also:* [Gauss's law](#gausss-law).

<a id="boundary-value-analysis"></a>**Boundary-value analysis** — Black-box test design that places tests just below, at and just above each boundary of the input ranges, where off-by-one errors (< versus <=) live. *First defined in* [05-09](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-09-software-engineering-practices.md).

<a id="branch"></a>**Branch** — A single element, or a path through one element, connecting two nodes of a circuit. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="branch-divergence"></a>**Branch divergence** — Threads of one warp taking different paths at a branch, which forces the warp to execute each path in turn with the other lanes masked off and lowers SIMD efficiency. *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [Warp](#warp).

<a id="branch-history-table-bht"></a>**Branch history table (BHT)** — An untagged table of 1-bit flags or 2-bit counters, indexed by low bits of the branch address, that records how branches behaved recently and predicts their direction. *First defined in* [14-07](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md).

<a id="branch-penalty"></a>**Branch penalty** — The cycles lost each time a branch or jump redirects fetch away from the predicted path; two cycles in the five-stage pipeline that resolves branches in EX. *First defined in* [14-06](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-06-pipelining-and-hazards.md).

<a id="branch-prediction"></a>**Branch prediction** — Guessing a branch's direction and target when it is fetched, so that the pipeline keeps fetching down the predicted path; a wrong guess costs a flush of the work done since. *First defined in* [14-07](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md). *See also:* [Speculative execution](#speculative-execution).

<a id="branch-target-buffer-btb"></a>**Branch target buffer (BTB)** — A tagged cache, looked up with the fetch address, that identifies control-transfer instructions before decode and supplies their last target so that fetch can redirect in the next cycle. *First defined in* [14-07](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md).

<a id="breakaway-point"></a>**Breakaway point** — A point on the real axis where two branches of a root locus meet and leave the axis (or arrive and join it, a break-in point); it satisfies N(s)D′(s) − D(s)N′(s) = 0 with K > 0. *First defined in* [15-06](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-06-root-locus.md). *See also:* [Root locus](#root-locus).

<a id="brents-method"></a>**Brent's method** — A bracketing root-finder (SciPy's brentq) that combines bisection's guaranteed convergence with faster secant and inverse-quadratic steps; it never leaves the bracket and typically needs a few times fewer evaluations than bisection. *First defined in* [05-03](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-03-scipy-sympy-matplotlib.md). *See also:* [Root-finding](#root-finding), [Bisection method](#bisection-method).

<a id="brent-kung-adder"></a>**Brent–Kung adder** — A parallel-prefix adder with an up-sweep tree and a down-sweep, using about 2n operators and regular wiring at the cost of 2 log2 n - 1 levels. *First defined in* [08-09](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md). *See also:* [Parallel-prefix adder](#parallel-prefix-adder), [Kogge–Stone adder](#kogge-stone-adder).

<a id="brewster-angle"></a>**Brewster angle** — The angle of incidence, tan θB = n₂/n₁ for nonmagnetic media, at which a wave polarized in the plane of incidence (TM) is fully transmitted; 56.3° from air into glass. Reflected light near it is mostly TE polarized. *First defined in* [13-06](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-06-reflection-and-transmission.md). *See also:* [Fresnel equations](#fresnel-equations).

<a id="bridge-rectifier"></a>**Bridge rectifier** — Four diodes arranged so that either polarity of a single winding drives the load the same way; current flows through two diodes in series, and each blocks about the winding's peak voltage. *First defined in* [10-01](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-01-diodes-and-diode-circuits.md).

<a id="bridge-tied-load"></a>**Bridge-tied load** — Driving a load between two amplifier outputs in antiphase instead of from one output to ground, which doubles the voltage swing and quadruples the power from a single supply; the usual arrangement in class D audio amplifiers. *First defined in* [12-07](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-07-output-stages.md). *See also:* [Class-D amplifier](#class-d-amplifier).

<a id="brillouin-zone"></a>**Brillouin zone** — The range of crystal wavevectors that describes every distinct Bloch state once, −π/d < k ≤ π/d in one dimension; band diagrams are plotted across it, and its boundaries are where Bragg reflection opens gaps. *First defined in* [09-01](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-01-crystals-and-energy-bands.md). *See also:* [Bloch's theorem](#blochs-theorem).

<a id="broadcasting"></a>**Broadcasting** — NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes; trailing axes must match or be 1, and size-1 axes are stretched without copying, so a column and a row combine into a full table. *First defined in* [05-02](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-02-numpy-and-vectorization.md).

<a id="bubble"></a>**Bubble** — An empty slot (a no-op) inserted into a pipeline stage by a stall or a flush; it moves through the pipeline doing nothing. *First defined in* [14-06](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-06-pipelining-and-hazards.md).

<a id="bubble-pushing"></a>**Bubble pushing** — Redrawing a gate by De Morgan's theorem (an AND with an output bubble equals an OR with input bubbles) so that inversion bubbles meet in pairs and cancel, making a NAND or NOR circuit easy to read. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md).

<a id="buffer-amplifier"></a>**Buffer amplifier** — A stage with a gain near 1 used to transform impedance, presenting a high input resistance to its source and a low output resistance to its load. *First defined in* [10-05](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-05-amplifier-fundamentals.md).

<a id="buffer-overflow"></a>**Buffer overflow** — Reading or writing past the end (or before the start) of an array or buffer, corrupting or leaking neighboring memory; a leading cause of security vulnerabilities in C and C++. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="built-in-field"></a>**Built-in field** — The electric field present in equilibrium wherever doping varies, of just the size, (kT/q)(1/N)(dN/dx), needed for drift to cancel diffusion; graded doping uses it to speed minority carriers across bipolar bases. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md).

<a id="built-in-potential"></a>**Built-in potential** — The electrostatic potential difference across a PN junction in equilibrium, V_bi = (kT/q) ln(N_A N_D/n_i²), equal to the difference of the two sides' Fermi levels before contact; about 0.6–0.9 V in silicon and not measurable with a voltmeter. *First defined in* [09-05](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-05-pn-junction-electrostatics.md).

<a id="bulk-charge-factor"></a>**Bulk-charge factor** — The factor m = 1 + C_dep/C_ox = 1 + 3T_ox/W_dmax (typically about 1.2) by which raising the channel potential also deepens the depletion charge; it lowers V_Dsat and I_Dsat and sets the subthreshold swing m × 60 mV/decade. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="burden-voltage"></a>**Burden voltage** — The voltage an ammeter drops across its internal resistance (shunt, fuse, leads) while measuring; it reduces the circuit's current by about R_A/R_th, the ammeter's counterpart of a voltmeter's loading error. *First defined in* [06-11](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-11-practical-dc-circuits-and-measurement.md). *See also:* [Loading effect](#loading-effect), [Current-sense shunt](#current-sense-shunt).

<a id="butterfly"></a>**Butterfly** — The FFT's basic computation, X[k] = G[k] + W·H[k] and X[k + N/2] = G[k] − W·H[k]: one complex multiplication by a twiddle factor, one addition and one subtraction producing two outputs. *First defined in* [16-04](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-04-the-fft.md). *See also:* [Twiddle factor](#twiddle-factor), [Fast Fourier transform (FFT)](#fast-fourier-transform-fft).

<a id="butterworth-response"></a>**Butterworth response** — The maximally flat filter response; a second-order Butterworth section has ζ = 0.707 (Q = 0.707), no peak, and −3.01 dB at its natural frequency. *First defined in* [02-04](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-04-forced-response-and-resonance.md).

<a id="bypass-capacitor"></a>**Bypass capacitor** — A capacitor placed across a bias element (typically an emitter or source resistor) so that it carries DC bias current but is a short circuit at signal frequencies, restoring the stage's full gain. *First defined in* [10-07](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-07-bjt-single-stage-amplifiers.md).

<a id="letter-c"></a>

## C

<a id="c-string"></a>**C string** — An array of char terminated by a zero byte; it needs strlen + 1 bytes of storage, and functions find its end by scanning for the zero, so a missing terminator or a too-small buffer causes overflows. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="cache-block"></a>**Cache block** — The unit of data a cache stores and moves, also called a line, typically 32 to 128 bytes; a miss brings in the whole block containing the requested address. *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md). *See also:* [Locality](#locality), [Tag (cache)](#tag-cache).

<a id="cache-coherence"></a>**Cache coherence** — The guarantee that all cores see a single, consistent sequence of values for each memory location despite private caches, maintained by a protocol enforcing the single-writer/multiple-reader and data-value invariants. *First defined in* [14-12](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-12-multicore-coherence-consistency.md). *See also:* [MESI protocol](#mesi-protocol), [Memory consistency model](#memory-consistency-model).

<a id="callee-saved-register"></a>**Callee-saved register** — A register whose value must survive a call (RISC-V s0–s11 and sp); a function that uses one must save it on entry and restore it before returning. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md). *See also:* [Caller-saved register](#caller-saved-register).

<a id="caller-saved-register"></a>**Caller-saved register** — A register a called function may overwrite freely (RISC-V t0–t6, a0–a7, ra); a caller that needs its value after a call must save it first. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md). *See also:* [Callee-saved register](#callee-saved-register).

<a id="calling-convention"></a>**Calling convention** — The part of an ABI that fixes how functions call each other — which registers carry arguments and return values, which must be preserved across calls, and how the stack is used. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md). *See also:* [Caller-saved register](#caller-saved-register), [Callee-saved register](#callee-saved-register).

<a id="capacitance"></a>**Capacitance** — The charge a pair of conductors holds per volt of potential difference, C = Q/V (farads); it depends only on geometry and the insulator, e.g. ε A/d for parallel plates and 2πεℓ/ln(b/a) for a coax. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="capacitance-per-unit-length"></a>**Capacitance per unit length** — The charge per metre on a long two-conductor structure divided by the voltage between the conductors, C' in F/m, such as 2 pi epsilon/ln(b/a) for a coaxial line; with the inductance per length it sets a transmission line's impedance and delay. *First defined in* [13-02](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-02-electrostatics-boundary-value-problems.md). *See also:* [Characteristic impedance](#characteristic-impedance).

<a id="capacitive-equivalent-thickness"></a>**Capacitive equivalent thickness** — The SiO₂-equivalent thickness of a whole gate stack in inversion (interfacial layer, high-k film, dipole layers and inversion layer), the quantity that sets drive current; the IRDS 2024 roadmap gives 1.0 nm for 2024–2025 and 0.9 nm from 2027. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md). *See also:* [Equivalent oxide thickness (EOT)](#equivalent-oxide-thickness-eot).

<a id="capacitive-sensing"></a>**Capacitive sensing** — Detecting a finger or object by the change it makes in an electrode's capacitance; self-capacitance sensing sees a finger add C_F to the pad's parasitic C_P, mutual-capacitance sensing sees the transmit-receive coupling fall. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="capture-cross-section"></a>**Capture cross section** — The effective target area σ (cm²) a trap presents to a passing carrier; the capture time is 1/(σ v_th N_t). Gold in silicon captures holes with σ_p ≈ 9×10⁻¹⁵ cm². *First defined in* [09-04](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-04-generation-recombination-continuity.md).

<a id="carry-chain"></a>**Carry chain** — Dedicated, hard-wired carry logic between neighboring FPGA logic cells that makes adders and counters much faster than the same logic built from lookup tables and general routing. *First defined in* [08-12](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-12-fpga-implementation-flow.md).

<a id="carry-lookahead-adder"></a>**Carry-lookahead adder** — An adder that computes carries directly from the bits' generate and propagate signals in two-level logic, usually in hierarchical groups of about 4 bits, instead of rippling them bit by bit. *First defined in* [08-09](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md). *See also:* [Generate and propagate](#generate-and-propagate), [Parallel-prefix adder](#parallel-prefix-adder).

<a id="carry-save-adder"></a>**Carry-save adder** — A row of independent full adders that reduces three numbers to two (a sum word and a carry word) in one full-adder delay, with no carry propagation; the building block of multiplier trees. *First defined in* [08-09](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md). *See also:* [Dadda tree](#dadda-tree).

<a id="carry-select-adder"></a>**Carry-select adder** — An adder that computes upper sum bits for both possible carry-ins in parallel and selects the right result with multiplexers once the real carry arrives, trading duplicated hardware for delay. *First defined in* [08-09](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md).

<a id="cascode"></a>**Cascode** — A common-source transistor followed by a common-gate transistor in series; the upper device multiplies the output resistance by about g_mr_o, raising the gain toward (g_mr_o)² at the cost of one more overdrive of headroom. *First defined in* [10-06](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-06-mos-single-stage-amplifiers.md). *See also:* [Intrinsic gain](#intrinsic-gain), [Source degeneration](#source-degeneration).

<a id="cascode-current-mirror"></a>**Cascode current mirror** — A current mirror with a second stacked transistor on each side, which holds the output transistor's drain at the reference transistor's drain voltage and raises the output resistance to about g_mr_o², at the cost of extra compliance voltage. *First defined in* [10-08](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-08-current-sources-and-mirrors.md). *See also:* [Cascode](#cascode), [Current mirror](#current-mirror).

<a id="catastrophic-cancellation"></a>**Catastrophic cancellation** — The loss of significant digits when subtracting two nearly equal floating-point numbers; avoided by algebraic rearrangement or series expansion. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="cauchy-distribution"></a>**Cauchy distribution** — The density 1/(π(1 + x²)), the ratio of two independent standard Gaussians; its tails are so heavy that it has no mean or variance, so the CLT does not apply and an average of Cauchy samples is still Cauchy. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="cauer-network"></a>**Cauer network** — An RC ladder model whose capacitors connect to a reference at each node, mirroring physical layers in series; unlike a Foster network it can be cascaded with models of further stages. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="causal-system"></a>**Causal system** — A system whose output at any time depends only on present and past input values; every real-time system is causal, and a linear system is causal exactly when an input that starts at t₁ produces no output before t₁ (initial rest). *First defined in* [11-02](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-02-system-properties.md). *See also:* [Latency](#latency).

<a id="cavity-resonator"></a>**Cavity resonator** — A closed conducting box (or dielectric body) that stores electromagnetic energy in standing-wave modes at discrete resonant frequencies, with quality factors of thousands from wall loss; the microwave counterpart of an LC tank. *First defined in* [13-10](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-10-waveguides-and-resonators.md). *See also:* [Quality factor](#quality-factor).

<a id="cccs"></a>**CCCS** — Current-controlled current source, i = β i_x, with dimensionless current gain β; SPICE element F. The core of a bipolar transistor's small-signal model and of a current mirror. *First defined in* [06-06](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-06-dependent-sources.md). *See also:* [Dependent source](#dependent-source).

<a id="ccdf"></a>**CCDF** — Complementary cumulative distribution function, P(X > x) = 1 − F(x); for signals, the fraction of time the instantaneous power exceeds each level above average. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="ccvs"></a>**CCVS** — Current-controlled voltage source, v = r i_x, with transresistance r in ohms; SPICE element H, controlled by the current through a named voltage source. *First defined in* [06-06](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-06-dependent-sources.md). *See also:* [Dependent source](#dependent-source).

<a id="cell-height"></a>**Cell height** — The height of a standard logic cell, set by the number of horizontal wiring tracks times the metal pitch; shorter cells raise logic density. *First defined in* [09-11](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-11-cmos-and-scaling.md).

<a id="central-difference"></a>**Central difference** — The numerical derivative (f(x + h) − f(x − h))/(2h), whose truncation error falls as h² rather than h. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="central-limit-theorem"></a>**Central limit theorem** — The standardized sum of many independent terms with finite variance tends to a Gaussian, whatever their distribution; accurate near the center, unreliable far into the tails. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="centroid"></a>**Centroid** — The balance point of a region or distribution, its first moment divided by its area (or total weight); the mean of a density and the Elmore delay are centroids. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md). *See also:* [Elmore delay](#elmore-delay).

<a id="chain-rule"></a>**Chain rule** — (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x))·g'(x); rates of nested quantities multiply, as in d/dt sin(ωt) = ω cos(ωt). *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="change-of-variables"></a>**Change of variables** — The rule f_Y(y) = Σ f_X(xᵢ)/|g′(xᵢ)| over the points xᵢ with g(xᵢ) = y, giving the density of Y = g(X); probability is conserved as the axis is stretched or compressed. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="channel-length-modulation"></a>**Channel-length modulation** — The shortening of a saturated MOSFET's effective channel as the pinch-off point moves toward the source with rising V_DS, which gives finite output resistance, often written I_D ∝ (1 + λV_DS). *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="characteristic-equation"></a>**Characteristic equation** — The polynomial equation obtained by substituting y = e^{st} into a linear constant-coefficient ODE, such as s² + 2αs + ω₀² = 0; its roots set the decay rates and oscillation frequencies of every natural response. *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="characteristic-impedance"></a>**Characteristic impedance** — Z0, the ratio of voltage to current for a single wave traveling along a transmission line (typically 50 Ω for coaxial cable and RF systems). For a lumped LC tank the analogous quantity is √(L/C), which sets the voltage swing per ampere of current step and the damping needed. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="characteristic-length"></a>**Characteristic length** — The length l_d ∝ (T_oxe W_dep X_j)^(1/3) over which the drain's electrostatic influence on the channel barrier decays; acceptable DIBL requires a gate length several times l_d, so oxide, depletion depth and junction depth must shrink with L. *First defined in* [09-10](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-10-short-channel-effects-and-leakage.md).

<a id="characteristic-polynomial"></a>**Characteristic polynomial** — det(A − λI), a degree-n polynomial in λ whose roots are the eigenvalues; for 2×2 it is λ² − (trace)λ + det. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md). *See also:* [Characteristic equation](#characteristic-equation).

<a id="charge-density"></a>**Charge density** — Charge per unit length (λ, C/m), area (σ, C/m²) or volume (ρ, C/m³), used to integrate the fields of continuous distributions. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="charge-pump-pll"></a>**Charge pump (PLL)** — The circuit after a PLL's phase–frequency detector that sources or sinks a current I_cp for the time between reference and divided edges; averaged over a reference period it delivers I_cp·Δθ/(2π), a gain of I_cp/(2π) A/rad into the loop filter. *First defined in* [15-12](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-12-control-applications-pll-regulators-thermal.md). *See also:* [Phase-locked loop (PLL)](#phase-locked-loop-pll).

<a id="charge-relaxation-time"></a>**Charge relaxation time** — The time constant τ = ε/σ with which free charge placed inside a conducting material decays away to its surface; about 10⁻¹⁹ s for copper and 0.18 ns for seawater. A material conducts at frequencies well below 1/(2πτ) and behaves as a dielectric well above it. *First defined in* [13-04](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-04-maxwells-equations.md). *See also:* [Continuity equation](#continuity-equation).

<a id="charge-sharing"></a>**Charge sharing** — Connecting capacitors at different voltages so their charge redistributes to a common voltage; charge is conserved but energy is lost (half, for equal capacitors), and it is how a DRAM cell is read onto its bit line. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="charge-control-model"></a>**Charge-control model** — Describing a device by its stored charge Q, with i = dQ/dt + Q/τ for a diode; exact for the total charge but approximate for switching events that depend on the charge at the junction edge. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="charge-coupled-device"></a>**Charge-coupled device** — An image sensor made of a dense array of MOS capacitors held in deep depletion, which collect photo-generated electrons in proportion to light and shift the charge packets to an output amplifier by sequencing the gate voltages. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="charged-device-model-cdm"></a>**Charged-device model (CDM)** — The component ESD test of JS-002, modeling a charged device discharging quickly to ground through one pin; the industry-recommended target is 250 V, trending lower for high-speed parts. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="chebyshevs-inequality"></a>**Chebyshev's inequality** — P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k² for any distribution with finite variance; a guarantee that is loose for any particular distribution (11.1% at 3σ against 0.27% for a Gaussian). *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="chi-square-distribution"></a>**Chi-square distribution** — The distribution of a sum of squared independent standard normals; with one degree of freedom it describes the instantaneous power of Gaussian noise, whose standard deviation is √2 times its mean. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="chiplet"></a>**Chiplet** — A die designed to be combined with other dies inside one package, so that a system can exceed the reticle limit or mix processes; chiplets communicate over die-to-die links. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="chopper-stabilization"></a>**Chopper stabilization** — Modulating a low-frequency signal above an amplifier's 1/f corner, amplifying it there and demodulating it, which removes offset and 1/f noise at the cost of switching artifacts; the basis of zero-drift amplifiers. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="chromatic-dispersion"></a>**Chromatic dispersion** — The spreading of a light pulse because different wavelengths travel at different speeds; about 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm and near zero at 1310 nm in standard single-mode fiber. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="circular-convolution"></a>**Circular convolution** — The N-point convolution of two sequences with indices taken modulo N, whose DFT is the product of the DFTs; it equals linear convolution when both are zero-padded to N ≥ L + M − 1. *First defined in* [16-03](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-03-the-dft.md). *See also:* [Circular shift](#circular-shift), [Overlap-add](#overlap-add), [Overlap-save](#overlap-save).
