<a id="direct-band-gap"></a>**Direct band gap** — A band gap whose conduction-band minimum lies at the same crystal momentum as the valence-band maximum (GaAs, GaN), so electrons and holes recombine by emitting light efficiently; indirect gaps (Si, Ge, SiC) need a phonon. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="direct-form-i-and-ii"></a>**Direct form I and II** — Block-diagram realizations of a difference equation; direct form I uses separate delay lines for input and output (2N delays for order N), direct form II runs the recursive part first so one line serves both (N delays, canonical); transposed direct form II rearranges it for better floating-point behavior. *First defined in* [11-04](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-04-lti-systems-and-differential-equations.md). *See also:* [Biquad](#biquad).

<a id="direct-memory-access-dma"></a>**Direct memory access (DMA)** — Data transfer between a device and memory performed by a DMA engine acting as a bus manager, following descriptors set up by software and interrupting on completion, so the CPU need not move the data itself. *First defined in* [14-11](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-11-io-buses-and-interconnect.md). *See also:* [Interrupt](#interrupt).

<a id="direct-time-of-flight"></a>**Direct time-of-flight** — Ranging by timing the round trip of a light pulse to a target, d = ct/2 (dToF); timing jitter Δt sets the depth resolution cΔt/2. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="direct-mapped-cache"></a>**Direct-mapped cache** — A cache in which each memory block can be placed in exactly one line, chosen by the index bits of its address; simple and fast but prone to conflict misses. *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md). *See also:* [Set-associative cache](#set-associative-cache).

<a id="direction-field"></a>**Direction field** — A plot of short segments with slope f(t, y) at a grid of points for y' = f(t, y); solutions run tangent to the segments, so the field shows their behavior before any algebra. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="directional-derivative"></a>**Directional derivative** — The rate of change of f along a unit vector u, D_u f = ∇f · u. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="directivity"></a>**Directivity** — The ratio of an antenna's maximum radiation intensity to the average over all directions, D = 4πU_max/P_rad; 1.5 for a Hertzian dipole, 1.64 (2.15 dBi) for a half-wave dipole. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Antenna gain](#antenna-gain), [Radiation pattern](#radiation-pattern).

<a id="directory-protocol"></a>**Directory protocol** — Cache coherence in which a directory at each block's home node records which caches hold the block, so requests and invalidations go only to those caches; scales to many cores at the cost of directory storage and extra hops. *First defined in* [14-12](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-12-multicore-coherence-consistency.md). *See also:* [Snooping](#snooping).

<a id="dirichlet-kernel"></a>**Dirichlet kernel** — The DTFT of a length-N rectangular sequence, e^{−jω(N−1)/2} sin(Nω/2)/sin(ω/2): a main lobe of null-to-null width 4π/N with sidelobes about 13 dB down; it is what truncation convolves every spectrum with. *First defined in* [11-07](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-07-discrete-time-fourier-transform.md). *See also:* [Window function](#window-function).

<a id="discount-factor"></a>**Discount factor** — D(t) = exp(−∫ r dt), the present value of one unit due at time t; it is exactly the integrating factor of the balance equation B' − r(t)B = deposits. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Integrating factor](#integrating-factor).

<a id="discrete-fourier-transform-dft"></a>**Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)** — X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} x[n] e^{−j2πkn/N}: N equally spaced samples of the DTFT of a length-N sequence, computed in N log N operations by the FFT. *First defined in* [11-07](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-07-discrete-time-fourier-transform.md). *See also:* [Discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT)](#discrete-time-fourier-transform-dtft), [Zero-padding](#zero-padding).

<a id="discrete-time-fourier-transform-dtft"></a>**Discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT)** — X(e^{jω}) = Σ x[n] e^{−jωn}, with inverse x[n] = (1/2π)∫ over one period of X(e^{jω}) e^{jωn} dω: the spectrum of a sequence, a continuous function of ω that is periodic with period 2π. *First defined in* [11-07](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-07-discrete-time-fourier-transform.md). *See also:* [Fourier transform](#fourier-transform), [Discrete-time frequency](#discrete-time-frequency).

<a id="discrete-time-frequency"></a>**Discrete-time frequency** — The frequency ω of a sequence e^{jωn} or cos(ωn), in rad/sample; it is defined only modulo 2π, so ω and ω + 2π give the same sequence and the fastest oscillation is at ω = π. Sampling a tone of f hertz at f_s gives ω = 2πf/f_s. *First defined in* [11-01](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-01-signals-classification-and-operations.md).

<a id="discrete-time-signal"></a>**Discrete-time signal** — A sequence x[n] defined only at integer indices n, often the samples x(nT_s) of a continuous-time signal; it is undefined, not zero, between samples. *First defined in* [11-01](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-01-signals-classification-and-operations.md). *See also:* [Continuous-time signal](#continuous-time-signal), [Sampling rate](#sampling-rate).

<a id="displacement-current"></a>**Displacement current** — The term ε₀ dΦ_E/dt that Maxwell added to Ampère's law; a changing electric field makes a magnetic field as a current does, so a charging capacitor's gap carries a displacement current equal to its lead current. *First defined in* [04-08](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-08-maxwell-preview.md).

<a id="dissipation-factor"></a>**Dissipation factor** — D = tan δ = R/|X| = 1/Q, the ratio of a component's loss to its reactance at a stated frequency; for a capacitor with series resistance, D = ωC·ESR. Capacitor datasheets quote it at a test frequency such as 120 Hz or 1 kHz. *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="distortionless-line"></a>**Distortionless line** — A transmission line satisfying Heaviside's condition R′/L′ = G′/C′, for which the attenuation and velocity are independent of frequency and Z₀ is real, so pulses arrive attenuated but undistorted. *First defined in* [13-08](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-08-transmission-lines-sinusoidal-steady-state.md). *See also:* [Propagation constant](#propagation-constant), [Telegrapher's equations](#telegraphers-equations).

<a id="distortionless-transmission"></a>**Distortionless transmission** — Passing a signal with only a gain and a delay, y = Kx(t − t₀), which requires a constant magnitude response and a phase that is linear in frequency (constant group delay). *First defined in* [11-06](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-06-continuous-time-fourier-transform.md). *See also:* [Group delay](#group-delay).

<a id="distributed-rc-line"></a>**Distributed RC line** — A wire whose resistance and capacitance are spread along its length; driven by a step, its far end reaches 50% at about 0.38 RC, so delay grows as length squared. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="disturbance-rejection"></a>**Disturbance rejection** — A feedback loop's ability to keep an unwanted input (a load, a supply change, an ambient change) from reaching the output; an output disturbance is multiplied by S = 1/(1 + L), so rejection is good only where the loop gain is large. *First defined in* [15-04](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-04-feedback-and-steady-state-error.md). *See also:* [Sensitivity function](#sensitivity-function).

<a id="dither"></a>**Dither** — A small random signal added before a quantizer so that the quantization error stops tracking the signal. Triangular-PDF dither two steps wide makes the mean and power of the total error independent of the input, at the cost of tripling the error power. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="divergence"></a>**Divergence** — ∇ · F, the net outflow of a vector field per unit volume at a point; a source density. Gauss's law states ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Flux](#flux).

<a id="divergence-theorem"></a>**Divergence theorem** — The total outward flux of a field through a closed surface equals the integral of its divergence over the enclosed volume; it turns local source density into a global balance. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Divergence](#divergence), [Flux](#flux).

<a id="domain-and-range"></a>**Domain and range** — The domain is the set of allowed inputs of a function; the range is the set of outputs it can produce. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="domain-specific-accelerator"></a>**Domain-specific accelerator** — A processor specialized for one class of workloads, such as neural networks, trading generality for much higher throughput and efficiency through dedicated datapaths, local memories and narrow number formats. *First defined in* [14-14](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-14-ai-accelerators.md). *See also:* [Systolic array](#systolic-array).

<a id="dominant-mode"></a>**Dominant mode** — The mode with the lowest cutoff frequency in a waveguide, TE₁₀ in a rectangular guide (f_c = c/2a); operating between its cutoff and the next mode's keeps the guide single-mode. *First defined in* [13-10](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-10-waveguides-and-resonators.md). *See also:* [Waveguide mode](#waveguide-mode).

<a id="dominant-poles"></a>**Dominant poles** — The poles closest to the imaginary axis, whose slowly decaying modes shape most of a response; a pair dominates when the other poles are several times (commonly more than five times) farther to the left. *First defined in* [15-03](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-03-time-response.md). *See also:* [Dominant-pole approximation](#dominant-pole-approximation).

<a id="dominant-pole-approximation"></a>**Dominant-pole approximation** — For a transfer function whose denominator is 1 + b_1s + b_2s² + …, with one pole far below the others, the low pole is about 1/b_1 and the next about b_1/b_2; it errs low when the poles are less than about a decade apart. *First defined in* [12-03](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-03-frequency-response-miller-poles-zeros.md). *See also:* [Gain-bandwidth product](#gain-bandwidth-product), [Miller effect](#miller-effect).

<a id="dominant-pole-compensation"></a>**Dominant-pole compensation** — Stabilizing a multi-pole feedback amplifier by making one pole so low that the loop gain falls to one before the other poles add much phase lag; lowering an existing pole costs less bandwidth than adding a new one. *First defined in* [12-06](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-06-stability-and-compensation.md). *See also:* [Miller compensation](#miller-compensation), [Phase margin](#phase-margin).

<a id="dont-care-condition"></a>**Don't-care condition** — An input combination whose output does not matter (because it never occurs or is ignored), marked X; it may be treated as 1 or 0 to simplify logic, but the built circuit then has a definite, unrequested output there. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md).

<a id="donor"></a>**Donor** — An impurity with one more valence electron than the atom it replaces (P, As or Sb in silicon), whose extra electron is bound by only tens of meV and is freed into the conduction band at room temperature, making the material n-type. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md). *See also:* [Acceptor](#acceptor), [Ionization energy](#ionization-energy).

<a id="dot-convention"></a>**Dot convention** — Schematic marks on one terminal of each coupled coil; a current entering one coil's dot induces a voltage positive at the other coil's dot, so the mutual term is +M di/dt when both currents enter (or leave) their dots and −M di/dt otherwise. *First defined in* [07-09](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-09-mutual-inductance-and-transformers.md). *See also:* [Mutual inductance](#mutual-inductance).

<a id="dot-product"></a>**Dot product** — a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b|cos θ; it measures how far two vectors point the same way and is zero for perpendicular vectors. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="double-integral"></a>**Double integral** — The integral of a function over a two-dimensional region, ∬ f dA; it sums a density (power per area, charge per area) over the region to give a total. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md).

<a id="drain-induced-barrier-lowering"></a>**Drain-induced barrier lowering** — The lowering of the source–channel barrier, and so of the threshold voltage, by the drain voltage in a short-channel MOSFET (DIBL), quoted in mV/V; it raises off-current exponentially. *First defined in* [09-10](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-10-short-channel-effects-and-leakage.md). *See also:* [Threshold roll-off](#threshold-roll-off), [Characteristic length](#characteristic-length).

<a id="drift"></a>**Drift** — The net motion of carriers caused by an electric field, superimposed on their random thermal motion; the drift velocity is μ𝓔 at low fields, and drift current density is q(nμ_n + pμ_p)𝓔. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md). *See also:* [Mobility](#mobility), [Diffusion](#diffusion).

<a id="drift-layer"></a>**Drift layer** — The thick, lightly doped region of a power device that holds the blocking voltage when off and carries the current when on; its thickness and doping set the breakdown voltage and much of the on-resistance. *First defined in* [09-13](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-13-compound-and-wide-bandgap-semiconductors.md).

<a id="drift-velocity"></a>**Drift velocity** — The small average velocity carriers acquire from a field on top of their fast random motion; about 74 µm/s for 1 A in 1 mm² of copper. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="drift-diffusion-equations"></a>**Drift–diffusion equations** — The transport model J_n = qnμ_n𝓔 + qD_n dn/dx and J_p = qpμ_p𝓔 − qD_p dp/dx which, with Poisson's equation and the continuity equations, describes semiconductor devices and is solved by device simulators. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md).

<a id="driving-point-impedance"></a>**Driving-point impedance** — The ratio V(s)/I(s) at a single port of a network, with input and output at the same pair of terminals; its poles and zeros are the network's natural frequencies with that port open and shorted. *First defined in* [07-04](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-04-laplace-domain-circuit-analysis.md). *See also:* [Transfer function](#transfer-function).

<a id="driving-point-resistance"></a>**Driving-point resistance** — The resistance seen looking into a node with respect to ground, equal to the diagonal entry R_jj of the resistance matrix G⁻¹; the voltage at node j per ampere injected there. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md). *See also:* [Thevenin resistance](#thevenin-resistance).

<a id="drude-model"></a>**Drude model** — The classical picture of conduction in which carriers accelerate in a field and lose their momentum in random collisions every τ on average, giving σ = ne²τ/m and Ohm's law. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="dsb-sc-modulation"></a>**DSB-SC modulation** — Double-sideband suppressed-carrier AM, x(t) cos(2πf_c t): the message multiplied by the carrier, with no carrier line; efficient, but it needs coherent demodulation with the carrier's frequency and phase. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [Coherent demodulation](#coherent-demodulation).

<a id="dtype"></a>**dtype** — The single element type of a NumPy array (int8, uint8, int64, float32, float64, complex128, bool), fixing its range, precision and memory use. *First defined in* [05-02](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-02-numpy-and-vectorization.md).

<a id="dual-circuit"></a>**Dual circuit** — The circuit obtained from a planar one by turning meshes into nodes, resistances into equal-valued conductances, voltage sources into current sources and series into parallel; its node voltages equal the original's mesh currents. *First defined in* [06-05](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-05-mesh-analysis.md). *See also:* [Mesh analysis](#mesh-analysis), [Nodal analysis](#nodal-analysis).

<a id="dual-dirac-model"></a>**Dual-Dirac model** — A model of jitter as two spikes DJ(δδ) apart blurred by Gaussian random jitter of rms σ, giving total jitter TJ(BER) = DJ(δδ) + 2·Q_BER·σ, where the industry convention defines Q(Q_BER) = BER (2Q_BER = 14.069 at 1e-12; the literal model gives 13.68). *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="dual-slope-adc"></a>**Dual-slope ADC** — An integrating converter that integrates the input for a fixed time and times the de-integration with a reference; its result is independent of R and C, and integrating over whole mains periods rejects hum. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="duality-fourier"></a>**Duality (Fourier)** — The symmetry of the Fourier pair: if x(t) ↔ X(jω), then X(jt) ↔ 2π x(−ω); so a pulse transforms to a sinc and a sinc to a pulse. *First defined in* [11-06](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-06-continuous-time-fourier-transform.md).

<a id="duality-principle"></a>**Duality principle** — Swapping AND with OR and 0 with 1 throughout a Boolean identity gives another valid identity, because every axiom's dual is also an axiom. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md).

<a id="duty-cycle"></a>**Duty cycle** — The fraction of time a block or signal is active; a block drawing current I for duty cycle D contributes D·I to the average current. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="dynamic-power"></a>**Dynamic power** — Power consumed by charging and discharging capacitances in switching circuits, P = αCV²f, independent of the resistance of the charging path. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md). *See also:* [Activity factor](#activity-factor).

<a id="dynamic-typing"></a>**Dynamic typing** — Types belong to objects, not to names, so a name can refer to values of different types over time; checked at run time (type hints document intent but do not enforce it). *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="dynamic-voltage-and-frequency-scaling-dvfs"></a>**Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)** — Lowering supply voltage and clock frequency together when full performance is not needed; because dynamic power scales roughly as V²f, power falls roughly as the cube of voltage. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="letter-e"></a>

## E

<a id="e-series-preferred-values"></a>**E-series (preferred values)** — The IEC 60063 series of standard component values with n values per decade spaced by about 10^(1/n), such as E12, E24 and E96, chosen so neighbouring values' tolerance bands roughly touch. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Tolerance](#tolerance).

<a id="early-effect"></a>**Early effect** — The rise of a bipolar transistor's collector current with V_CE because the widening base–collector depletion region thins the neutral base; it gives the device a finite output resistance. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md). *See also:* [Early voltage](#early-voltage).

<a id="early-voltage"></a>**Early voltage** — The voltage V_A at which extrapolated I_C–V_CE characteristics meet the voltage axis, equal to Q'_B/C'_jC for a uniform base; the output resistance is V_A/I_C and the intrinsic gain V_A/V_T, typically tens of volts. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="ebers-moll-model"></a>**Ebers–Moll model** — The superposition model of a bipolar transistor driven by both V_BE and V_BC, I_C = I_S(e^(V_BE/V_T) − 1) − I_S(1 + 1/β_R)(e^(V_BC/V_T) − 1), valid in all operating regions and the core of SPICE bipolar models. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="eddy-currents"></a>**Eddy currents** — Currents induced in bulk conductors by changing magnetic flux; they cause braking, heating and core loss, which laminated and ferrite cores reduce. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="effective-aperture"></a>**Effective aperture** — The area A_e = Gλ²/(4π) from which a receiving antenna collects power, P_r = S·A_e; for a fixed gain it shrinks as λ², for a fixed physical area the gain grows as 1/λ². *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Antenna gain](#antenna-gain), [Friis transmission equation](#friis-transmission-equation).

<a id="effective-density-of-states"></a>**Effective density of states** — The number of states per volume, N_C (or N_V), that a band would have if all its states sat at the band edge, chosen so that n = N_C e^(−(E_C − E_F)/kT); N_C = 2(2π m_dn kT/h²)^(3/2), about 3.2×10¹⁹ cm⁻³ in silicon at 300 K. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md). *See also:* [Density of states](#density-of-states), [Density-of-states effective mass](#density-of-states-effective-mass).

<a id="effective-mass"></a>**Effective mass** — The mass m\* = ħ²/(d²E/dk²) with which an electron in a band responds to external forces, set by the band's curvature; light effective masses mean high mobility. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="effective-number-of-bits-enob"></a>**Effective number of bits (ENOB)** — (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02, the resolution of an ideal ADC with the same measured signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio as a real one. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="efficiency"></a>**Efficiency** — The ratio of output power to input power, η = P_out/P_in, of a converter or distribution path; efficiencies of stages in series multiply. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="eigenfunction-of-an-lti-system"></a>**Eigenfunction of an LTI system** — A signal that passes through every LTI system unchanged in shape, multiplied only by a complex constant: zⁿ → H(z)zⁿ in discrete time and e^{st} → H(s)e^{st} in continuous time. Sinusoids are sums of two such signals. *First defined in* [11-04](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-04-lti-systems-and-differential-equations.md). *See also:* [System function](#system-function), [Frequency response](#frequency-response).

<a id="eigenvalue"></a>**Eigenvalue** — A number λ for which Ax = λx has a nonzero solution x; the roots of det(A − λI) = 0. They sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md). *See also:* [Eigenvector](#eigenvector), [Characteristic polynomial](#characteristic-polynomial).

<a id="eigenvector"></a>**Eigenvector** — A nonzero vector x that a matrix only scales, Ax = λx; any nonzero multiple is also an eigenvector. In eigenvector coordinates a diagonalizable matrix acts as independent scalings. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md).

<a id="einstein-relation"></a>**Einstein relation** — D/μ = kT/q for non-degenerate carriers, derived from the requirement of zero current in equilibrium; 25.85 mV at 300 K. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md). *See also:* [Diffusion coefficient](#diffusion-coefficient), [Mobility](#mobility).

<a id="eirp"></a>**EIRP** — (Effective isotropic radiated power.) The transmitter power times the antenna gain in a given direction, P_t·G_t, the power an isotropic antenna would need to produce the same peak power density; regulators set limits in EIRP. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Antenna gain](#antenna-gain).

<a id="elasticity-sensitivity"></a>**Elasticity (sensitivity)** — The dimensionless ratio of relative changes, S = d ln y / d ln x = (x/y)(dy/dx); for y = kxⁿ it equals n. Engineers call it sensitivity, economists elasticity. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="electric-charge"></a>**Electric charge** — The property that makes matter feel electric forces; it comes in two signs, is conserved, and is quantized in multiples of the elementary charge. Measured in coulombs (1 C = 1 A·s). *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="electric-current"></a>**Electric current** — The rate at which charge crosses a surface, I = dQ/dt (amperes); conventional current points the way positive charge would move, opposite to electron motion in a metal. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="electric-dipole"></a>**Electric dipole** — Charges ±q a distance d apart, with dipole moment p = qd pointing from − to +; its far field falls as 1/r³, and in a uniform field it feels torque pE sin θ but no net force. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="electric-displacement"></a>**Electric displacement** — The field D = ε₀E + P = εE (C/m²), whose flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed free charge; its normal component is continuous across a boundary without free charge. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="electric-energy-density"></a>**Electric energy density** — The energy stored per unit volume in an electric field, u = ½εE² (J/m³); integrated over space it equals a capacitor's ½CV², and in a vacuum gap it equals the electrostatic pressure on the conductors. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="electric-field"></a>**Electric field** — The force per unit charge a small test charge would feel at a point, E = F/q (V/m); a point charge's field is q/(4πε₀r²) pointing away from a positive charge. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="electric-flux"></a>**Electric flux** — The surface integral of the electric field's normal component, Φ = ∬ E · n̂ dA (V·m); it counts field lines crossing a surface, and through a closed surface it equals the enclosed charge over ε₀. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md). *See also:* [Flux](#flux), [Gauss's law](#gausss-law).

<a id="electric-potential"></a>**Electric potential** — Potential energy per unit charge, V = U/q (volts, J/C), defined because the electrostatic field is conservative; V_b − V_a = −∫ E · dl, a point charge gives k_e q/r, and potentials add as scalars. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md). *See also:* [Conservative field](#conservative-field), [Equipotential](#equipotential).

<a id="electric-power"></a>**Electric power** — The rate of energy transfer, p = dw/dt = vi, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s = 1 V·A). *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Passive sign convention](#passive-sign-convention), [Average power](#average-power).

<a id="electrical-engineering"></a>**Electrical engineering** — The discipline of using electricity and electromagnetism to move and convert energy and to sense, move, store and process information. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="electrical-oxide-thickness"></a>**Electrical oxide thickness** — The effective gate-dielectric thickness in inversion, T_oxe = T_ox + W_dpoly/3 + T_inv/3, including poly-gate depletion and the inversion-layer centroid; typically 6–10 Å more than the physical oxide. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="electromagnetic-wave"></a>**Electromagnetic wave** — Self-sustaining oscillating E and B fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, with E = cB; speed c/√ε_r in a dielectric. Radio, light and board signals are all such waves. *First defined in* [04-08](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-08-maxwell-preview.md).

<a id="electromigration"></a>**Electromigration** — The slow drift of metal atoms pushed by the electron current at high current density, forming voids and hillocks; it caps the DC current density in on-chip wires, especially power grids. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="electron-affinity"></a>**Electron affinity** — The energy χ = E_0 − E_C needed to lift an electron from the conduction-band edge to the vacuum level; 4.05 eV for silicon. Unlike the work function, it does not depend on doping. *First defined in* [09-01](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-01-crystals-and-energy-bands.md). *See also:* [Work function](#work-function), [Vacuum level](#vacuum-level).

<a id="electron-volt"></a>**Electron-volt** — The energy an electron gains (or the work done on it) crossing 1 V, exactly 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J since 2019; the natural unit for band gaps, photon energies and per-electron energies. Also written electronvolt. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="electronic-design-automation-eda"></a>**Electronic design automation (EDA)** — The software used to design and verify chips and boards, covering simulation, synthesis, place-and-route, timing and verification; dominated commercially by Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens EDA. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="electrostatic-discharge-esd"></a>**Electrostatic discharge (ESD)** — The sudden flow of charge between objects at different potentials, typically a spark from a charged person or device; ICs are protected on-chip and qualified against standard ESD models. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="electrostatic-equilibrium"></a>**Electrostatic equilibrium** — The state of a conductor whose free charges have stopped moving; the field inside the metal is zero, net charge sits on the surface, and the field just outside is perpendicular with magnitude σ/ε₀. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="element-law"></a>**Element law** — The relation between an element's terminal voltage and current (its constitutive relation), such as v = Ri; with KCL and KVL it determines every voltage and current in a circuit. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [i–v characteristic](#i-v-characteristic).

<a id="elementary-charge"></a>**Elementary charge** — The charge of a proton, e = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C exactly (an electron carries −e); one coulomb is 6.242 × 10¹⁸ elementary charges. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="elliptic-filter"></a>**Elliptic filter** — A filter with equiripple passband and stopband, obtained by placing zeros on the jω axis just beyond the passband; it meets a magnitude specification with the lowest order of the classical families, at the cost of large group-delay variation. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [Butterworth response](#butterworth-response), [Bessel filter](#bessel-filter).

<a id="elmore-delay"></a>**Elmore delay** — The first moment (time centroid) of a network's impulse response, computed directly from its resistances and capacitances; a fast, somewhat pessimistic interconnect delay estimate. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="emitter-degeneration"></a>**Emitter degeneration** — A resistor in series with a bipolar transistor's emitter, which provides negative feedback that stabilizes the bias against β, V_BE and temperature, at the cost of headroom and gain. *First defined in* [10-03](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-03-bjt-dc-operation-and-biasing.md). *See also:* [Source degeneration](#source-degeneration).

<a id="emitter-follower"></a>**Emitter follower** — The common-collector bipolar stage, with the input at the base and the output at the emitter; gain (β + 1)R_E'/(R_sig + r_π + (β + 1)R_E'), input resistance r_π + (β + 1)R_E' and output resistance about r_e + R_sig/(β + 1). *First defined in* [10-07](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-07-bjt-single-stage-amplifiers.md). *See also:* [Buffer amplifier](#buffer-amplifier), [Source follower](#source-follower).

<a id="emitter-injection-efficiency"></a>**Emitter injection efficiency** — The fraction γ of a bipolar transistor's emitter current carried by majority carriers injected into the base; set by the ratio of emitter to base Gummel numbers and limited by band-gap narrowing in the emitter. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="emulation"></a>**Emulation** — Running a chip design on specialized hardware (emulators or FPGA prototypes) thousands to millions of times faster than simulation, so software can run before tapeout. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="endianness"></a>**Endianness** — The order of a multi-byte value's bytes in memory or on a wire; little-endian stores the least significant byte first (x86, most Arm MCUs), big-endian the most significant first (network byte order). *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="energy-band"></a>**Energy band** — A range of closely spaced allowed electron energies in a crystal, formed when each atomic level of N coupled atoms splits into N levels; each band holds two electrons per primitive cell. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="energy-per-bit"></a>**Energy per bit** — The energy (typically pJ/bit) consumed to move, store or process one bit; power = energy per bit × data rate. A key efficiency metric for links, memories and accelerators. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="energy-signal"></a>**Energy signal** — A signal with finite, nonzero energy E = ∫|x|² dt (or Σ|x[n]|²), and hence zero average power; transients and pulses are energy signals. *First defined in* [11-01](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-01-signals-classification-and-operations.md). *See also:* [Power signal](#power-signal).

<a id="energy-spectral-density"></a>**Energy spectral density** — |X(f)|², the energy per hertz of a finite-energy signal; by Parseval its integral over all frequency is the signal's energy. *First defined in* [11-06](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-06-continuous-time-fourier-transform.md). *See also:* [Parseval's relation](#parsevals-relation).

<a id="energy-delay-product"></a>**Energy-delay product** — Energy per task times execution time (EDP), or times its square (ED²P); ED²P is roughly unchanged by voltage scaling, so it compares architectures independently of their operating points. *First defined in* [14-01](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-01-performance-power-iron-law.md).

<a id="engineering-change-order-eco"></a>**Engineering change order (ECO)** — A late design change made with minimal disruption, often by rewiring spare gates through metal-layer changes only. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="enhancement-mode-transistor"></a>**Enhancement-mode transistor** — A MOSFET with no channel at zero gate voltage, so it is off unless the gate is driven past a threshold of the right sign; standard logic transistors are enhancement mode. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="envelope-detector"></a>**Envelope detector** — A diode charging a capacitor that discharges through a resistor, which tracks the peaks of an AM signal; its time constant must be much longer than the carrier period but at most √(1 − m²)/(mω_m) to avoid diagonal clipping. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [Amplitude modulation (AM)](#amplitude-modulation-am).

<a id="epitaxy"></a>**Epitaxy** — Growth of a crystalline layer on a crystalline substrate so that the layer continues the substrate's lattice; a mismatched layer is strained until, beyond a critical thickness, misfit dislocations relax it. *First defined in* [09-01](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-01-crystals-and-energy-bands.md). *See also:* [Lattice mismatch](#lattice-mismatch).

<a id="equilibrium-solution"></a>**Equilibrium solution** — A constant solution y\* of an autonomous equation y' = f(y), where f(y\*) = 0; it is stable if f'(y\*) < 0, with local time constant −1/f'(y\*), and unstable if f'(y\*) > 0. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="equipotential"></a>**Equipotential** — A surface (or line) of constant potential; moving along it takes no work, field lines cross it at right angles, and every conductor in equilibrium is one. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="equivalent-noise-bandwidth-enbw"></a>**Equivalent noise bandwidth (ENBW)** — The width of an ideal brick-wall filter passing the same white-noise power as a real filter, ∫₀^∞ |H(f)|² df divided by the passband gain; (π/2) f_c for one pole. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="equivalent-noise-resistance"></a>**Equivalent noise resistance** — The resistance whose thermal noise 4kTR equals a device's or amplifier's input-referred noise power density; γ/g_m for a MOSFET and 1/(2g_m) for a bipolar transistor. *First defined in* [12-10](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-10-noise-in-circuits.md). *See also:* [Input-referred noise](#input-referred-noise), [Thermal noise](#thermal-noise).

<a id="equivalent-oxide-thickness-eot"></a>**Equivalent oxide thickness (EOT)** — The SiO₂ thickness giving the same capacitance per area as a gate stack, EOT = Σ t_i × 3.9/ε_r,i; a 2 nm HfO₂ layer (ε_r = 25) counts as 0.312 nm. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="equivalent-resistance"></a>**Equivalent resistance** — The single resistance that has the same voltage–current relation at a pair of terminals as a network of resistors; it says nothing about the network's internal currents. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md).

<a id="equivalent-series-inductance-esl"></a>**Equivalent series inductance (ESL)** — The inductance in series with a real capacitor, set by its current loop through terminations and package; above the self-resonant frequency it dominates, so the part behaves as an inductor, and paralleling N parts divides it by N. *First defined in* [07-01](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-01-capacitors-and-inductors.md). *See also:* [Equivalent series resistance (ESR)](#equivalent-series-resistance-esr), [Decoupling capacitor](#decoupling-capacitor).

<a id="equivalent-series-resistance-esr"></a>**Equivalent series resistance (ESR)** — The resistance in series with a real capacitor's ideal capacitance (electrodes, terminations, dielectric loss); it dissipates ripple current as heat and sets the impedance at the self-resonant frequency. *First defined in* [07-01](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-01-capacitors-and-inductors.md). *See also:* [Equivalent series inductance (ESL)](#equivalent-series-inductance-esl), [Self-resonant frequency](#self-resonant-frequency).

<a id="equivalent-states"></a>**Equivalent states** — Two states of an FSM that produce the same output sequence for every input sequence; they can be merged without changing the machine's behavior. *First defined in* [08-08](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-08-finite-state-machines.md). *See also:* [Partition refinement](#partition-refinement).

<a id="ergodicity"></a>**Ergodicity** — The property that time averages along one sample function converge to ensemble averages; it licenses measuring a process with one long recording. Unit-to-unit offsets are not ergodic. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="error-budget"></a>**Error budget** — A table of every error source's contribution to a system's output (each source times its gain to the output), combined by worst case or by root-sum-square. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Root-sum-square (RSS)](#root-sum-square-rss), [Worst-case analysis](#worst-case-analysis).

<a id="error-log"></a>**Error log** — A running record of every mistake, its cause and the rule that prevents it, used to target review and to avoid repeating errors. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="error-vector-magnitude"></a>**Error vector magnitude** — EVM, the RMS distance between transmitted (or received) constellation points and their ideal positions, relative to the signal, often quoted in dB. It sets the highest usable QAM order. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="espresso"></a>**Espresso** — The heuristic two-level logic minimizer developed at IBM and UC Berkeley (Brayton, Hachtel, McMullen and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, 1984), iterating expand, irredundant and reduce steps to find near-minimal multiple-output covers. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md).

<a id="esr-zero"></a>**ESR zero** — The zero at s = −1/(R_ESR·C) created by a capacitor's equivalent series resistance; above f = 1/(2π·R_ESR·C) the capacitor looks resistive. Some older linear regulators relied on it for stability, which ties their stability to a window of ESR. *First defined in* [07-04](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-04-laplace-domain-circuit-analysis.md).

<a id="essential-prime-implicant"></a>**Essential prime implicant** — A prime implicant that covers at least one minterm no other prime implicant covers, so every cover must include it. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md).

<a id="estimator"></a>**Estimator** — A rule for computing a parameter's value from data, such as the sample mean; the result, an estimate, is itself a random variable with a sampling distribution. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="eulers-formula"></a>**Euler's formula** — e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ for real θ. It connects exponentials and sinusoids and makes r∠θ and re^{jθ} the same number. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="eulers-method"></a>**Euler's method** — The simplest numerical ODE solver, y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n); first-order accurate, and on y' = −y/τ stable only for steps h < 2τ. Its implicit (backward) form is stable for any step. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="evanescent-wave"></a>**Evanescent wave** — A field that decays exponentially away from an interface instead of propagating, as on the far side of a totally reflecting boundary; it carries no average power across the interface but can couple to a nearby structure. *First defined in* [13-06](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-06-reflection-and-transmission.md). *See also:* [Total internal reflection](#total-internal-reflection).

<a id="even-and-odd-signals"></a>**Even and odd signals** — An even signal satisfies x(−t) = x(t) and an odd one x(−t) = −x(t); every signal splits uniquely into x_e = (x(t) + x(−t))/2 and x_o = (x(t) − x(−t))/2, whose energies add. *First defined in* [11-01](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-01-signals-classification-and-operations.md).

<a id="exception"></a>**Exception** — An object signalling an error that stops normal execution until handled by try/except; raising one with a clear message is how code refuses invalid input instead of returning a wrong value. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="excitation-table"></a>**Excitation table** — For each present-to-next transition of a flip-flop (0→0, 0→1, 1→0, 1→1), the inputs that produce it, with don't cares; used to design sequential circuits with JK, T or SR flip-flops. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md). *See also:* [JK flip-flop](#jk-flip-flop), [State table](#state-table).

<a id="existence-and-uniqueness-theorem"></a>**Existence and uniqueness theorem** — A linear first-order IVP with continuous coefficients has exactly one solution on the whole interval of continuity; a nonlinear one y' = f(t, y) has a unique local solution when f and ∂f/∂y are continuous (Picard–Lindelöf). *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="expectation"></a>**Expectation** — The probability-weighted average of a random variable, Σ k·p(k) or ∫ x·f(x) dx; its long-run average over many independent trials, also called the mean. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="exponential-distribution"></a>**Exponential distribution** — The waiting time to the first event of a Poisson process with rate r, P(T > t) = e^(−rt), with mean 1/r; the model behind constant failure rates. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md). *See also:* [Memoryless property](#memoryless-property), [FIT (failures in time)](#fit-failures-in-time).

<a id="exponential-function"></a>**Exponential function** — The function eˣ (e ≈ 2.71828), whose rate of change equals its value; physical decays are written y₀e^(−t/τ) with time constant τ. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md). *See also:* [Natural logarithm](#natural-logarithm), [Half-life](#half-life).

<a id="exponential-moving-average-ema"></a>**Exponential moving average (EMA)** — The first-order recursion y[n] = y[n − 1] + α(x[n] − y[n − 1]), with impulse response α(1 − α)^n, DC gain 1, a time constant of about 1/α − 1/2 samples and the white-noise reduction of a moving average of length (2 − α)/α; with α a power of 2 it needs one stored value, a shift and two additions per sample. *First defined in* [16-01](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-01-discrete-time-systems-review.md). *See also:* [IIR filter](#iir-filter), [Moving-average filter](#moving-average-filter).

<a id="exponential-response-formula"></a>**Exponential response formula** — For p(D)y = e^{st} with p(s) ≠ 0, a particular solution is y = e^{st}/p(s); when s is a simple root of p, y = t e^{st}/p'(s) instead (the resonant case). *First defined in* [02-04](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-04-forced-response-and-resonance.md).

<a id="extraction-efficiency"></a>**Extraction efficiency** — The fraction of photons generated inside an LED that escape the chip; limited by total internal reflection at the high-index surface and raised by shaping and texturing. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="letter-f"></a>

## F

<a id="fabless"></a>**Fabless** — A chip company that designs chips but outsources manufacturing to foundries (and assembly and test to OSATs). *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md). *See also:* [Foundry](#foundry).

<a id="false-sharing"></a>**False sharing** — Coherence misses caused by different cores writing different data that happen to share a cache block, so the block moves between caches although no variable is shared; fixed by padding or aligning data to blocks. *First defined in* [14-12](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-12-multicore-coherence-consistency.md). *See also:* [Coherence miss](#coherence-miss).

<a id="far-field"></a>**Far field** — The region far enough from an antenna (r ≫ λ and r > 2D²/λ for an antenna of size D) that the fields fall as 1/r, are transverse to the radial direction, and have a pattern independent of distance. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Radiation pattern](#radiation-pattern).

<a id="faraday-cage"></a>**Faraday cage** — A closed conducting enclosure; its empty interior has zero electrostatic field whatever the outside charges, and it shields both ways only when grounded. Seams, apertures and low-frequency magnetic fields limit real shields. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="faradays-law"></a>**Faraday's law** — The EMF around a closed loop equals minus the rate of change of magnetic flux through it, ℰ = −N dΦ/dt; changing flux makes the electric field non-conservative, so voltage then depends on the path. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md). *See also:* [Lenz's law](#lenzs-law).

<a id="fast-fourier-transform-fft"></a>**Fast Fourier transform (FFT)** — Any algorithm that computes the DFT in O(N log N) operations instead of N²; the radix-2 Cooley–Tukey FFT splits an N-point DFT into two N/2-point DFTs recursively, using (N/2)log₂N butterflies. *First defined in* [16-04](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-04-the-fft.md). *See also:* [Butterfly](#butterfly), [Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)](#discrete-fourier-transform-dft).

<a id="fastspice"></a>**FastSPICE** — A class of transistor-level circuit simulators that partition the circuit and use simplified or tabulated device models to gain speed and capacity, at some loss of accuracy relative to SPICE. *First defined in* [06-04](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-04-nodal-analysis.md). *See also:* [SPICE](#spice).

<a id="fault-coverage"></a>**Fault coverage** — The fraction of modeled faults (for example stuck-at faults) that a set of test patterns detects. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md). *See also:* [Defect level (DPPM)](#defect-level-dppm).

<a id="feed-forward-equalizer-ffe"></a>**Feed-forward equalizer (FFE)** — An FIR filter in a receiver that approximately inverts the channel; taps acting on samples before the main cursor (precursor taps) cancel precursor intersymbol interference, at the cost of one symbol of latency per precursor tap and of noise enhancement where the channel's response is low. *First defined in* [16-02](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-02-dtft-and-z-transform-for-dsp.md). *See also:* [Decision-feedback equalizer (DFE)](#decision-feedback-equalizer-dfe), [Precursor tap](#precursor-tap), [Noise enhancement](#noise-enhancement).

<a id="feedback-topology"></a>**Feedback topology** — The way a feedback amplifier mixes the fed-back signal at its input (series, as a voltage, or shunt, as a current) and samples its output (shunt, the voltage, or series, the current); series connections raise an impedance by 1 + T and shunt connections lower it. *First defined in* [12-05](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-05-feedback-topologies.md). *See also:* [Return ratio](#return-ratio).

<a id="fence"></a>**Fence** — An instruction that orders memory operations, preventing specified earlier accesses from being reordered after specified later ones (for example RISC-V FENCE, x86 MFENCE). *First defined in* [14-12](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-12-multicore-coherence-consistency.md). *See also:* [Memory consistency model](#memory-consistency-model).

<a id="fermi-energy"></a>**Fermi energy** — The highest occupied electron energy at absolute zero, E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^(2/3) for a free-electron gas (about 7 eV in copper); at finite temperature the Fermi level is the energy whose occupation probability is one half. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="fermi-estimate"></a>**Fermi estimate** — An order-of-magnitude estimate built from rounded assumptions and simple multiplication, used to sanity-check calculations and claims. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="fermi-level"></a>**Fermi level** — The energy E_F at which a state would be occupied with probability one half; in equilibrium it is constant throughout a system, and its position relative to the band edges sets the electron and hole concentrations. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md). *See also:* [Fermi–Dirac distribution](#fermi-dirac-distribution), [Intrinsic Fermi level](#intrinsic-fermi-level).

<a id="fermi-level-pinning"></a>**Fermi-level pinning** — The weak dependence of Schottky barrier height on metal work function, caused by interface states that hold the Fermi level near a fixed energy in the gap; for silicon Hu fits φ_Bn ≈ 0.7 V + 0.2(ψ_M − 4.75 V). *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="fermi-dirac-distribution"></a>**Fermi–Dirac distribution** — The probability f(E) = 1/(1 + e^((E − E_F)/kT)) that an electron state of energy E is occupied in equilibrium; it falls from 0.9 to 0.1 over about 4.4 kT and reduces to the Boltzmann factor far above E_F. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="fermi-dirac-integral"></a>**Fermi–Dirac integral** — The function F_1/2(η) = (2/√π)∫₀^∞ √x dx/(1 + e^(x − η)) that gives the carrier density of a parabolic band with any Fermi level, n = N_C F_1/2((E_F − E_C)/kT); it reduces to e^η when η ≪ −1. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md).

<a id="ferromagnetism"></a>**Ferromagnetism** — Strong, spontaneous alignment of atomic magnetic moments in domains (iron, nickel, cobalt, ferrites), giving high permeability, saturation and hysteresis. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="ficks-law"></a>**Fick's law** — The statement that a diffusion flux is proportional to, and directed down, the concentration gradient, F = −D dn/dx; it follows from a random walk. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md).

<a id="field-programmable-gate-array-fpga"></a>**Field-programmable gate array (FPGA)** — A chip of lookup tables, flip-flops, block RAMs, DSP blocks and I/O joined by programmable routing, configured after manufacture by loading a bitstream. *First defined in* [08-11](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-11-memories-and-programmable-logic.md). *See also:* [Lookup table (LUT)](#lookup-table-lut), [Block RAM](#block-ram), [Bitstream](#bitstream).

<a id="fill-factor"></a>**Fill factor** — The ratio of a solar cell's maximum output power to the product V_oc I_sc, measuring how square its I–V curve is; about 0.75 is typical, and higher for an ideal cell. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="final-value-theorem"></a>**Final-value theorem** — f(∞) = lim sF(s) as s → 0, valid only if f actually settles, that is, every pole of sF(s) lies in the open left half-plane; applied to an unstable or oscillating signal it gives a wrong answer. *First defined in* [02-05](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-05-laplace-transform-for-odes.md). *See also:* [Initial-value theorem](#initial-value-theorem), [DC gain](#dc-gain).

<a id="finfet"></a>**FinFET** — A multigate MOSFET whose channel is a thin vertical silicon fin with the gate draped over its sidewalls and top; its width is 2H_fin + W_fin per fin and comes in whole fins. *First defined in* [09-12](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-12-finfet-gaa-cfet-backside-power.md).

<a id="finite-state-machine-fsm"></a>**Finite state machine (FSM)** — A sequential circuit described by a finite set of states, a next-state function of the present state and inputs, an output function and a reset state; implemented as a state register with next-state and output logic. *First defined in* [08-08](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-08-finite-state-machines.md). *See also:* [Moore machine](#moore-machine), [Mealy machine](#mealy-machine), [State diagram](#state-diagram).

<a id="finite-difference-method"></a>**Finite-difference method** — Approximating derivatives by differences on a grid; for Laplace's equation each grid potential equals the average of its four neighbours to second order in the spacing, giving linear equations that a computer, or a grid of equal resistors, solves. *First defined in* [13-02](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-02-electrostatics-boundary-value-problems.md). *See also:* [Laplace's equation](#laplaces-equation).

<a id="finite-time-blow-up"></a>**Finite-time blow-up** — A solution of a nonlinear ODE reaching infinity at a finite time although the equation is smooth, as for y' = y² with y = 1/(1 − t); it signals superlinear positive feedback. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="fir-filter"></a>**FIR filter** — A finite impulse response filter, y[n] = Σ h[k] x[n − k] over finitely many taps; always BIBO-stable, it costs one multiply-accumulate per tap per sample and, if symmetric, has exactly linear phase. *First defined in* [11-03](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-03-convolution.md). *See also:* [Multiply-accumulate (MAC)](#multiply-accumulate-mac), [Latency](#latency).

<a id="first-order-circuit"></a>**First-order circuit** — A circuit whose behavior is described by a first-order differential equation, typically one with a single (equivalent) capacitor or inductor. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="first-silicon-success"></a>**First-silicon success** — A chip's first manufactured version (A0) being functionally correct and shippable without a respin; reported for a minority of IC/ASIC projects in industry surveys. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="fit-failures-in-time"></a>**FIT (failures in time)** — A failure rate of one failure per 10^9 device-hours; soft-error rates of memories are quoted in FIT per megabit. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="five-transistor-ota"></a>**Five-transistor OTA** — The simplest operational transconductance amplifier, a differential pair with a current-mirror load and a tail source; gain g_m(r_o2 ∥ r_o4), small common-mode gain about 1/(2g_m3R_SS), and the first stage of the classic two-stage op-amp. *First defined in* [12-02](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-02-active-loads-cascodes-multistage.md). *See also:* [Current-mirror load](#current-mirror-load), [Common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR)](#common-mode-rejection-ratio-cmrr).

<a id="fixed-point-arithmetic"></a>**Fixed-point arithmetic** — Representing fractions as integers with an agreed scale 2^−f, so integer hardware does the arithmetic; additions are direct, products must be rescaled, and rounding, overflow and saturation are managed by the programmer. *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md). *See also:* [Q format](#q-format), [Saturation arithmetic](#saturation-arithmetic).

<a id="flat-band-voltage"></a>**Flat-band voltage** — The gate voltage at which the semiconductor's bands are flat up to the surface, V_FB = ψ_g − ψ_s − Q_ox/C_ox; about −1 V for an n⁺ poly gate on p-type silicon. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="flicker-1-f-noise"></a>**Flicker (1/f) noise** — Noise whose power spectral density falls as 1/f, so every decade of frequency carries equal power; dominant at low frequencies in MOSFETs. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="flicker-noise"></a>**Flicker noise** — Noise whose power spectral density rises as 1/f toward low frequency, from carriers trapped and released at interfaces; strong in MOSFETs, it contributes equal power in every decade and is characterized by its corner frequency with the white floor. *First defined in* [12-10](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-10-noise-in-circuits.md). *See also:* [Thermal noise](#thermal-noise), [Input-referred noise](#input-referred-noise).

<a id="floating-point-number"></a>**Floating-point number** — A number stored as sign, exponent and fraction in binary; IEEE 754 binary64 (Python float, C double) has 53 significant bits (about 16 decimal digits), so most decimals such as 0.1 are approximated. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="floor-division"></a>**Floor division** — Division that rounds the quotient down toward minus infinity (Python's //), paired with a remainder (%) that takes the divisor's sign; −7 // 2 is −4 in Python but C's integer division gives −3. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="flush"></a>**Flush** — Discarding instructions fetched down a wrong path (after a taken branch, under predict-not-taken) by turning them into bubbles before they change any state. *First defined in* [14-06](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-06-pipelining-and-hazards.md).

<a id="flux"></a>**Flux** — The surface integral of a vector field's normal component, ∬ F · dA, measuring how much of the field passes through a surface. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md).

<a id="flyback-diode"></a>**Flyback diode** — A diode placed across an inductive load so that, when the driving switch opens, the inductor's current circulates through the diode, clamping the switch voltage to about one diode drop above the supply. Also called a freewheeling diode. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="foldback-current-limiting"></a>**Foldback current limiting** — Output short-circuit protection whose current limit falls as the voltage across the output device rises, so that a short circuit, which puts the full supply across the device, draws much less current than a normal peak and stays inside the safe operating area. *First defined in* [12-07](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-07-output-stages.md). *See also:* [Safe operating area](#safe-operating-area).

<a id="folded-cascode"></a>**Folded cascode** — A single-stage op-amp in which the input pair's signal currents are folded into common-gate cascode devices of the opposite type, giving cascode output resistance with more headroom than a telescopic cascode; its load capacitance sets the dominant pole, so GBW = g_m1/(2πC_L). *First defined in* [12-08](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-08-op-amp-internals.md). *See also:* [Two-stage op-amp](#two-stage-op-amp), [Telescopic cascode amplifier](#telescopic-cascode-amplifier).

<a id="forced-beta"></a>**Forced beta** — The ratio I_C/I_B imposed on a saturated bipolar transistor by its circuit, smaller than the device's β; switches are designed with a forced beta near 10 so every device saturates. *First defined in* [10-03](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-03-bjt-dc-operation-and-biasing.md).

<a id="force-current-analogy"></a>**Force–current analogy** — The mapping of a mechanical system onto a circuit with force ↔ current and velocity ↔ voltage (mass ↔ C to ground, damping ↔ conductance, stiffness ↔ 1/L); elements sharing a velocity become parallel elements, so the circuit keeps the mechanism's topology. *First defined in* [15-01](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-01-modeling-dynamic-systems.md). *See also:* [Force–voltage analogy](#force-voltage-analogy).

<a id="force-voltage-analogy"></a>**Force–voltage analogy** — The mapping of a mass–spring–damper onto a series RLC circuit (force ↔ voltage, velocity ↔ current, mass ↔ L, damping ↔ R, compliance 1/k_s ↔ C); it turns mechanical systems into circuits that SPICE can simulate. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="form-factor"></a>**Form factor** — RMS value divided by the rectified average; π/(2√2) ≈ 1.111 for a sine. Average-responding meters assume this value. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="formal-verification"></a>**Formal verification** — Using mathematical proof (model checking, equivalence checking) to show that a design satisfies a property for all possible inputs, instead of testing examples. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="forward-error-correction-fec"></a>**Forward error correction (FEC)** — Adding redundant symbols so the receiver can correct errors without retransmission; it lets links run at a raw BER near 1e-4 and still deliver 1e-13 or better. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="forward-transit-time"></a>**Forward transit time** — The ratio τ_F = Q_F/I_C of stored excess charge to collector current in a forward-active bipolar transistor, the sum of emitter, base (W_B²/2D_B for a uniform base) and collector delays; it sets the diffusion capacitance and limits f_T. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="forward-active-mode"></a>**Forward-active mode** — The amplifying region of a bipolar transistor, with the base–emitter junction forward biased and the base–collector junction reverse biased, where the collector current is set by V_BE and nearly independent of V_CE. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="forward-active-region"></a>**Forward-active region** — The bipolar operating region with the base-emitter junction forward-biased and the base-collector junction reverse-biased, where I_C ≈ βI_B and the collector acts as a current source. *First defined in* [10-03](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-03-bjt-dc-operation-and-biasing.md).

<a id="forwarding-bypassing"></a>**Forwarding (bypassing)** — Routing a result from a later pipeline register (EX/MEM or MEM/WB) directly to the inputs of an instruction that needs it, instead of waiting for it to be written to the register file. *First defined in* [14-06](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-06-pipelining-and-hazards.md).

<a id="foster-network"></a>**Foster network** — An RC model written as a series chain of parallel R–C pairs, Z(t) = Σ Rᵢ(1 − e^(−t/τᵢ)); it is a modal (eigenvalue) expansion whose nodes have no physical meaning, so it cannot be cascaded with other stages. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="foundry"></a>**Foundry** — A company that manufactures chips designed by its customers, supplying them with a process and its PDK. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="four-point-probe"></a>**Four-point probe** — A sheet-resistance measurement with four collinear probes, driving current through the outer pair and measuring voltage across the inner pair so that contact resistance drops out; for a thin film R_s = (π/ln 2)(V/I) ≈ 4.532 V/I. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md). *See also:* [Sheet resistance](#sheet-resistance).

<a id="four-resistor-bias"></a>**Four-resistor bias** — The standard discrete BJT bias, a base divider with an emitter resistor (and a collector resistor), giving I_E = (V_Th − V_BE)/(R_E + R_Th/(β + 1)), nearly independent of β when R_Th is much less than (β + 1)R_E. *First defined in* [10-03](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-03-bjt-dc-operation-and-biasing.md).

<a id="four-terminal-kelvin-measurement"></a>**Four-terminal (Kelvin) measurement** — Measuring a resistance or current with one pair of leads that forces the current and a separate pair, attached at the element itself, that senses the voltage while carrying almost no current, so lead, contact and copper resistances drop out. *First defined in* [06-11](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-11-practical-dc-circuits-and-measurement.md). *See also:* [Current-sense shunt](#current-sense-shunt), [Remote sensing](#remote-sensing).

<a id="four-valued-logic"></a>**Four-valued logic** — The simulation model in which each bit is 0, 1, X (unknown) or Z (undriven); 0 dominates AND and 1 dominates OR, other combinations with X or Z give X, and === compares the four values literally. *First defined in* [08-05](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-05-verilog-and-testbenches.md).

<a id="fourier-coefficient"></a>**Fourier coefficient** — The amplitude of one harmonic in a periodic signal, b_n = (2/T)∫ x(t) sin(nωt) dt (and a_n with cosine), found by orthogonality. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="fourier-series"></a>**Fourier series** — The representation of a periodic signal as a sum of complex exponentials at multiples of its fundamental frequency, x(t) = Σ c_k e^{jkω₀t}, with c_k = (1/T₀)∫ x(t) e^{−jkω₀t} dt found by orthogonality. *First defined in* [11-05](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-05-fourier-series.md). *See also:* [Fourier coefficient](#fourier-coefficient), [Harmonic](#harmonic), [Line spectrum](#line-spectrum).

<a id="fourier-transform"></a>**Fourier transform** — X(jω) = ∫ x(t) e^{−jωt} dt, with inverse x(t) = (1/2π)∫ X(jω) e^{jωt} dω: the spectrum of an aperiodic signal, obtained as the limit of the Fourier series as the period grows; X(f) = X(j2πf) in hertz. *First defined in* [11-06](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-06-continuous-time-fourier-transform.md). *See also:* [Fourier series](#fourier-series), [Convolution theorem](#convolution-theorem).

<a id="fowler-nordheim-tunneling"></a>**Fowler–Nordheim tunneling** — Tunneling through a triangular barrier formed when a strong field tilts an insulator's band; the current rises steeply with field (about seven orders of magnitude from 7 to 10 MV/cm in SiO₂) and is used to program and erase flash. *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="fp8"></a>**FP8** — The two 8-bit floating-point formats used for AI, E4M3 (largest value 448, no infinities, one NaN code per sign) and E5M2 (largest value 57 344, IEEE-style specials), standardized by the Open Compute Project in 2023. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md). *See also:* [bfloat16](#bfloat16), [Block floating point](#block-floating-point).

<a id="freeze-out"></a>**Freeze-out** — The recapture of carriers by their dopants at low temperature, when kT becomes small compared with the ionization energy; lightly doped silicon begins to lose carriers this way below about 100 K. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md).

<a id="frequency-prewarping"></a>**Frequency prewarping** — Replacing 2/T in the Tustin substitution by ω_p/tan(ω_pT/2), so the discrete controller matches the continuous one exactly at the chosen frequency ω_p (usually crossover or a notch frequency) despite frequency warping. *First defined in* [15-11](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-11-digital-control.md). *See also:* [Tustin transformation](#tustin-transformation), [Frequency warping](#frequency-warping).

<a id="frequency-resolution"></a>**Frequency resolution** — The smallest separation at which two spectral components appear as distinct peaks; for a record of duration T it is about 1/T hertz with a rectangular window, and roughly twice that with a Hamming window. *First defined in* [11-07](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-07-discrete-time-fourier-transform.md). *See also:* [Window function](#window-function), [Zero-padding](#zero-padding).

<a id="frequency-response"></a>**Frequency response** — The complex gain H(jω) of a linear system at angular frequency ω. Its magnitude scales a sinusoid's amplitude and its angle shifts the sinusoid's phase. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Corner frequency](#corner-frequency).

<a id="frequency-warping"></a>**Frequency warping** — The nonlinear frequency map of the bilinear transform, Ω = (2/T) tan(ω/2): nearly linear well below the sample rate, compressing the whole analog axis into ω < π; corrected at one chosen frequency by prewarping. *First defined in* [11-09](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-09-z-transform.md). *See also:* [Bilinear transform](#bilinear-transform).

<a id="frequency-division-multiplexing-fdm"></a>**Frequency-division multiplexing (FDM)** — Sharing a medium by giving each message its own carrier frequency slot, separated by guard bands sized for the selection filters' transition width; OFDM is its digital form. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md).

<a id="fresnel-equations"></a>**Fresnel equations** — The reflection and transmission coefficients of a plane wave at a planar interface as functions of angle, separately for TE (perpendicular) and TM (parallel) polarization; they follow from continuity of the tangential fields. *First defined in* [13-06](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-06-reflection-and-transmission.md). *See also:* [Brewster angle](#brewster-angle), [Snell's law](#snells-law).

<a id="friis-transmission-equation"></a>**Friis transmission equation** — P_r/P_t = G_t·G_r·(λ/4πR)² for antennas in each other's far field in free space; the free-space path loss is 20 log₁₀(4πR/λ) dB. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Effective aperture](#effective-aperture), [EIRP](#eirp).
