<a id="fubinis-theorem"></a>**Fubini's theorem** — For well-behaved integrands, a double integral can be evaluated as two nested single integrals in either order; reversing the order can turn an impossible integral into an easy one. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Double integral](#double-integral).

<a id="full-adder"></a>**Full adder** — A block that adds two bits and a carry in, giving S = A XOR B XOR Cin (three-input parity) and Cout = majority(A, B, Cin) = G + P·Cin. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md). *See also:* [Generate and propagate](#generate-and-propagate), [Ripple-carry adder](#ripple-carry-adder).

<a id="full-power-bandwidth"></a>**Full-power bandwidth** — The highest frequency at which an amplifier can deliver a sine of a given peak amplitude V_p without slew-rate limiting, SR/(2πV_p). *First defined in* [10-09](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-09-real-op-amps-nonidealities.md). *See also:* [Slew rate](#slew-rate).

<a id="full-well-capacity"></a>**Full-well capacity** — The largest number of electrons a pixel can hold before saturating; it caps the maximum signal-to-noise ratio at its square root. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md).

<a id="fully-associative-cache"></a>**Fully associative cache** — A cache with a single set, in which any block may occupy any line; it has no conflict misses but needs a tag comparator per line. *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md). *See also:* [Set-associative cache](#set-associative-cache).

<a id="fully-differential-amplifier"></a>**Fully differential amplifier** — An amplifier with differential inputs and differential outputs, which doubles the output swing, rejects common-mode noise and even-order distortion, and needs common-mode feedback to set its output common-mode level. *First defined in* [12-08](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-08-op-amp-internals.md). *See also:* [Common-mode feedback](#common-mode-feedback).

<a id="function"></a>**Function** — A rule that assigns exactly one output to each allowed input; in engineering both input and output usually carry units (for example voltage as a function of time). *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md). *See also:* [Domain and range](#domain-and-range), [Inverse function](#inverse-function).

<a id="function-prototype"></a>**Function prototype** — A C declaration giving a function's name, return type and parameter types without its body, so that other translation units can call it; usually placed in a header file. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="functional-completeness"></a>**Functional completeness** — The property of a set of gates that every Boolean function can be built from it; {AND, OR, NOT} is complete, and so are NAND alone and NOR alone, while AND and OR together are not (they cannot make NOT). *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md).

<a id="functional-coverage"></a>**Functional coverage** — A measure of which specified behaviors, input combinations or corner cases a verification run has actually exercised; used to decide when verification is complete. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="fundamental-frequency"></a>**Fundamental frequency** — The reciprocal of a periodic signal's fundamental (smallest) period, f₀ = 1/T₀; all of the signal's harmonics lie at its integer multiples. *First defined in* [11-05](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-05-fourier-series.md).

<a id="fundamental-period"></a>**Fundamental period** — The smallest positive shift that leaves a periodic signal unchanged; a sum of continuous-time periodic signals is periodic only if their periods have a rational ratio, and a discrete-time sinusoid only if ω/2π is rational. *First defined in* [11-01](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-01-signals-classification-and-operations.md).

<a id="fundamental-theorem-of-calculus"></a>**Fundamental theorem of calculus** — Part 1, the accumulated area ∫_a^x f has derivative f(x); part 2, ∫_a^b f = F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F. Integration and differentiation are inverse operations. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="fused-multiply-add-fma"></a>**Fused multiply-add (FMA)** — An operation that computes a × b + c with a single rounding, more accurate than a separate multiply and add and the building block of dot products. *First defined in* [14-04](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-04-computer-arithmetic-and-number-formats.md).

<a id="letter-g"></a>

## G

<a id="gain-crossover-frequency"></a>**Gain crossover frequency** — The frequency ω_c at which a loop gain's magnitude |L(jω)| equals 1 (0 dB); the phase margin is read there, and it sets the loop's speed (closed-loop bandwidth is typically 1 to 2 times ω_c). *First defined in* [15-07](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-07-frequency-domain-design.md). *See also:* [Phase margin](#phase-margin).

<a id="gain-margin"></a>**Gain margin** — How far a loop gain's magnitude is below one, in decibels, at the frequency where its phase reaches −180°, −20·log|T(jω180)|; the extra loop gain the loop could tolerate before oscillating. A typical target is at least 10 dB. *First defined in* [12-06](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-06-stability-and-compensation.md). *See also:* [Phase margin](#phase-margin), [Crossover frequency](#crossover-frequency).

<a id="gain-bandwidth-product"></a>**Gain-bandwidth product** — For an op-amp with a single dominant pole, the constant product of open-loop gain and frequency above the pole, equal to the unity-gain frequency; a closed loop's bandwidth is the gain-bandwidth product divided by the noise gain. *First defined in* [10-09](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-09-real-op-amps-nonidealities.md). *See also:* [Noise gain](#noise-gain).

<a id="gain-bandwidth-product-gbw"></a>**Gain–bandwidth product (GBW)** — For a dominant-pole amplifier, the product of DC gain and bandwidth, A0·fa, equal to the unity-gain frequency; with feedback, closed-loop bandwidth ≈ GBW divided by the noise gain 1/β. Datasheets quote it as a typical value, sometimes at a stated gain. *First defined in* [07-07](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-07-frequency-response-and-bode-plots.md). *See also:* [Loop gain](#loop-gain).

<a id="gate-equivalent-ge"></a>**Gate equivalent (GE)** — A unit of logic area equal to one two-input NAND gate in a named cell library; a block's gate count is its area divided by the NAND2 area. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md).

<a id="gate-all-around-transistor"></a>**Gate-all-around transistor** — A MOSFET whose gate completely surrounds each channel (GAA), as a nanowire or a stack of nanosheets, giving the strongest electrostatic control of the channel. *First defined in* [09-12](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-12-finfet-gaa-cfet-backside-power.md).

<a id="gate-induced-drain-leakage"></a>**Gate-induced drain leakage** — Band-to-band tunneling current in the drain under the gate edge when the gate is low and the drain high (GIDL); it needs band bending beyond the gap and a surface field near 10⁶ V/cm, and grows steeply with drain-to-gate voltage and thinner oxides. *First defined in* [09-10](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-10-short-channel-effects-and-leakage.md).

<a id="gauge-factor"></a>**Gauge factor** — The ratio of a strain gauge's fractional resistance change to the strain, GF = (ΔR/R)/ε; about 2 for metal-foil gauges. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md).

<a id="gausss-law"></a>**Gauss's law** — The electric flux out of any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀; with symmetry it gives fields of spheres, lines and planes in one line. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Divergence theorem](#divergence-theorem).

<a id="gaussian-distribution"></a>**Gaussian distribution** — The normal (bell-curve) distribution with density e^(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²))/(σ√(2π)); thermal noise and sums of many independent small effects follow it. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md). *See also:* [Q-function](#q-function).

<a id="gaussian-elimination"></a>**Gaussian elimination** — Solving Ax = b by subtracting multiples of rows to reach an upper-triangular system, then back-substituting; it costs about (2/3)n³ flops for an n×n system. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md). *See also:* [Pivot](#pivot), [LU factorization](#lu-factorization).

<a id="gaussian-surface"></a>**Gaussian surface** — An imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss's law, ideally one on which the field is constant and perpendicular (or parallel, carrying no flux), such as a sphere, coaxial cylinder or pillbox. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="generate-and-propagate"></a>**Generate and propagate** — In an adder column, generate G = AB means the column produces a carry by itself, and propagate P = A XOR B means it passes an incoming carry on, so Cout = G + P·Cin; the basis of all fast adders. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md).

<a id="generation"></a>**Generation** — The creation of electron–hole pairs, thermally (balanced by recombination in equilibrium) or by light or high fields; net generation occurs where np < n_i², as in a reverse-biased depletion region. *First defined in* [09-04](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-04-generation-recombination-continuity.md). *See also:* [Recombination](#recombination).

<a id="geometric-distribution"></a>**Geometric distribution** — The number of independent trials up to and including the first success, with PMF (1 − q)^(k−1) q; it is memoryless. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="geometric-evaluation"></a>**Geometric evaluation** — Reading a frequency response from a pole–zero plot: |H(jω)| is the product of the distances from jω to the zeros divided by the product of the distances to the poles, and the phase is the sum of the zero angles minus the sum of the pole angles. *First defined in* [11-08](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-08-laplace-transform-and-system-functions.md). *See also:* [Poles and zeros](#poles-and-zeros), [Frequency response](#frequency-response).

<a id="geometric-mean"></a>**Geometric mean** — The nth root of the product of n numbers; used to summarize benchmark speed ratios because the ratio of two machines' geometric means does not depend on the reference machine. *First defined in* [14-01](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-01-performance-power-iron-law.md).

<a id="geometric-series"></a>**Geometric series** — Σ a r^k, which sums to a/(1 − r) for |r| < 1 and diverges otherwise; models reflections, feedback loops, digital filters and annuities. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="gibbs-phenomenon"></a>**Gibbs phenomenon** — The persistent overshoot, about 9 % of the jump, of truncated Fourier series near a discontinuity; it narrows but does not shrink as harmonics are added. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="glitch"></a>**Glitch** — A brief unintended pulse on a signal while logic settles; harmless on data sampled by flip-flops after settling, but dangerous on clocks, asynchronous resets and signals leaving the clock domain, and a waste of energy everywhere. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md).

<a id="global-history"></a>**Global history** — A shift register of the outcomes of the most recent conditional branches, used by correlating predictors such as gshare to give the same branch different predictions in different contexts. *First defined in* [14-07](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md).

<a id="gradient"></a>**Gradient** — The vector of partial derivatives ∇f; it points in the direction of steepest increase, its length is that steepest rate, and it is perpendicular to level curves. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="gradient-descent"></a>**Gradient descent** — Minimizing a function by repeated steps x ← x − η∇f; stable only for step sizes below 2 divided by the largest curvature, and slow when the condition number is large. The workhorse of neural-network training. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="gradual-channel-approximation"></a>**Gradual-channel approximation** — The assumption that the potential along a MOSFET channel varies slowly compared with the vertical field, so each slice of channel behaves as a MOS capacitor biased by the local channel potential; it yields the long-channel I–V equations. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="graphical-convolution"></a>**Graphical convolution** — Evaluating a convolution integral by flipping one signal, sliding it across the other and integrating the product over the overlap, region by region between breakpoints at the sums of the signals' edges. *First defined in* [11-03](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-03-convolution.md).

<a id="graphics-processing-unit-gpu"></a>**Graphics processing unit (GPU)** — A throughput-oriented processor with many simple cores grouped into streaming multiprocessors, which hides memory latency by running tens of thousands of threads; used for graphics, scientific computing and AI. *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [SIMT](#simt), [Streaming multiprocessor (SM)](#streaming-multiprocessor-sm).

<a id="gray-code"></a>**Gray code** — An ordering of the 2^n bit patterns in which consecutive values differ in exactly one bit; the reflected binary Gray code is G = B XOR (B >> 1), used for encoders and for pointers that cross clock domains. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md).

<a id="grounding"></a>**Grounding** — Connecting a conductor to a large charge reservoir (the earth or a circuit's ground plane) that can supply or absorb charge freely, fixing its potential and draining the charge induced on its outer surface. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="group-delay"></a>**Group delay** — τg = −d∠H/dω, the delay of the envelope of a narrowband signal passing through a system; constant group delay means a pulse keeps its shape. For a single pole it equals the time constant at low frequency. *First defined in* [07-07](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-07-frequency-response-and-bode-plots.md).

<a id="group-velocity"></a>**Group velocity** — The speed dω/dβ at which a narrowband signal's envelope, and its energy and information, travel; equal to the phase velocity only in a non-dispersive medium. *First defined in* [13-05](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-05-plane-waves.md). *See also:* [Phase velocity](#phase-velocity).

<a id="gshare"></a>**gshare** — A correlating branch predictor that indexes a table of 2-bit counters by the XOR of the branch address and the global history. *First defined in* [14-07](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md). *See also:* [Global history](#global-history).

<a id="guard-bits"></a>**Guard bits** — Extra high-order bits in an accumulator that keep a sum of many terms from overflowing; a sum of N terms needs ceil(log2 N) of them beyond the width of one term. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md). *See also:* [Fixed-point arithmetic](#fixed-point-arithmetic), [Integer overflow](#integer-overflow).

<a id="guard-round-and-sticky-bits"></a>**Guard, round and sticky bits** — The three bits a floating-point adder keeps below the significand when aligning operands — the first two shifted-out bits plus an OR of all the rest — which suffice for correct rounding. *First defined in* [14-04](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-04-computer-arithmetic-and-number-formats.md).

<a id="guide-wavelength"></a>**Guide wavelength** — The wavelength of a mode along a waveguide, λ_g = 2π/β = λ/√(1 − (f_c/f)²), longer than the free-space wavelength and growing without limit as the frequency approaches cutoff. *First defined in* [13-10](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-10-waveguides-and-resonators.md). *See also:* [Waveguide mode](#waveguide-mode).

<a id="gummel-number"></a>**Gummel number** — The base charge integral G_B = ∫(n_i²/n_iB²)(p/D_B) dx (s/cm⁴) that sets a bipolar transistor's saturation current, I_S = qA_E n_i²/G_B; for a uniform silicon base it is the base dopant count per area divided by D_B. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="gummel-plot"></a>**Gummel plot** — A semilog plot of collector and base current against V_BE; its 60 mV/decade slopes, intercepts and the spacing between the curves give I_S, the Gummel numbers and the current gain, and show gain fall-off at low and high current. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="gustafsons-law"></a>**Gustafson's law** — The scaled speedup σ + N(1 − σ) obtained when the problem grows with the number of processors N and σ is the serial fraction of the parallel run; it grows linearly with N, unlike Amdahl's fixed-problem speedup. *First defined in* [14-01](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-01-performance-power-iron-law.md). *See also:* [Amdahl's law](#amdahls-law).

<a id="letter-h"></a>

## H

<a id="h-parameters"></a>**h-parameters** — Hybrid parameters with I1 and V2 as inputs; h11 input impedance (output shorted), h12 reverse voltage ratio, h21 forward current gain (β for a bipolar transistor, hfe), h22 output admittance (input open). *First defined in* [07-10](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-10-two-port-networks.md). *See also:* [Two-port network](#two-port-network).

<a id="half-adder"></a>**Half adder** — A block that adds two bits, giving sum S = A XOR B and carry C = AB. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md). *See also:* [Full adder](#full-adder).

<a id="half-circuit"></a>**Half-circuit** — One half of a symmetric circuit analyzed alone, using the fact that for differential signals the symmetry plane (such as a pair's tail node) is a virtual ground, and for common-mode signals each half sees twice the shared impedance. *First defined in* [12-01](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-01-differential-pairs.md). *See also:* [Differential pair](#differential-pair).

<a id="half-life"></a>**Half-life** — The time for an exponentially decaying quantity to halve, τ ln 2 ≈ 0.693τ; for growth the same expression is the doubling time. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="half-power-bandwidth"></a>**Half-power bandwidth** — The width ω₂ − ω₁ of the band over which a resonant response stays within 1/√2 of its peak (half the power); for a second-order band-pass it equals ω₀/Q exactly, with ω₁ω₂ = ω₀². *First defined in* [02-04](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-04-forced-response-and-resonance.md). *See also:* [Quality factor](#quality-factor).

<a id="half-wave-symmetry"></a>**Half-wave symmetry** — The property x(t + T₀/2) = −x(t), under which every even harmonic, including DC, is zero; zero-mean square and triangle waves have it. *First defined in* [11-05](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-05-fourier-series.md).

<a id="hall-effect"></a>**Hall effect** — The transverse voltage V_H = IB/(nqt) across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field; its sign gives the carrier type and its size the carrier density, and semiconductor Hall plates make magnetic sensors. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="hall-mobility"></a>**Hall mobility** — The mobility obtained from a Hall measurement, μ_H = |R_H|/ρ; it differs from the drift mobility by the Hall factor, which depends on the scattering mechanism. *First defined in* [09-03](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-03-drift-and-diffusion.md). *See also:* [Hall effect](#hall-effect).

<a id="hamming-code"></a>**Hamming code** — A single-error-correcting code whose check bits sit at power-of-two positions, so the syndrome of a word with one flipped bit is that bit's position; Hamming(7,4) protects 4 data bits with 3 check bits. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md). *See also:* [SEC-DED](#sec-ded), [Hamming distance](#hamming-distance).

<a id="hamming-distance"></a>**Hamming distance** — The number of bit positions in which two words differ; a code whose words are at least d_min apart detects up to d_min − 1 errors or corrects up to floor((d_min − 1)/2). *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md). *See also:* [Hamming code](#hamming-code), [Parity bit](#parity-bit).

<a id="hardware-description-language-hdl"></a>**Hardware description language (HDL)** — A language such as Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL for describing digital hardware structure and behavior, used for simulation and synthesis. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="harmonic"></a>**Harmonic** — A component of a periodic signal at an integer multiple k of its fundamental frequency; the k-th harmonic of a real signal is a sinusoid of amplitude 2|c_k|. *First defined in* [11-05](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-05-fourier-series.md).

<a id="harmonic-distortion"></a>**Harmonic distortion** — Output at integer multiples of an input sinusoid's frequency, produced by nonlinearity; HD2 ≈ (a₂/2a₁)A and HD3 ≈ (a₃/4a₁)A² from the Taylor coefficients. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md). *See also:* [Total harmonic distortion (THD)](#total-harmonic-distortion-thd).

<a id="harmonic-series"></a>**Harmonic series** — Σ 1/k, which diverges (slowly, like ln n) even though its terms shrink to zero. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="harvard-architecture"></a>**Harvard architecture** — An organization with separate instruction and data memories (or caches), so that an instruction can be fetched in the same cycle as a data access. *First defined in* [14-05](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-05-single-cycle-datapath.md).

<a id="hash-table"></a>**Hash table** — A key-value store that computes each key's array slot with a hash function, giving O(1) average lookup; collisions are resolved by chaining or open addressing, and the table resizes as its load factor grows. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md). *See also:* [Load factor](#load-factor).

<a id="hazard"></a>**Hazard** — The possibility of a momentary wrong output after an input change, caused by unequal path delays; a static-1 hazard dips to 0 when the output should stay 1, and is removed in two-level logic by adding consensus terms. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md). *See also:* [Glitch](#glitch), [Consensus theorem](#consensus-theorem).

<a id="hazard-rate"></a>**Hazard rate** — The failure rate among survivors, h(t) = f(t)/R(t); constant for the exponential, falling for infant mortality, rising for wear-out. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="header-file"></a>**Header file** — A C file (.h) of declarations (prototypes, types, macros) that a module offers, included by its users; wrapped in an include guard so its contents are processed once per translation unit. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="heap-memory"></a>**Heap (memory)** — The region for dynamic allocation (malloc, calloc, realloc, free), whose blocks live until freed; flexible in size but subject to leaks, fragmentation and unpredictable allocation time. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="helmholtz-equation"></a>**Helmholtz equation** — The phasor wave equation ∇²E + k²E = 0 with k = ω√(µε), obtained by combining Maxwell's two curl equations in a source-free uniform region; its solutions are waves travelling at 1/√(µε). *First defined in* [13-04](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-04-maxwells-equations.md). *See also:* [Maxwell's equations](#maxwells-equations).

<a id="helmholtz-theorem"></a>**Helmholtz theorem** — A smooth vector field that decays fast enough at infinity is determined uniquely by its divergence and its curl, and is the sum of a gradient and a curl; the reason Maxwell's equations specify both for each field. *First defined in* [13-01](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-01-vector-calculus-refresher.md). *See also:* [Divergence](#divergence), [Curl](#curl).

<a id="hertzian-dipole"></a>**Hertzian dipole** — An infinitesimal current element I·ℓ (ℓ ≪ λ), the building block of radiation; its far field varies as sin θ, it has directivity 1.5 (1.76 dBi) and radiation resistance (2π/3)η(ℓ/λ)². *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Radiation resistance](#radiation-resistance).

<a id="hessian"></a>**Hessian** — The matrix of second partial derivatives of a function; its determinant and signs classify critical points as minima, maxima or saddles. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="heterojunction"></a>**Heterojunction** — A junction between two different semiconductors, with steps in the conduction and valence bands at the interface; used to confine carriers, separate them from dopants and block unwanted injection. *First defined in* [09-13](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-13-compound-and-wide-bandgap-semiconductors.md).

<a id="heterojunction-bipolar-transistor"></a>**Heterojunction bipolar transistor** — A bipolar transistor whose emitter and base are different semiconductors, such as a SiGe base on a silicon emitter; the narrower base gap raises n_iB² and the gain, which designers trade for heavier base doping and a graded drift field. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="hidden-state"></a>**Hidden state** — Values held in a notebook kernel's memory that the visible code, read top to bottom, does not explain (from deleted, edited or out-of-order cells); cured by restarting the kernel and running all cells. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md).

<a id="high-bandwidth-memory-hbm"></a>**High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)** — DRAM built as a stack of dies joined by through-silicon vias and connected to a processor over a very wide interface on a silicon interposer (1024 bits per stack in HBM3, 2048 in HBM4), giving bandwidths of about 1–2 TB/s per stack. *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md).

<a id="high-electron-mobility-transistor"></a>**High-electron-mobility transistor** — A field-effect transistor whose channel is a two-dimensional electron gas at a heterojunction (HEMT), modulated by a gate on the barrier; used in RF amplifiers and, in GaN, in fast power switches. *First defined in* [09-13](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-13-compound-and-wide-bandgap-semiconductors.md).

<a id="high-k-dielectric"></a>**High-k dielectric** — An insulator with permittivity well above SiO₂'s 3.9 (HfO₂ and ZrO₂ about 25), used in transistor gates and DRAM capacitors to get high capacitance from a physically thicker, less leaky film. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="high-level-injection"></a>**High-level injection** — The regime in which injected minority carriers become comparable with the majority density, so quasi-neutrality raises the majority density too and the diode current rises only as e^(qV/2kT); in silicon it begins near 2V_T ln(N/n_i). *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md). *See also:* [Low-level injection](#low-level-injection).

<a id="hold-time"></a>**Hold time** — The minimum time a flip-flop's data input must stay stable after the active clock edge; the hold constraint t_ccq + t_cd ≥ t_hold does not involve the clock period, so a violation cannot be fixed by slowing the clock. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md).

<a id="hole"></a>**Hole** — An empty state near the top of an otherwise full valence band, which carries current as a positive charge with positive effective mass; holes are the carriers of p-type silicon and PMOS transistors. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="homogeneity"></a>**Homogeneity** — Scaling property of a linear system, f(a x) = a f(x); in a circuit with one source, every response is proportional to the source. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Linearity](#linearity), [Unit-output method](#unit-output-method).

<a id="hot-plug-overshoot"></a>**Hot-plug overshoot** — The voltage spike, up to nearly twice the supply, when a supply is connected through cable inductance to low-loss (ceramic) input capacitors that form a lightly damped series RLC; cured with a lossy bulk capacitor or other damping. *First defined in* [07-03](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-03-second-order-rlc-transients.md).

<a id="htol"></a>**HTOL** — High-temperature operating life test; JEDEC JESD47G (2009) specifies at least 125 °C junction temperature for 1000 h on 3 lots of 77 units with zero failures (the HTOL row of the current revision, Rev N listed Aug 2026, was not checked). *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="huge-page"></a>**Huge page** — A page much larger than the base page (such as RISC-V's 4 MiB Sv32 megapages or 2 MiB and 1 GiB Sv39 superpages), mapped by a leaf entry at a higher page-table level to increase TLB reach. *First defined in* [14-10](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-10-virtual-memory.md). *See also:* [TLB reach](#tlb-reach).

<a id="human-body-model-hbm"></a>**Human-body model (HBM)** — The component ESD test of ANSI/ESDA/JEDEC JS-001, modeling a charged person as 100 pF discharged through 1.5 kΩ (peak current 0.667 A per kV); the industry-recommended qualification target is 1 kV. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="hybrid-model"></a>**Hybrid-π model** — The small-signal model of a bipolar transistor with transconductance g_m = I_C/V_T, input resistance r_π = β/g_m, input capacitance C_π = τ_F g_m + C_jE, output resistance r_o = V_A/I_C, feedback capacitance C_μ and series resistances. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="hyperbolic-functions"></a>**Hyperbolic functions** — cosh x = (e^x + e^−x)/2, sinh x = (e^x − e^−x)/2 and tanh = sinh/cosh, linked by cosh² − sinh² = 1; they describe catenaries, overdamped responses, transmission-line input impedance and the differential pair's tanh transfer curve. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="hypothesis-test"></a>**Hypothesis test** — A decision rule that rejects a null hypothesis when data would be sufficiently unlikely under it, with a stated significance level α (false-alarm probability). *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="hysteresis-magnetic"></a>**Hysteresis (magnetic)** — The dependence of a ferromagnet's B on its magnetic history, traced as a B–H loop; soft materials (cores) have narrow loops, hard materials (permanent magnets) wide ones. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="hysteresis-switching"></a>**Hysteresis (switching)** — The difference between the input level at which a switching circuit changes state on a rising input and the level at which it changes back on a falling input; it should exceed the input noise's peak-to-peak value. *First defined in* [10-10](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-10-op-amp-application-circuits.md).

<a id="letter-i"></a>

## I

<a id="iq"></a>**I/Q (in-phase/quadrature)** — Representation of a bandpass signal by two baseband components, in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q), which together form one complex sample stream I + jQ; the native signal format of modern radios. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Error vector magnitude](#error-vector-magnitude).

<a id="ideal-current-source"></a>**Ideal current source** — An element that maintains a specified current regardless of the voltage across it; a 0 A source is an open circuit. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Ideal voltage source](#ideal-voltage-source).

<a id="ideal-diode-equation"></a>**Ideal diode equation** — The Shockley relation I = I_s(e^(qV_A/kT) − 1) derived from minority-carrier diffusion in the neutral regions, with I_s = Aqn_i²(D_p/(L_pN_D) + D_n/(L_nN_A)) for a long diode; the current rises tenfold per 59.5 mV at 300 K. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md). *See also:* [Reverse saturation current](#reverse-saturation-current), [Law of the junction](#law-of-the-junction).

<a id="ideal-low-pass-filter"></a>**Ideal low-pass filter** — A filter passing |ω| < W unchanged and removing all else; its impulse response sin(Wt)/(πt) is noncausal and not absolutely integrable, and its step response overshoots to 1.0895 (Gibbs). *First defined in* [11-06](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-06-continuous-time-fourier-transform.md).

<a id="ideal-transformer"></a>**Ideal transformer** — A lossless, perfectly coupled transformer with infinite magnetizing inductance; V2/V1 = N2/N1, I2/I1 = N1/N2, complex power passes unchanged and impedances scale by the square of the turns ratio. It does not pass DC. *First defined in* [07-09](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-09-mutual-inductance-and-transformers.md). *See also:* [Turns ratio](#turns-ratio), [Reflected impedance](#reflected-impedance).

<a id="ideal-voltage-source"></a>**Ideal voltage source** — An element that maintains a specified voltage between its terminals regardless of the current through it; a 0 V source is a short circuit. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Ideal current source](#ideal-current-source), [Internal resistance](#internal-resistance).

<a id="ideal-diode-controller"></a>**Ideal-diode controller** — An integrated circuit that drives a MOSFET so that it conducts like a diode with a forward drop of tens of millivolts and blocks reverse current, replacing ORing and reverse-polarity diodes. *First defined in* [10-01](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-01-diodes-and-diode-circuits.md).

<a id="ideality-factor"></a>**Ideality factor** — The factor η in I ∝ e^(qV/ηkT) that summarizes a measured diode characteristic; 1 for diffusion current, 2 for depletion-region recombination or high-level injection, with values between where mechanisms mix. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="iir-filter"></a>**IIR filter** — An infinite impulse response (recursive) digital filter, whose output feeds back into future outputs; it achieves sharp responses with few multiply-accumulates but must be checked for stability, has nonlinear phase and is sensitive to coefficient rounding. *First defined in* [11-04](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-04-lti-systems-and-differential-equations.md). *See also:* [FIR filter](#fir-filter), [Biquad](#biquad).

<a id="illegal-state"></a>**Illegal state** — A code of an FSM's state register that corresponds to no state of the design; reachable only through faults such as missing reset, timing violations or upsets, and handled by reset or recovery logic. *First defined in* [08-08](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-08-finite-state-machines.md). *See also:* [Single-event upset (SEU)](#single-event-upset-seu), [One-hot encoding](#one-hot-encoding).

<a id="illusion-of-competence"></a>**Illusion of competence** — The mistaken feeling of mastery produced by recognizing familiar material (for example, while re-reading a solution), as opposed to being able to recall and apply it unaided. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="image-frequency"></a>**Image frequency** — The input frequency on the other side of the local oscillator that mixes to the same IF as the wanted signal: f_RF + 2f_IF for a high-side LO; it must be filtered before mixing, because afterward it is inseparable. *First defined in* [11-11](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-11-modulation-and-filtering-applications.md). *See also:* [Superheterodyne receiver](#superheterodyne-receiver).

<a id="imaginary-unit"></a>**Imaginary unit** — The number j defined by j² = −1 (written i in mathematics; EE uses j because i denotes current). Multiplying by j rotates a complex number 90° counterclockwise. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="immediate"></a>**Immediate** — A constant encoded inside an instruction, such as ADDI's 12-bit signed value or a branch's offset; in RISC-V every immediate is sign-extended from instruction bit 31. *First defined in* [14-02](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-02-isa-risc-v-arm-x86.md). *See also:* [Sign extension](#sign-extension).

<a id="immediate-generator"></a>**Immediate generator** — The datapath block that reassembles an instruction's scattered immediate bits for its format and sign-extends them to 32 bits. *First defined in* [14-05](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-05-single-cycle-datapath.md).

<a id="impact-ionization"></a>**Impact ionization** — The creation of an electron–hole pair by a carrier that has gained more than about the bandgap energy from a strong field; the multiplication process behind avalanche breakdown and avalanche photodiodes. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="impedance"></a>**Impedance** — The ratio Z = V/I of voltage phasor to current phasor for an element or network, in ohms. Resistor R, inductor jωL, capacitor 1/(jωC). *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Reactance](#reactance), [Phasor](#phasor).

<a id="impedance-and-frequency-scaling"></a>**Impedance and frequency scaling** — Turning a normalized filter prototype (1 Ω, 1 rad/s) into a design without changing its response shape; impedance scaling by k multiplies R and L by k and divides C by k, frequency scaling by k_f divides L and C by k_f. *First defined in* [07-08](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-08-filters-and-resonance.md).

<a id="impedance-matching"></a>**Impedance matching** — Inserting a lossless network between a source and a load so that each sees the impedance that transfers maximum power (or minimizes reflection, or noise); exact at one frequency with two elements, over a band with more. *First defined in* [13-09](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-09-smith-chart-and-matching.md). *See also:* [L-network](#l-network), [Bode–Fano limit](#bode-fano-limit).

<a id="impedance-of-free-space"></a>**Impedance of free space** — η₀ = √(µ₀/ε₀) ≈ 376.7 Ω, the ratio E/H in a plane wave in vacuum; η₀/√ε_r in a dielectric. *First defined in* [04-08](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-08-maxwell-preview.md).

<a id="implicant"></a>**Implicant** — A product term that is 1 only where the function is 1 (or don't care); geometrically, a subcube of the input cube lying inside the on-set. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md).

<a id="implicit-differentiation"></a>**Implicit differentiation** — Differentiating both sides of an equation that defines y in terms of x, treating y as a function of x; used to differentiate ln x, arctan x and curves such as circles. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="improper-integral"></a>**Improper integral** — An integral over an infinite interval or of an unbounded integrand, defined as a limit; it converges if the limit is finite (for example ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges only for p > 1). *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="impulse"></a>**Impulse** — The time integral of force, J = ∫F dt (N·s), equal to the change in momentum; a short, violent impact and a longer, gentler stop can carry the same impulse. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="impulse-invariance"></a>**Impulse invariance** — Converting a CT system to DT by sampling its impulse response, h[n] = T h(nT), which maps each pole s to z = e^{sT}; it preserves the impulse response's shape but aliases the frequency response. *First defined in* [11-09](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-09-z-transform.md). *See also:* [Bilinear transform](#bilinear-transform).

<a id="impulse-response"></a>**Impulse response** — h(t), a system's output when the input is δ(t) with zero initial conditions; its transform is the transfer function, and the output for any input is the convolution h \* x. *First defined in* [02-05](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-05-laplace-transform-for-odes.md). *See also:* [Convolution](#convolution), [Transfer function](#transfer-function).

<a id="in-place-computation"></a>**In-place computation** — An FFT organization in which each butterfly writes its two outputs back to the memory locations of its two inputs, so the transform needs only N words of data memory. *First defined in* [16-04](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-04-the-fft.md). *See also:* [Butterfly](#butterfly).

<a id="incidence-matrix"></a>**Incidence matrix** — The branch-by-node matrix of a circuit graph, with +1 at each branch's start node and −1 at its end node. Its rank is n − 1 for a connected graph, the conductance matrix is AᵀCA, and its left null space holds the loop currents. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="inclusion-exclusion-principle"></a>**Inclusion–exclusion principle** — P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), which corrects the double counting of outcomes in both events. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="incremental-resistance"></a>**Incremental resistance** — The slope dv/di of a nonlinear element's i–v curve at an operating point, the resistance a small signal sees; for a diode it is about V_T/I. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="incrementally-linear-system"></a>**Incrementally linear system** — A system whose output is a linear system's output plus a fixed zero-input response, y = L{x} + y₀, such as an amplifier with offset or a linear circuit with initial stored energy; differences of outputs obey superposition. *First defined in* [11-02](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-02-system-properties.md). *See also:* [Linearity](#linearity), [Zero-input response](#zero-input-response).

<a id="indeterminate-form"></a>**Indeterminate form** — An expression such as 0/0, ∞/∞ or ∞ − ∞ whose form alone does not determine a limit; it must be resolved by algebra, standard limits or L'Hôpital's rule. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="indicator-variable"></a>**Indicator variable** — A random variable equal to 1 if an event occurs and 0 otherwise, so its expectation is the event's probability; counts are sums of indicators. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="indirect-band-gap"></a>**Indirect band gap** — A band gap whose conduction-band minimum lies at a different crystal momentum from the valence-band maximum (Si, Ge, SiC), so radiative recombination needs a phonon and light emission is weak, although absorption above the gap remains strong. *First defined in* [09-01](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-01-crystals-and-energy-bands.md). *See also:* [Direct band gap](#direct-band-gap).

<a id="inductance"></a>**Inductance** — Flux linkage per ampere, L = NΦ/i (henries), so that v = L di/dt; a long solenoid has µ₀N²A/ℓ, a core with reluctance R has N²/R. It scales as turns squared. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="inductive-kick"></a>**Inductive kick** — The large voltage an inductor develops (v = L di/dt) when its current is interrupted abruptly; it can arc switch contacts or break down transistors unless a flyback path is provided. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md). *See also:* [Flyback diode](#flyback-diode).

<a id="initial-rest"></a>**Initial rest** — The condition that a system's output is zero until its input becomes nonzero; with it, a constant-coefficient differential or difference equation defines a causal LTI system. *First defined in* [11-04](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-04-lti-systems-and-differential-equations.md).

<a id="initial-condition-source"></a>**Initial-condition source** — In the s-domain model of a capacitor or inductor, the source that carries the stored energy into the analysis; L·i(0⁻) in series with sL (or i(0⁻)/s in parallel with 1/sL), and v(0⁻)/s in series with 1/sC (or C·v(0⁻) in parallel with sC). In time it is an impulse of flux linkage or charge. *First defined in* [07-04](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-04-laplace-domain-circuit-analysis.md).

<a id="initial-value-problem"></a>**Initial-value problem** — A differential equation together with the value of the unknown at a starting time, y(t₀) = y₀, which fixes the arbitrary constant of the general solution. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="initial-value-theorem"></a>**Initial-value theorem** — f(0⁺) = lim sF(s) as s → ∞, valid when F(s) is strictly proper; it checks an inverse transform's starting value without inverting. *First defined in* [02-05](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-05-laplace-transform-for-odes.md). *See also:* [Final-value theorem](#final-value-theorem).

<a id="injection-efficiency"></a>**Injection efficiency** — The fraction of a forward-biased junction's current carried by carriers injected into the lightly doped side; close to 1 for a strongly one-sided junction and the basis of a bipolar transistor's current gain. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="input-bias-current"></a>**Input bias current** — I_B, the small DC current flowing into (or, for PNP input stages, out of) each op-amp input; through a resistance R it produces an error I_B R that is amplified like a signal. *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Input offset current](#input-offset-current), [Input offset voltage](#input-offset-voltage).

<a id="input-common-mode-range"></a>**Input common-mode range** — The range of common-mode input voltage over which every transistor of a differential stage, including its tail source, stays in its active (saturation) region, so that gain and CMRR hold. *First defined in* [12-01](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-01-differential-pairs.md). *See also:* [Differential pair](#differential-pair), [Rail-to-rail](#rail-to-rail).

<a id="input-impedance"></a>**Input impedance** — The impedance seen looking into a transmission line of length ℓ terminated in Z_L, Z₀(Z_L + jZ₀ tan βℓ)/(Z₀ + jZ_L tan βℓ) for a lossless line; it repeats every half wavelength and inverts (Z₀²/Z_L) at a quarter wavelength. *First defined in* [13-08](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-08-transmission-lines-sinusoidal-steady-state.md). *See also:* [Characteristic impedance](#characteristic-impedance), [Quarter-wave transformer](#quarter-wave-transformer).

<a id="input-offset-current"></a>**Input offset current** — I_OS, the difference between an op-amp's two input bias currents; it is the error that remains when the two inputs see equal resistances (a compensation resistor R1∥R2 at the + input). *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Input bias current](#input-bias-current).

<a id="input-offset-voltage"></a>**Input offset voltage** — V_OS, the small DC voltage that, applied between an op-amp's inputs, would bring its output to zero; modeled as a source in series with the + input and amplified by the noise gain (OPA187 10 µV max, LM358 7 mV max at 25 °C). *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Noise gain](#noise-gain), [Input bias current](#input-bias-current).

<a id="input-resistance"></a>**Input resistance** — The resistance seen looking into an amplifier's input terminals; with the source resistance it forms the input divider that sets how much of the source signal reaches the amplifier. *First defined in* [10-05](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-05-amplifier-fundamentals.md). *See also:* [Output resistance](#output-resistance), [Loading effect](#loading-effect).

<a id="input-referred-noise"></a>**Input-referred noise** — An amplifier's output noise divided by its gain, expressed as an equivalent noise source at the input so it can be compared directly with the signal; in a chain, each later stage's contribution is divided by the gain ahead of it. *First defined in* [12-10](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-10-noise-in-circuits.md). *See also:* [Equivalent noise resistance](#equivalent-noise-resistance), [Noise figure](#noise-figure).

<a id="insertion-loss"></a>**Insertion loss** — The reduction in delivered signal caused by inserting a component (a filter) into a matched path, in dB; for one resonator between equal terminations it is −20 lg(1 − Q_L/Q_u), so low loss needs an unloaded Q far above the loaded Q the bandwidth demands. *First defined in* [07-08](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-08-filters-and-resonance.md). *See also:* [Loaded Q](#loaded-q).

<a id="instruction-format"></a>**Instruction format** — The layout of an instruction's bits into fields (opcode, registers, function codes, immediate); RV32I has six (R, I, S, B, U, J), with the register fields in the same positions in all of them. *First defined in* [14-02](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-02-isa-risc-v-arm-x86.md).

<a id="instruction-level-parallelism-ilp"></a>**Instruction-level parallelism (ILP)** — The parallelism among the instructions of a single sequential program, the number that could execute at once if only true dependences constrained them; superscalar and out-of-order hardware extract it without help from the programmer. *First defined in* [14-08](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-08-out-of-order-and-superscalar.md). *See also:* [Dataflow limit](#dataflow-limit), [Superscalar](#superscalar).

<a id="instruction-set-architecture-isa"></a>**Instruction-set architecture (ISA)** — The contract between hardware and software, namely the instructions, registers, memory model and exceptions a program can rely on, independent of how a processor implements them. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="instrumentation-amplifier"></a>**Instrumentation amplifier** — A differential amplifier with high input resistance on both inputs and gain set by one resistor, classically two non-inverting stages followed by a difference amplifier, G = (1 + 2R/R_G)(R2/R1); its first stage multiplies the CMRR by its gain. *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR)](#common-mode-rejection-ratio-cmrr).

<a id="integer-overflow"></a>**Integer overflow** — A result outside a fixed-width integer type's range; in NumPy arrays and C it wraps around modulo 2^n (uint8 200 + 100 = 44) rather than raising an error. *First defined in* [05-02](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-02-numpy-and-vectorization.md).

<a id="integer-promotion"></a>**Integer promotion** — C's rule that integer types narrower than int (char, short, int8_t, uint8_t, int16_t, uint16_t) are converted to int before arithmetic, so uint8_t 200 + 100 is the int 300. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="integral-action"></a>**Integral action** — A controller term proportional to the time integral of the error, K_i ∫e dt (K_i/s); it can hold a constant output with zero error, so it removes steady errors to steps of reference and of disturbances entering downstream of it. *First defined in* [15-04](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-04-feedback-and-steady-state-error.md). *See also:* [System type](#system-type).

<a id="integral-test"></a>**Integral test** — For a positive decreasing f with a_k = f(k), Σ a_k converges exactly when ∫ f dx does, and the tail after n terms lies between ∫ from n+1 to ∞ and ∫ from n to ∞ of f. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="integrated-device-manufacturer-idm"></a>**Integrated device manufacturer (IDM)** — A chip company that both designs and manufactures its own chips in its own fabs. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="integrating-factor"></a>**Integrating factor** — A multiplier (e^{t/τ} for τ x' + x = u) that turns the left side of a first-order linear ODE into an exact derivative, giving the general solution as an integral of the input. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="integration-by-parts"></a>**Integration by parts** — ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du, the product rule in reverse; used for products such as x e^x, ln x and e^(ax) cos bx. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="integrator"></a>**Integrator** — A circuit or algorithm whose output is the running integral of its input, such as an op-amp with capacitive feedback, v_out = −(1/RC)∫ v_in dt, or a digital accumulator. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md). *See also:* [Integrator (op-amp)](#integrator-op-amp).

<a id="integrator-op-amp"></a>**Integrator (op-amp)** — An op-amp circuit with a capacitor in the feedback path and a resistor at the input, giving v_out = −(1/RC)∫v_in dt; a resistor across the capacitor makes it a "leaky" integrator (a first-order low-pass). *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="integrator-windup"></a>**Integrator windup** — The build-up of a controller's integral term while the actuator is saturated and the error stays large; when the output finally reaches the setpoint, the oversized integral keeps the actuator saturated, causing a large overshoot and slow recovery. *First defined in* [15-08](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-08-pid-control.md). *See also:* [Anti-windup](#anti-windup).

<a id="interface-traps"></a>**Interface traps** — Electronic states at the semiconductor–dielectric interface whose charge changes with surface potential; they stretch C–V curves, degrade subthreshold slope and add noise. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="interference"></a>**Interference** — The addition of waves arriving with different phases; constructive where path differences are whole wavelengths, destructive at half-wavelengths, redistributing (not destroying) energy. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="interleaving"></a>**Interleaving** — Mixing different problem types within a practice session, which forces choosing the method and improves later performance even though it feels harder during practice. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="intermediate-value-theorem"></a>**Intermediate value theorem** — A continuous function on [a, b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b); in particular, a sign change guarantees a root in between. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md). *See also:* [Bisection method](#bisection-method).

<a id="intermodulation-distortion"></a>**Intermodulation distortion** — Output at sums and differences of input frequencies produced by nonlinearity; with two tones, second-order products fall at f₁ ± f₂ and third-order products at 2f₁ − f₂ and 2f₂ − f₁, close to the signals themselves. *First defined in* [11-02](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-02-system-properties.md). *See also:* [Harmonic distortion](#harmonic-distortion).

<a id="internal-inductance"></a>**Internal inductance** — The part of a conductor's inductance due to magnetic energy stored inside the conductor itself; µ₀/8π = 50 nH/m for a round nonmagnetic wire with uniform current, whatever its radius, and vanishing at high frequency as the skin effect pushes the current to the surface. *First defined in* [13-03](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-03-magnetostatics-and-inductance.md). *See also:* [Inductance](#inductance).

<a id="internal-model-principle"></a>**Internal model principle** — A loop tracks or rejects a class of signals with zero steady error only if its loop gain contains a model of their generator, 1/s for constants, 1/s² for ramps, 1/(s² + ω₀²) for sinusoids of frequency ω₀. *First defined in* [15-04](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-04-feedback-and-steady-state-error.md). *See also:* [Integral action](#integral-action).

<a id="internal-resistance"></a>**Internal resistance** — The series resistance in the model of a real source (an ideal source in series with R_int), which makes the terminal voltage fall as v = V_oc − i R_int under load. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Open-circuit voltage](#open-circuit-voltage), [Short-circuit current](#short-circuit-current).

<a id="internal-stability"></a>**Internal stability** — Stability of every transfer function inside a feedback loop (reference to output, disturbance to output, reference to control effort); it rules out unstable modes hidden by pole–zero cancellation. *First defined in* [15-05](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-05-stability-routh-hurwitz.md). *See also:* [Pole–zero cancellation](#pole-zero-cancellation).

<a id="interpreter"></a>**Interpreter** — A program that reads source code and executes it at run time (Python compiles it to bytecode first), with no separate build step; mistakes surface only when the offending line runs. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="interrupt"></a>**Interrupt** — An asynchronous signal from a device or timer that makes the processor trap to a handler between instructions, so software need not poll; each one costs a fixed overhead for the trap and the handler. *First defined in* [14-11](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-11-io-buses-and-interconnect.md). *See also:* [Polling](#polling), [Interrupt coalescing](#interrupt-coalescing), [Trap (processor)](#trap-processor).

<a id="interrupt-coalescing"></a>**Interrupt coalescing** — Raising one interrupt for several device events, after a count or a timeout, to cut the CPU cost of interrupts at high event rates at the price of added latency. *First defined in* [14-11](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-11-io-buses-and-interconnect.md). *See also:* [Interrupt](#interrupt).

<a id="intrinsic-carrier-concentration"></a>**Intrinsic carrier concentration** — The electron (and equal hole) density of a pure semiconductor, n_i = √(N_c N_v) e^(−E_g/2kT); about 9.65×10⁹ cm⁻³ for silicon at 300 K and rising several hundredfold by 400 K. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="intrinsic-fermi-level"></a>**Intrinsic Fermi level** — The Fermi level E_i of an undoped semiconductor, where n = p = n_i; it lies near mid-gap, offset by (kT/2)ln(N_V/N_C), and serves as the reference in n = n_i e^((E_F − E_i)/kT). *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md). *See also:* [Intrinsic carrier concentration](#intrinsic-carrier-concentration).

<a id="intrinsic-gain"></a>**Intrinsic gain** — g_m·r_o, the largest voltage gain a single transistor can provide, set by its transconductance and output resistance. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md). *See also:* [Transconductance](#transconductance).

<a id="intrinsic-impedance"></a>**Intrinsic impedance** — The ratio of electric to magnetic field in a uniform plane wave, η = √(jωµ/(σ + jωε)); √(µ/ε) for a lossless medium (376.7 Ω in free space), and small and at 45° for a good conductor. *First defined in* [13-05](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-05-plane-waves.md). *See also:* [Impedance of free space](#impedance-of-free-space), [Uniform plane wave](#uniform-plane-wave).

<a id="inverse-function"></a>**Inverse function** — The function that undoes a one-to-one function, so that f⁻¹(f(x)) = x; for example ln undoes exp. Solving an equation for a variable applies an inverse. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="inverse-matrix"></a>**Inverse matrix** — A⁻¹ with A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I, existing exactly when det A ≠ 0. Computed by Gauss–Jordan elimination at about 2n³ flops; for solving systems, LU is cheaper and more accurate. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="inversion-layer"></a>**Inversion layer** — A thin layer of minority carriers at a semiconductor surface, induced when the surface potential exceeds about 2φ_B; it inverts the surface's conductivity type and forms a MOSFET's channel. *First defined in* [09-08](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-08-mos-capacitor.md).

<a id="invertible-system"></a>**Invertible system** — A system for which distinct inputs give distinct outputs, so an inverse system can recover the input; the inverse may still be noncausal or unstable, as for an echo channel whose echo is stronger than its direct path. *First defined in* [11-02](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-02-system-properties.md).

<a id="ionization-coefficient"></a>**Ionization coefficient** — The number of electron–hole pairs a carrier creates per unit distance in a given field, α = α_0 e^(−E_0/E); in silicon about 6.6×10³ cm⁻¹ for electrons and 2.8×10³ cm⁻¹ for holes at 3×10⁵ V/cm. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="ionization-energy"></a>**Ionization energy** — For a dopant, the energy needed to free its bound carrier into the band, E_C − E_D for donors and E_A − E_V for acceptors; 45 meV for phosphorus and boron in silicon, about twice the hydrogen-model estimate of 26 meV. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md).

<a id="ipc"></a>**IPC** — (Instructions per cycle.) The reciprocal of CPI; the measure quoted for processors that complete more than one instruction per cycle. *First defined in* [14-01](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-01-performance-power-iron-law.md).

<a id="ir-drop"></a>**IR drop** — The voltage lost along a power-distribution network by current flowing through its resistance, so circuits far from the supply connections see less than the nominal supply voltage. *First defined in* [06-04](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-04-nodal-analysis.md). *See also:* [Electromigration](#electromigration).

<a id="iron-law-of-performance"></a>**Iron law of performance** — Execution time equals instruction count times average cycles per instruction times clock period, T = IC × CPI / f; each factor is owned by a different part of the design (compiler and ISA, microarchitecture, circuits and process). *First defined in* [14-01](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-01-performance-power-iron-law.md). *See also:* [CPI](#cpi).

<a id="iterative-refinement"></a>**Iterative refinement** — Improving a computed solution of Ax = b by computing the residual r = b − Ax in higher precision, solving A d = r with the existing (often low-precision) factors, and updating x ← x + d; it converges when κ·u_low is well below 1. *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md).

<a id="i-v-characteristic"></a>**i–v characteristic** — The plot of all (voltage, current) pairs an element permits; a resistor's is a line through the origin, an ideal voltage source's a vertical line, an ideal current source's a horizontal line. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="letter-j"></a>

## J

<a id="jacobian"></a>**Jacobian** — The determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of a change of variables; its magnitude is the local area or volume scale factor, r for polar and ρ² sin φ for spherical coordinates. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md).

<a id="jensens-inequality"></a>**Jensen's inequality** — For a convex function g, E[g(X)] ≥ g(E[X]); averaging through an exponential or square law raises the result, so leakage or failure rate at the average input underestimates the average. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="jitter"></a>**Jitter** — The deviation of a signal's edges from their ideal times, split into unbounded Gaussian random jitter (RJ) and bounded deterministic jitter (DJ). *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md). *See also:* [Dual-Dirac model](#dual-dirac-model).

<a id="jitter-transfer"></a>**Jitter transfer** — The closed-loop transfer T = L/(1 + L) of a PLL or clock-recovery loop from input (reference) jitter to output jitter; low-pass, with peaking near the loop bandwidth that shrinks as phase margin grows and adds in decibels along a chain of identical stages. *First defined in* [15-12](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-12-control-applications-pll-regulators-thermal.md). *See also:* [Phase-locked loop (PLL)](#phase-locked-loop-pll), [Jitter](#jitter).

<a id="jk-flip-flop"></a>**JK flip-flop** — A flip-flop whose inputs J and K hold (00), reset (01), set (10) or toggle (11) the output at the clock edge, Q⁺ = JQ̄ + K̄Q; in standard-cell chips it is a D flip-flop with logic in front. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md). *See also:* [T flip-flop](#t-flip-flop), [Excitation table](#excitation-table).

<a id="johnson-counter"></a>**Johnson counter** — A twisted-ring counter that feeds the complement of its last stage back to its first, giving 2n states from n flip-flops with one bit changing per step. *First defined in* [08-07](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md). *See also:* [Ring counter](#ring-counter).

<a id="joint-distribution"></a>**Joint distribution** — The joint PMF p(x, y) or PDF f(x, y) of two or more random variables, giving the probability of any combination of values; marginals alone do not determine it. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="jointly-gaussian"></a>**Jointly Gaussian** — Variables whose joint density is the multivariate normal; their marginals and linear combinations are Gaussian, and for them uncorrelated means independent. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="joule-heating"></a>**Joule heating** — The conversion of electrical energy to heat in a resistance, P = I²R = V²/R, or locally p = J · E = ρJ² per unit volume. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="jump-conditions"></a>**Jump conditions** — The values an impulse imposes at t = 0⁺ on an Nth-order differential equation's solution; only the highest derivative contains the impulse, so the next lower derivative jumps by the impulse weight over the leading coefficient and lower derivatives are continuous. *First defined in* [11-04](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-04-lti-systems-and-differential-equations.md).

<a id="jump-discontinuity"></a>**Jump discontinuity** — A point where both one-sided limits exist but differ, as for the unit step at t = 0 or a capacitor's current at a switching instant. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="junction-capacitance"></a>**Junction capacitance** — The small-signal capacitance of a reverse-biased junction, ε/W per unit area, from charge uncovered at the depletion edges; about 1 fF/µm² at W = 0.1 µm, falling with reverse bias. *First defined in* [09-05](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-05-pn-junction-electrostatics.md). *See also:* [C–V profiling](#c-v-profiling).

<a id="junction-temperature"></a>**Junction temperature** — The temperature of a chip's active devices (T_J), the quantity reliability and performance limits are set on; it exceeds the case and ambient temperatures by the heat flow times the thermal resistances in between. *First defined in* [15-01](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-01-modeling-dynamic-systems.md).

<a id="junction-voltage-limiting"></a>**Junction voltage limiting** — A Newton-iteration safeguard in SPICE device models that compresses large steps in a pn-junction voltage above a critical voltage to a logarithmic step, preventing the exponential current law from overflowing or stalling convergence. *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md).

<a id="jupyter-notebook"></a>**Jupyter notebook** — A document (.ipynb, stored as JSON) of Markdown and code cells whose code runs in a separate kernel process; it saves outputs with the code, so a saved notebook shows results that may not match a fresh run. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md). *See also:* [Hidden state](#hidden-state).

<a id="jury-stability-test"></a>**Jury stability test** — An algebraic test, the discrete counterpart of Routh–Hurwitz, for whether all roots of a polynomial in z lie inside the unit circle; for z² + a₁z + a₀ it reduces to |a₀| < 1 and 1 ± a₁ + a₀ > 0. *First defined in* [15-11](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-11-digital-control.md). *See also:* [Stability triangle](#stability-triangle).

<a id="letter-k"></a>

## K

<a id="kahan-summation"></a>**Kahan summation** — Compensated summation that carries each addition's rounding error forward in a correction variable, giving an error bound independent of the number of terms at four operations per element. *First defined in* [14-04](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-04-computer-arithmetic-and-number-formats.md). *See also:* [Pairwise summation](#pairwise-summation).

<a id="kalman-filter"></a>**Kalman filter** — The optimal linear estimator of a state-space system's state from noisy measurements (Kalman, 1960), alternating model-based prediction with measurement correction; widely used in navigation, tracking and sensor fusion. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="karnaugh-map"></a>**Karnaugh map** — A truth table drawn as a grid whose rows and columns are labelled in Gray code, so that cells differing in one variable are adjacent (including across the edges); rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells are product terms. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md). *See also:* [Prime implicant](#prime-implicant), [Gray code](#gray-code).

<a id="kernel-gpu"></a>**Kernel (GPU)** — A function launched on a GPU over a grid of thread blocks, each thread running the same code on its own data. *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [SIMT](#simt).

<a id="kinetic-energy"></a>**Kinetic energy** — The energy of motion, ½mv² for translation and ½Iω² for rotation; by the work–energy theorem, net work equals its change. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="kirchhoffs-current-law-kcl"></a>**Kirchhoff's current law (KCL)** — The algebraic sum of the currents entering a node is zero at every instant; it follows from charge conservation and the lumped assumption that nodes store no charge. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL)](#kirchhoffs-voltage-law-kvl), [Lumped-matter discipline](#lumped-matter-discipline).

<a id="kirchhoffs-voltage-law-kvl"></a>**Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL)** — The algebraic sum of the voltages around any loop is zero at every instant; it follows from Faraday's law when no changing magnetic flux links the loop outside the elements. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Kirchhoff's current law (KCL)](#kirchhoffs-current-law-kcl), [Lumped-matter discipline](#lumped-matter-discipline).

<a id="kirk-effect"></a>**Kirk effect** — Base push-out at high current density, when mobile electrons in the collector depletion region cancel its donor charge near J = qN_C v_sat; the effective base widens, the transit time rises and f_T and gain collapse. *First defined in* [09-07](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-07-bipolar-junction-transistor.md).

<a id="kogge-stone-adder"></a>**Kogge–Stone adder** — A parallel-prefix adder with the minimum log2 n levels and fan-out 1, at the cost of about n log2 n operators and many long wires. *First defined in* [08-09](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md). *See also:* [Parallel-prefix adder](#parallel-prefix-adder), [Brent–Kung adder](#brent-kung-adder).
