<a id="quine-mccluskey-method"></a>**Quine–McCluskey method** — A tabular algorithm for two-level minimization that merges terms differing in one bit (grouped by their number of 1s) to find all prime implicants, then selects a cover from a prime implicant chart. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md). *See also:* [Petrick's method](#petricks-method), [Prime implicant](#prime-implicant).

<a id="quotient-rule"></a>**Quotient rule** — (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g², valid where g ≠ 0. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="letter-r"></a>

## R

<a id="race-condition"></a>**Race condition** — A situation in which a simulation result depends on the arbitrary order in which concurrent processes execute, typically from blocking assignments in clocked blocks that read each other's outputs. *First defined in* [08-05](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-05-verilog-and-testbenches.md).

<a id="race-to-idle"></a>**Race to idle** — Running a task at full speed and then power-gating the hardware, instead of running it slowly; it uses less energy when leakage or the power of the rest of the system is large. *First defined in* [14-01](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-01-performance-power-iron-law.md). *See also:* [Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)](#dynamic-voltage-and-frequency-scaling-dvfs).

<a id="radian"></a>**Radian** — The angle that subtends an arc equal to the radius; 2π rad = 360° and 1 rad ≈ 57.30°. Calculus formulas for sin and cos hold only in radians. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="radiation-efficiency"></a>**Radiation efficiency** — The fraction of the power accepted by an antenna that it radiates, R_rad/(R_rad + R_loss); small antennas have low radiation resistance and hence often low efficiency. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Radiation resistance](#radiation-resistance), [Antenna gain](#antenna-gain).

<a id="radiation-pattern"></a>**Radiation pattern** — The angular distribution of an antenna's radiated power (or field) in the far field, usually normalized to its maximum and characterized by its half-power beamwidth, nulls and sidelobes. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Directivity](#directivity).

<a id="radiation-resistance"></a>**Radiation resistance** — The resistance that, carrying the antenna's terminal current, would dissipate the power it radiates, R_rad = 2P_rad/|I₀|²; about 73 Ω for a half-wave dipole and well under 1 Ω for electrically small antennas. *First defined in* [13-11](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-11-radiation-and-antennas.md). *See also:* [Hertzian dipole](#hertzian-dipole), [Radiation efficiency](#radiation-efficiency).

<a id="radiative-recombination"></a>**Radiative recombination** — Band-to-band recombination that emits a photon, at rate B(np − n_i²); weak in indirect-gap silicon (B = 1.1×10⁻¹⁴ cm³/s) and strong in direct-gap GaAs (7×10⁻¹⁰ cm³/s), where it powers LEDs and lasers. *First defined in* [09-04](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-04-generation-recombination-continuity.md).

<a id="radius-of-convergence"></a>**Radius of convergence** — The distance from a power series' center within which it converges; it equals the distance to the nearest singularity, including complex ones. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="radix-4-fft"></a>**Radix-4 FFT** — An FFT that splits the DFT four ways at each stage; its 4-point butterflies need only trivial internal twiddles, so it uses (3N/8)log₂N complex multiplications, 75% of radix-2. *First defined in* [16-04](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-04-the-fft.md). *See also:* [Fast Fourier transform (FFT)](#fast-fourier-transform-fft).

<a id="rail-to-rail"></a>**Rail-to-rail** — Describes an op-amp input whose common-mode range includes both supply rails (usually with complementary input pairs and a crossover region), or an output that swings to within millivolts of the rails at light load. *First defined in* [10-09](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-09-real-op-amps-nonidealities.md).

<a id="rail-to-rail-input"></a>**Rail-to-rail input** — An input stage whose common-mode range reaches both supply rails, usually by placing NMOS and PMOS differential pairs in parallel so one pair works near each rail; its transconductance, offset and CMRR change where the pairs hand over. *First defined in* [12-08](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-08-op-amp-internals.md). *See also:* [Constant-gm input stage](#constant-gm-input-stage), [Input common-mode range](#input-common-mode-range).

<a id="random-dopant-fluctuation"></a>**Random dopant fluctuation** — The variation of transistor properties, chiefly threshold voltage, caused by the random number and placement of dopant atoms in a small channel; the count is Poisson-distributed, so a mean of N atoms varies by about √N. *First defined in* [09-02](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-02-carriers-doping-fermi-level.md).

<a id="random-process"></a>**Random process** — A rule assigning a waveform to each outcome of an experiment; at any fixed time its value is a random variable, and the collection of waveforms is the ensemble. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="random-seed"></a>**Random seed** — The starting value of a pseudo-random generator (np.random.default_rng(seed)); the same seed reproduces the same numbers, making simulations and tests repeatable. *First defined in* [05-02](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-02-numpy-and-vectorization.md).

<a id="random-variable"></a>**Random variable** — A function that assigns a number to each outcome of a random experiment, such as the number of bit errors in a packet or the noise voltage at a sampling instant. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="random-walk"></a>**Random walk** — The running sum (integral) of white noise, whose spread grows as √t without bound; it models accumulated phase error in free-running oscillators. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="rank"></a>**Rank** — The number of pivots of a matrix, equal to the dimension of its column space (and of its row space). Numerically, the rank counts singular values above a stated tolerance. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md). *See also:* [Column space](#column-space), [Null space](#null-space), [Rank–nullity theorem](#rank-nullity-theorem).

<a id="rank-nullity-theorem"></a>**Rank–nullity theorem** — For an m×n matrix of rank r, dim C(A) + dim N(A) = r + (n − r) = n. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="ratio-test"></a>**Ratio test** — A series converges if |a_{k+1}/a_k| tends to a limit below 1 and diverges if above 1; suited to factorials and powers. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="rayleigh-criterion"></a>**Rayleigh criterion** — Two point sources are just resolved when one's diffraction peak falls on the other's first dark ring, 1.22λ/D apart in angle; in lithography the analogous limit is CD = k₁λ/NA with k₁ ≥ 0.25. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="rayleigh-distribution"></a>**Rayleigh distribution** — The distribution of the envelope R of a complex Gaussian signal, f(r) = (2r/P̄)e^(−r²/P̄), when the power R² is exponential with mean P̄; mean √(πP̄)/2. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="reactance"></a>**Reactance** — The imaginary part X of an impedance Z = R + jX, in ohms. Positive for inductors (ωL), negative for capacitors (−1/(ωC)). *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="reactive-power"></a>**Reactive power** — Q = V_rms I_rms sin θ (var), the amplitude of the energy exchanged back and forth between source and reactive elements at twice the line frequency; positive for inductive loads, negative for capacitive. *First defined in* [07-06](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-06-ac-power-and-power-factor.md).

<a id="read-only-memory-rom"></a>**Read-only memory (ROM)** — A memory whose contents are fixed at manufacture (or programmed once); as logic, a 2^n by m ROM implements any n-input, m-output function by storing its truth table. *First defined in* [08-11](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-11-memories-and-programmable-logic.md). *See also:* [Lookup table (LUT)](#lookup-table-lut).

<a id="real-time-constraint"></a>**Real-time constraint** — The requirement that a DSP system finish each sample or block before the next arrives, on average and in the worst case; budgeted as cycles available per sample (f_clk/f_s) against cycles needed (operations per sample divided by operations per cycle, plus overhead). *First defined in* [16-01](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-01-discrete-time-systems-review.md). *See also:* [Multiply-accumulate (MAC)](#multiply-accumulate-mac).

<a id="reciprocity"></a>**Reciprocity** — In a linear network of resistors (and other reciprocal elements), the response at node k to a current injected at node j equals the response at j to the same current injected at k; mathematically, the resistance matrix G⁻¹ is symmetric. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="recombination"></a>**Recombination** — The annihilation of an electron–hole pair, by emitting a photon (radiative), through a trap level (Shockley–Read–Hall) or by giving the energy to a third carrier (Auger); net recombination occurs where np > n_i². *First defined in* [09-04](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-04-generation-recombination-continuity.md). *See also:* [Generation](#generation), [Minority-carrier lifetime](#minority-carrier-lifetime).

<a id="recombination-current"></a>**Recombination current** — The extra forward current from electron–hole recombination inside the depletion region, about (qn_iW/2τ)(e^(qV/2kT) − 1), dominant at low forward bias in silicon; in reverse bias the same traps produce generation leakage. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="recovery-time"></a>**Recovery time** — The minimum time between the release of an asynchronous reset or set and the next active clock edge, the reset's analogue of setup time. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md).

<a id="rectangular-form"></a>**Rectangular form** — Writing a complex number by its components, z = x + jy. Convenient for addition and subtraction. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Polar form](#polar-form).

<a id="rectifier"></a>**Rectifier** — A circuit that converts alternating voltage to a voltage of one polarity, using diodes (or transistors switched as diodes) to pass one or both half-cycles. *First defined in* [10-01](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-01-diodes-and-diode-circuits.md).

<a id="recursive-moving-sum"></a>**Recursive moving sum** — Computing the sum of the last N samples as s[n] = s[n − 1] + x[n] − x[n − N], two additions per sample at any N; its input–output map is FIR, but it hides an accumulator with a pole at z = 1, so it is exact only in integer (wraparound) arithmetic and never forgets a stored error. *First defined in* [16-01](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-01-discrete-time-systems-review.md). *See also:* [Internal stability](#internal-stability), [Wraparound](#wraparound), [Moving-average filter](#moving-average-filter).

<a id="reduction-of-order"></a>**Reduction of order** — Finding a second solution of a linear ODE by writing y = u(t)y₁(t) with a known solution y₁; for a repeated characteristic root it gives te^{−αt}. *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="reed-solomon-code"></a>**Reed–Solomon code** — A block code over m-bit symbols; RS(n, k) sends n symbols with k data symbols and corrects up to t = (n − k)/2 wrong symbols per codeword, as in Ethernet's RS(544,514). *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="reference-direction"></a>**Reference direction** — The arrow (for current) or the + and − marks (for voltage) chosen before solving a circuit; a negative result means the actual direction or polarity is opposite to the reference. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="reference-model"></a>**Reference model** — An executable model of the ISA that runs one instruction at a time, used to check a processor design by comparing their results instruction by instruction. *First defined in* [14-05](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-05-single-cycle-datapath.md).

<a id="reference-node-ground"></a>**Reference node (ground)** — The node chosen as zero volts, relative to which every other node voltage is quoted; a bookkeeping choice that need not be connected to the earth. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Voltage](#voltage), [Grounding](#grounding).

<a id="reflected-impedance"></a>**Reflected impedance** — The impedance a secondary circuit presents at the primary of coupled coils, (ωM)²/Z22 with Z22 the secondary loop impedance; its resistance is positive and its reactance has the opposite sign to Z22's. Through an ideal transformer a load reflects as (N1/N2)² Z_L. *First defined in* [07-09](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-09-mutual-inductance-and-transformers.md).

<a id="reflection-coefficient"></a>**Reflection coefficient** — Γ = (R − Z0)/(R + Z0), the ratio of reflected to incident wave voltage at a termination R on a line of characteristic impedance Z0; +1 for an open, −1 for a short, 0 for a matched load. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="regeneration"></a>**Regeneration** — Restoring a signal to clean logic levels at each stage, so that noise does not accumulate along a chain; the key advantage of digital over analog processing. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="region-of-convergence-roc"></a>**Region of convergence (ROC)** — The set of s for which a Laplace (or z-) transform's integral converges absolutely; for the Laplace transform a vertical strip bounded by poles, a right half-plane for right-sided signals and a left half-plane for left-sided ones. The same algebraic X(s) with different ROCs describes different signals. *First defined in* [11-08](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-08-laplace-transform-and-system-functions.md). *See also:* [Bilateral Laplace transform](#bilateral-laplace-transform).

<a id="register"></a>**Register** — A group of flip-flops sharing a clock that stores a multi-bit word, usually with an enable that lets it hold its value instead of loading a new one. *First defined in* [08-07](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md). *See also:* [Shift register](#shift-register).

<a id="register-file"></a>**Register file** — A small, fast memory of a processor's registers with several read and write ports used in the same cycle; its area grows roughly as the square of the number of ports. *First defined in* [08-11](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-11-memories-and-programmable-logic.md).

<a id="register-renaming"></a>**Register renaming** — Mapping each architectural register written by an instruction to a new physical register from a free list, recorded in a register alias (map) table, so that only true dependences remain between instructions. *First defined in* [14-08](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-08-out-of-order-and-superscalar.md). *See also:* [Name dependence](#name-dependence), [Out-of-order execution](#out-of-order-execution).

<a id="regression-line"></a>**Regression line** — The conditional mean E[Y | X = x] = μ_Y + ρ(σ_Y/σ_X)(x − μ_X) of jointly Gaussian variables, the best prediction of Y from X; the remaining spread is σ_Y√(1 − ρ²). *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="regression-test"></a>**Regression test** — A test kept permanently in a suite to make sure a fixed bug or a verified behavior does not silently return; in chip design, the nightly regression is the whole suite of such tests. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md).

<a id="related-rates"></a>**Related rates** — Rates of change linked by differentiating a relationship among quantities with respect to time, for example i = V dC/dt for a moving-plate capacitor. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="relative-degree"></a>**Relative degree** — The number of poles minus the number of zeros of a transfer function, n − m; the gain falls as 1/ωⁿ⁻ᵐ at high frequency, and physical systems have relative degree of at least 1. *First defined in* [15-02](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-02-transfer-functions-and-block-diagrams.md). *See also:* [Transfer function](#transfer-function), [Poles and zeros](#poles-and-zeros).

<a id="relative-permeability"></a>**Relative permeability** — The factor µ_r in B = µ_r µ₀ H for a linear magnetic material; near 1 for most materials, hundreds to tens of thousands for ferromagnets below saturation. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="relative-permittivity"></a>**Relative permittivity** — The factor ε_r by which a material's polarization reduces the field of a given free charge, so that ε = ε_r ε₀; about 11.7 for silicon and 3.9 for thermal SiO₂. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="relaxation-oscillator"></a>**Relaxation oscillator** — An oscillator without a resonator, in which a capacitor charges until a threshold, a comparator switches, and the capacitor discharges to a second threshold; its period is set by an RC time constant and the thresholds (an op-amp astable, the 555 timer). *First defined in* [12-09](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-09-oscillators.md). *See also:* [Schmitt trigger](#schmitt-trigger).

<a id="relocation"></a>**Relocation** — A note in an object file saying that an instruction or data word depends on a symbol's final address; the linker computes the address and patches the field. *First defined in* [14-03](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md).

<a id="reluctance"></a>**Reluctance** — The magnetic-circuit analogue of resistance, R = l/(µ_r µ₀ A) (A/Wb); flux = NI/R, series reluctances add, and a small air gap often dominates a core's reluctance. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="remote-sensing"></a>**Remote sensing** — Connecting a supply's feedback (sense) inputs to the load's terminals with separate wires so that it regulates the voltage at the load, raising its own output by the drop in the current-carrying wires. *First defined in* [06-11](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-11-practical-dc-circuits-and-measurement.md). *See also:* [Four-terminal (Kelvin) measurement](#four-terminal-kelvin-measurement), [Negative feedback](#negative-feedback).

<a id="removable-discontinuity"></a>**Removable discontinuity** — A point where a function's limit exists but its value is missing or different; redefining the value as the limit removes it (for example sin x/x at 0). *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="reorder-buffer-rob"></a>**Reorder buffer (ROB)** — A queue holding every in-flight instruction in program order; instructions finish in any order but retire from its head in order, which makes speculation and exceptions precise. Its size bounds the instruction window. *First defined in* [14-08](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-08-out-of-order-and-superscalar.md). *See also:* [Precise exception](#precise-exception), [Out-of-order execution](#out-of-order-execution).

<a id="repeater"></a>**Repeater** — A buffer inserted along a long on-chip wire to break it into shorter segments, converting delay that grows with the square of length into delay that grows linearly. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="reproducibility"></a>**Reproducibility** — The property that someone else can regenerate a result from the recorded code, data and environment and get the same numbers; achieved by scripting every step, pinning versions, seeding randomness and fingerprinting data. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md).

<a id="requantization"></a>**Requantization** — Converting a wide integer accumulator result back to a narrow format by multiplying by the combined scale factors (usually a fixed-point multiply and shift) and rounding. *First defined in* [14-04](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-04-computer-arithmetic-and-number-formats.md).

<a id="requirement"></a>**Requirement** — A statement of what a system must do (functional) or how well (non-functional, e.g. power, latency, reliability); good requirements are specific, measurable, testable, unambiguous and free of design. *First defined in* [05-09](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-09-software-engineering-practices.md). *See also:* [Traceability](#traceability).

<a id="reservation-station"></a>**Reservation station** — An issue-queue entry, introduced in Tomasulo's algorithm, where a dispatched instruction waits for its source operands and from which it issues to an execution unit once they are ready. *First defined in* [14-08](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-08-out-of-order-and-superscalar.md). *See also:* [Out-of-order execution](#out-of-order-execution).

<a id="reset-synchronizer"></a>**Reset synchronizer** — Two flip-flops that assert a domain's reset asynchronously but release it on the domain's clock edge, so every flip-flop in the domain leaves reset in the same cycle. *First defined in* [08-10](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-10-timing-metastability-cdc.md).

<a id="residual"></a>**Residual** — The difference between a measured value and a model's prediction (or, in root-finding, the value f(x) at a claimed root); random residuals at the noise level mean the model is adequate, while a systematic pattern means physics is missing. *First defined in* [05-03](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-03-scipy-sympy-matplotlib.md).

<a id="resistance"></a>**Resistance** — The ratio of voltage to current for a resistor, R = v/i, in ohms (V/A); for a uniform conductor R = ρL/A. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Conductance](#conductance), [Ohm's law](#ohms-law).

<a id="resistance-reflection"></a>**Resistance reflection** — The rule that a resistance in a bipolar transistor's emitter appears multiplied by β + 1 when seen from the base, and a resistance in the base appears divided by β + 1 when seen from the emitter. *First defined in* [10-07](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-07-bjt-single-stage-amplifiers.md).

<a id="resistivity"></a>**Resistivity** — The material property ρ = 1/σ (Ω·m) that sets resistance R = ρL/A; copper is 1.68 µΩ·cm in bulk and rises with temperature and in wires narrower than its mean free path. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="resolution-measurement"></a>**Resolution (measurement)** — The smallest change an instrument can display or report (one count of the least significant digit); it says nothing about accuracy, which the specification bounds separately. *First defined in* [06-11](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-11-practical-dc-circuits-and-measurement.md). *See also:* [Meter accuracy specification](#meter-accuracy-specification).

<a id="resonance"></a>**Resonance** — The condition in an LC-containing circuit where inductive and capacitive reactances cancel (ω₀ = 1/√(LC) in a series RLC), making the impedance purely resistive and the response peak. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="respin"></a>**Respin** — A new manufacturing pass of a chip with corrected masks after a bug or shortfall is found in silicon, either metal-only or full-layer. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="responsivity"></a>**Responsivity** — A photodetector's output current per unit optical power, R = ηeλ/(hc) = ηλ[µm]/1.24 A/W, where η is the quantum efficiency (electrons per incident photon). *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="reticle-limit"></a>**Reticle limit** — The largest area one lithography exposure can print, 26 mm × 33 mm ≈ 858 mm² on standard scanners (half that with High-NA EUV); it caps the size of a single die without stitching. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md). *See also:* [Chiplet](#chiplet).

<a id="retrieval-practice"></a>**Retrieval practice** — Learning by actively recalling information (self-testing, solving problems) rather than re-reading it; the "testing effect" is among the most robust findings in learning science. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="retrograde-doping"></a>**Retrograde doping** — A channel doping profile with a lightly doped surface layer over a heavily doped region, which fixes the depletion width, makes the body effect nearly linear and reduces impurity scattering in the channel. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="return-loss"></a>**Return loss** — −20 lg|S11| (or |Γ|), in positive dB, the ratio of incident to reflected power at a port; 20 dB means 1% of the power is reflected. *First defined in* [07-10](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-10-two-port-networks.md). *See also:* [S-parameters](#s-parameters), [Reflection coefficient](#reflection-coefficient).

<a id="return-ratio"></a>**Return ratio** — The loop gain measured at one controlled source, without splitting the circuit into A and β, by replacing the source with an independent one of value s_c and finding the value P·x_r its controlling variable would call for, T = −P·x_r/s_c. *First defined in* [12-05](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-05-feedback-topologies.md). *See also:* [Asymptotic-gain formula](#asymptotic-gain-formula), [Loop gain](#loop-gain).

<a id="return-address-stack-ras"></a>**Return-address stack (RAS)** — A small hardware stack that pushes the return address at each call and pops it to predict each return's target, which a BTB alone predicts poorly. *First defined in* [14-07](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md).

<a id="reverse-recovery"></a>**Reverse recovery** — The transient when a conducting PN diode is switched to reverse bias, in which stored minority charge first sustains a reverse current set by the circuit (the storage phase) and then decays; it limits switching speed and causes loss in power converters. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md). *See also:* [Storage time](#storage-time).

<a id="reverse-saturation-current"></a>**Reverse saturation current** — The constant I_s in the diode equation, the reverse current of an ideal diode, set by minority carriers generated within about a diffusion length of the junction; proportional to n_i² and so very small in silicon and steeply temperature dependent. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="richardson-constant"></a>**Richardson constant** — The prefactor K = 4πqmk²/h³ of the thermionic-emission current, 120 A/(cm²·K²) for the free-electron mass and about 100 for silicon in Hu's usage. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="ridge-point"></a>**Ridge point** — The arithmetic intensity (FLOP per byte) at which a machine's peak compute equals its memory bandwidth times the intensity; below it a workload is memory-bound, above it compute-bound. *First defined in* [14-14](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-14-ai-accelerators.md). *See also:* [Arithmetic intensity](#arithmetic-intensity).

<a id="riemann-sum"></a>**Riemann sum** — An approximation of accumulated quantity, Σ f(x_k\*) Δx, from samples of f on a partition; left, right, midpoint and trapezoid are common choices. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md). *See also:* [Definite integral](#definite-integral).

<a id="right-half-plane-zero"></a>**Right-half-plane zero** — A transfer-function zero with positive real part, typically from two signal paths of opposite sign (such as a Miller capacitor feeding the input forward around an inverting stage); it makes a step response start in the wrong direction and costs phase in a feedback loop. *First defined in* [07-04](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-04-laplace-domain-circuit-analysis.md). *See also:* [Poles and zeros](#poles-and-zeros).

<a id="ring-buffer"></a>**Ring buffer** — A fixed-size array used as a FIFO queue whose read and write positions wrap around; with free-running unsigned counters and a power-of-two size, the count is head − tail and the slot is counter AND (size − 1). Standard between interrupts and main loops. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="ring-counter"></a>**Ring counter** — A shift register whose output feeds its input, initialized with a single 1, so the 1 circulates through n states of n flip-flops with one-hot outputs. *First defined in* [08-07](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md). *See also:* [Johnson counter](#johnson-counter).

<a id="ring-oscillator"></a>**Ring oscillator** — An odd number of inverters connected in a loop, which oscillates with period 2Nτ_d; foundries use it to measure gate delay. *First defined in* [09-11](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-11-cmos-and-scaling.md).

<a id="ringing"></a>**Ringing** — A decaying oscillation after a switching edge, caused by energy sloshing between an inductance and a capacitance; its frequency is about 1/(2π√(LC)) and its decay is set by how resistance compares with √(L/C). *First defined in* [07-03](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-03-second-order-rlc-transients.md).

<a id="ripple-counter"></a>**Ripple counter** — A counter in which each flip-flop is clocked by the output of the previous one; it needs no counting logic but its outputs settle one clock-to-Q delay per stage after the clock, passing through transient states. *First defined in* [08-07](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md). *See also:* [Synchronous counter](#synchronous-counter).

<a id="ripple-voltage"></a>**Ripple voltage** — The peak-to-peak variation of a rectifier's smoothed output, about I_L/fC for a half-wave and I_L/2fC for a full-wave peak rectifier. *First defined in* [10-01](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-01-diodes-and-diode-circuits.md).

<a id="ripple-carry-adder"></a>**Ripple-carry adder** — An n-bit adder made of n full adders with each carry out feeding the next carry in; small, but its delay grows linearly with n because a carry may have to travel through every column. *First defined in* [08-04](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md).

<a id="risc-v"></a>**RISC-V** — An open, royalty-free ISA maintained by RISC-V International, built as a small base integer set (RV32I, RV64I) plus optional standard extensions (M, A, F, D, C, V and others) and bundled into profiles such as RVA23. *First defined in* [14-02](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-02-isa-risc-v-arm-x86.md).

<a id="rise-time"></a>**Rise time** — The time a response takes to go from 10 % to 90 % of its total change; τ·ln 9 ≈ 2.2τ for a single pole, so t_r ≈ 0.35/f_3dB. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="rms-value"></a>**RMS value** — Root-mean-square value, √(average of v²). For a sinusoid of amplitude V_m it is V_m/√2; it is the value that delivers the same average power to a resistor as a DC voltage of that size. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="roofline-model"></a>**Roofline model** — A performance bound that plots attainable throughput against arithmetic intensity as the lesser of peak compute and memory bandwidth times intensity, showing at a glance whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound. *First defined in* [14-15](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-15-roofline-and-benchmarks.md). *See also:* [Arithmetic intensity](#arithmetic-intensity), [Ridge point](#ridge-point).

<a id="root-locus"></a>**Root locus** — The set of paths traced in the s-plane by a closed-loop system's poles as a parameter, usually the loop gain K, runs from zero to infinity; the branches start at the open-loop poles and end at the open-loop zeros or at infinity. *First defined in* [15-06](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-06-root-locus.md). *See also:* [Angle condition](#angle-condition), [Magnitude condition](#magnitude-condition).

<a id="root-sum-of-squares-rss"></a>**Root sum of squares (RSS)** — Combining independent error contributions as the square root of the sum of their squares; less pessimistic than adding them worst-case. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="root-finding"></a>**Root-finding** — Solving f(x) = 0 numerically, the way a nonlinear circuit (a diode with a resistor) is solved; bracketing methods need an interval where f changes sign, while guess-based methods need a good starting point and can fail silently. *First defined in* [05-03](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-03-scipy-sympy-matplotlib.md). *See also:* [Bisection method](#bisection-method), [Brent's method](#brents-method), [Newton's method](#newtons-method).

<a id="root-sum-square-rss"></a>**Root-sum-square (RSS)** — Combining independent random contributions as the square root of the sum of their squares, because their variances add; it gives a total at a stated confidence level only if each input is given at that same level. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Error budget](#error-budget), [Worst-case analysis](#worst-case-analysis).

<a id="roots-of-unity"></a>**Roots of unity** — The N complex numbers e^{j2πk/N} (k = 0 … N−1) whose N-th power is 1, equally spaced on the unit circle. They are the twiddle factors of the FFT. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="round-to-nearest-ties-to-even"></a>**Round to nearest, ties to even** — IEEE 754's default rounding rule — round to the nearer representable number, and on an exact tie to the one whose last bit is 0 — which avoids the systematic drift of always rounding halves up (banker's rounding). *First defined in* [14-04](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-04-computer-arithmetic-and-number-formats.md).

<a id="routh-array"></a>**Routh array** — A table built from a polynomial's coefficients, two rows of alternate coefficients followed by rows of cross-multiplied differences; the number of sign changes in its first column equals the number of right-half-plane roots. *First defined in* [15-05](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-05-stability-routh-hurwitz.md). *See also:* [Routh–Hurwitz criterion](#routh-hurwitz-criterion).

<a id="routh-hurwitz-criterion"></a>**Routh–Hurwitz criterion** — A polynomial has all roots in the open left half-plane if and only if every entry in the first column of its Routh array is positive; for a cubic this reduces to positive coefficients with a₂a₁ > a₃a₀. *First defined in* [15-05](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-05-stability-routh-hurwitz.md). *See also:* [Routh array](#routh-array), [Characteristic polynomial](#characteristic-polynomial).

<a id="routing"></a>**Routing** — The implementation step that connects every net through the available wires and switches (an FPGA's programmable interconnect, or an ASIC's metal layers), resolving competition for wires. *First defined in* [08-12](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-12-fpga-implementation-flow.md). *See also:* [Placement](#placement), [Routing congestion](#routing-congestion).

<a id="routing-congestion"></a>**Routing congestion** — Demand by more nets than the wiring in a region can carry; routers resolve it by pushing nets onto longer paths, which adds delay, and a congested design can fail to route at all. *First defined in* [08-12](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-12-fpga-implementation-flow.md). *See also:* [Routing](#routing).

<a id="rtl"></a>**RTL** — Register-transfer level, the description of digital logic in an HDL (Verilog/SystemVerilog) as registers and the logic between them, from which synthesis produces gates. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="rule-of-three"></a>**Rule of three** — With zero failures in n independent trials, the 95% upper confidence bound on the failure probability is about 3/n. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="runge-kutta-method"></a>**Runge–Kutta method** — An explicit one-step ODE integrator that combines several slope evaluations within each step; the classical RK4 method uses four and is fourth-order accurate. *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md).

<a id="r-2r-ladder"></a>**R–2R ladder** — A resistor network of series R and shunt 2R sections in which each node sees R looking onward, so currents halve at every rung; the basis of many digital-to-analog converters. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md).

<a id="letter-s"></a>

## S

<a id="s-parameters"></a>**S-parameters** — Scattering parameters relating reflected to incident waves at ports terminated in a reference impedance (usually 50 Ω); S11 is the input reflection coefficient and S21 the forward transmission. Reciprocal networks have S12 = S21; lossless ones conserve power. *First defined in* [07-10](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-10-two-port-networks.md). *See also:* [Reflection coefficient](#reflection-coefficient), [Insertion loss](#insertion-loss), [Return loss](#return-loss).

<a id="s-plane"></a>**s-plane** — The complex plane of the Laplace variable s = σ + jω: the horizontal axis is the growth or decay rate (s⁻¹), the vertical axis the oscillation frequency (rad/s); the imaginary axis carries the frequency response. *First defined in* [11-08](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-08-laplace-transform-and-system-functions.md). *See also:* [Poles and zeros](#poles-and-zeros).

<a id="saddle-point"></a>**Saddle point** — An equilibrium whose matrix has real eigenvalues of opposite sign (negative determinant); trajectories approach along one eigenvector and leave along the other, so it is unstable. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="safe-operating-area"></a>**Safe operating area** — The region of collector-emitter voltage and current (for a given case temperature and pulse length) in which a power transistor may operate, bounded by maximum current, maximum voltage, the power hyperbola and, for bipolar devices, the second-breakdown limit. Abbreviated SOA. *First defined in* [12-07](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-07-output-stages.md). *See also:* [Second breakdown](#second-breakdown), [Thermal runaway](#thermal-runaway).

<a id="sallen-key-filter"></a>**Sallen–Key filter** — An active second-order section (Sallen and Key, 1955) with two resistors, two capacitors and a non-inverting amplifier of gain K; ω0 = 1/√(R1R2C1C2). At unity gain with equal resistors Q = ½√(C1/C2); with equal components Q = 1/(3 − K). *First defined in* [07-08](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-08-filters-and-resonance.md). *See also:* [Biquad](#biquad).

<a id="sample-function"></a>**Sample function** — One waveform of a random process, such as the noise recorded from one particular amplifier. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="sample-space"></a>**Sample space** — The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, such as every possible error pattern in a block of bits; events are subsets of it. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="sample-variance"></a>**Sample variance** — S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n − 1), unbiased for σ² because one degree of freedom is used up estimating the mean. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="sample-and-hold"></a>**Sample-and-hold** — A circuit that connects a capacitor to a signal through a switch (sample), then disconnects it to hold the voltage while it is converted; its settling and kT/C noise limit ADC accuracy. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="sampling-rate"></a>**Sampling rate** — The number of samples taken per second, f_s = 1/T_s, in samples per second (SPS) or hertz; it sets the highest frequency a sampled signal can represent unambiguously, f_s/2. *First defined in* [11-01](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-01-signals-classification-and-operations.md).

<a id="sampling-theorem"></a>**Sampling theorem** — A signal band-limited to f_M is uniquely determined by its samples taken at f_s > 2f_M and can be rebuilt from them by ideal low-pass filtering (sinc interpolation); sampling copies the spectrum at every multiple of f_s, and the condition keeps the copies apart. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Nyquist rate](#nyquist-rate), [Aliasing (sampling)](#aliasing-sampling).

<a id="sanitizer"></a>**Sanitizer** — Compiler-inserted run-time checks (UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, AddressSanitizer) that report undefined behavior and memory errors with the source line; used in testing, at roughly 2x run-time cost. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="saturation-arithmetic"></a>**Saturation arithmetic** — Arithmetic that clamps results to the largest or smallest representable value instead of wrapping around, so an overflowing signal clips rather than jumping to the opposite extreme. *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="saturation-current"></a>**Saturation current** — The current at which an inductor's core approaches saturation and its inductance has fallen by a stated percentage (set by the datasheet); beyond it the current rises much faster than v/L predicts. *First defined in* [07-01](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-01-capacitors-and-inductors.md). *See also:* [Saturation flux density](#saturation-flux-density).

<a id="saturation-flux-density"></a>**Saturation flux density** — The flux density B_s at which a ferromagnetic core is fully magnetized; beyond it the core adds nothing and inductance collapses. About 0.49 T for N87 ferrite at 25 °C (0.39 T at 100 °C), 1.5–1.8 T for silicon steel. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="saturation-region"></a>**Saturation region** — The MOSFET operating region with V_DS above V_Dsat = (V_GS − V_TH)/m, where the channel is pinched off at the drain and the current is nearly independent of V_DS; not the same as a bipolar transistor's saturation. *First defined in* [09-09](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-09-long-channel-mosfet.md).

<a id="scale-factor"></a>**Scale factor** — In an orthogonal coordinate system, the factor h_i that converts a step du_i in a coordinate into a distance h_i·du_i; (1, ρ, 1) for cylindrical and (1, r, r·sinθ) for spherical coordinates. It appears inside the derivatives of the divergence and curl. *First defined in* [13-01](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-01-vector-calculus-refresher.md). *See also:* [Divergence](#divergence), [Curl](#curl).

<a id="scale-length"></a>**Scale length** — The length λ over which a disturbance of the channel potential decays along a thin-body transistor; for a double gate λ² = (ε_s/2ε_ox)t_si t_ox + t_si²/8, and roll-off and DIBL scale as e^(−L/2λ). *First defined in* [09-12](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-12-finfet-gaa-cfet-backside-power.md). *See also:* [Characteristic length](#characteristic-length), [Drain-induced barrier lowering](#drain-induced-barrier-lowering).

<a id="scalloping-loss"></a>**Scalloping loss** — The drop in the largest DFT bin when a tone falls between bins; for a rectangular window it reaches 2/π (−3.92 dB) halfway between bins. *First defined in* [16-03](../courses/16-digital-signal-processing/chapters/16-03-the-dft.md). *See also:* [Spectral leakage](#spectral-leakage).

<a id="schmitt-trigger"></a>**Schmitt trigger** — A comparator with positive feedback that gives two switching thresholds, so a slowly varying, noisy input switches the output once instead of chattering; the threshold separation is its hysteresis. *First defined in* [10-10](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-10-op-amp-application-circuits.md). *See also:* [Hysteresis (switching)](#hysteresis-switching).

<a id="schottky-barrier"></a>**Schottky barrier** — The energy barrier φ_B that carriers in a metal face to enter a semiconductor's band at a metal–semiconductor junction; ideally ψ_M − χ but pinned near 0.7 V on n-type silicon by interface states, with φ_Bn + φ_Bp ≈ E_g. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md). *See also:* [Fermi-level pinning](#fermi-level-pinning).

<a id="schottky-diode"></a>**Schottky diode** — A metal–semiconductor rectifier whose current is thermionic emission of majority carriers; it has a saturation current 10³–10⁸ times a PN diode's, a lower forward drop and almost no stored charge, at the cost of higher leakage. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="schrodinger-equation"></a>**Schrodinger equation** — The wave equation of quantum mechanics, −(ħ²/2m)ψ″ + Vψ = Eψ in its time-independent 1-D form; its allowed solutions give the energy levels of wells, atoms and crystals. (Written Schrödinger in the text.) *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="scrambler"></a>**Scrambler** — A circuit that XORs data with a pseudo-random sequence so that long runs of identical bits become unlikely, giving a receiver transitions to recover the clock from; the descrambler applies the same sequence to restore the data. *First defined in* [08-07](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md). *See also:* [Pseudo-random bit sequence (PRBS)](#pseudo-random-bit-sequence-prbs).

<a id="sec-ded"></a>**SEC-DED** — Single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting; a Hamming code plus an overall parity bit (minimum distance 4), as in the (72,64) code of DDR4-generation server memory, which corrects one flipped bit per word and flags two; DDR5 ECC modules give each 32-bit subchannel 4 or 8 check bits. *First defined in* [08-01](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md). *See also:* [Hamming code](#hamming-code).

<a id="second-breakdown"></a>**Second breakdown** — Failure of a bipolar power transistor at high collector-emitter voltage when current concentrates in a hot spot that heats and draws still more current, a local thermal runaway; it limits the safe operating area below the average-power hyperbola. *First defined in* [12-07](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-07-output-stages.md). *See also:* [Safe operating area](#safe-operating-area), [Thermal runaway](#thermal-runaway).

<a id="second-derivative"></a>**Second derivative** — The derivative of the derivative, f''(x) or d²y/dx²; it measures curvature (concavity) and, for position, acceleration. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="second-derivative-test"></a>**Second derivative test** — At a critical point, f'' < 0 indicates a local maximum and f'' > 0 a local minimum; f'' = 0 is inconclusive. The size of f'' measures how sharp the optimum is. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="second-harmonic-distortion"></a>**Second-harmonic distortion** — The ratio HD2 of a nonlinear device's output at twice the input frequency to its fundamental; v̂/(4V_T) for a bipolar transistor and v̂/(4V_ov) for a square-law MOSFET driven by a sine of amplitude v̂. *First defined in* [10-04](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-04-small-signal-models.md). *See also:* [Harmonic distortion](#harmonic-distortion).

<a id="second-order-circuit"></a>**Second-order circuit** — A circuit whose behavior is described by a second-order differential equation, typically one with two independent storage elements (a capacitor and an inductor, or two capacitors that cannot be combined); its natural response has two characteristic roots. *First defined in* [07-03](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-03-second-order-rlc-transients.md).

<a id="self-checking-testbench"></a>**Self-checking testbench** — A testbench that compares the design's outputs with independently computed expected values and reports pass or fail automatically, rather than relying on a human reading waveforms. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="self-resonant-frequency"></a>**Self-resonant frequency** — The frequency at which an inductor's winding capacitance resonates with its inductance; above it the part behaves as a capacitor, not an inductor. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="semantic-versioning"></a>**Semantic versioning** — MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers where MAJOR signals incompatible changes, MINOR compatible new features and PATCH compatible fixes. *First defined in* [05-09](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-09-software-engineering-practices.md).

<a id="semi-insulating-substrate"></a>**Semi-insulating substrate** — An undoped or compensated wafer (for example GaAs, with about 10⁸ Ω·cm intrinsic resistivity) that barely conducts, so microwave circuits built on it lose little signal to the substrate. *First defined in* [09-13](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-13-compound-and-wide-bandgap-semiconductors.md).

<a id="semilog-plot"></a>**Semilog plot** — A graph with one logarithmic axis (usually the vertical); an exponential function plots as a straight line on it. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="sensitivity-function"></a>**Sensitivity function** — S(s) = 1/(1 + L(s)), the transfer function from reference to error in a unity-feedback loop; it scales how much of a disturbance reaches the output and how strongly plant variations affect the closed loop. Small |S| means good tracking and rejection. *First defined in* [15-02](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-02-transfer-functions-and-block-diagrams.md). *See also:* [Complementary sensitivity](#complementary-sensitivity), [Desensitivity factor](#desensitivity-factor).

<a id="sensitivity-peak"></a>**Sensitivity peak** — M_s = max |S(jω)| = 1/(min |1 + L(jω)|), the reciprocal of the Nyquist plot's closest approach to −1; a single robustness number that guarantees GM ≥ M_s/(M_s − 1) and PM ≥ 2 arcsin(1/(2M_s)). *First defined in* [15-07](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-07-frequency-domain-design.md). *See also:* [Sensitivity function](#sensitivity-function).

<a id="separable-equation"></a>**Separable equation** — A first-order equation y' = a(t)b(y), solved by integrating dy/b(y) = a(t) dt; constant solutions where b(y) = 0 must be checked separately. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="separation-of-variables"></a>**Separation of variables** — Solving a partial differential equation by trying products of one-variable functions; each factor satisfies an ordinary differential equation with a separation constant, and boundary conditions select a series of such products. *First defined in* [13-02](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-02-electrostatics-boundary-value-problems.md). *See also:* [Laplace's equation](#laplaces-equation), [Fourier series](#fourier-series).

<a id="separation-principle"></a>**Separation principle** — With state feedback acting on observer estimates, the closed-loop eigenvalues are those of A − BK together with those of A − LC, so the controller and the observer can be designed independently. *First defined in* [15-10](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-10-state-space-introduction.md). *See also:* [Pole placement](#pole-placement), [State observer](#state-observer).

<a id="sequence"></a>**Sequence** — An ordered list a₁, a₂, a₃, …; it converges to L if its terms approach L as n grows. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="sequential-consistency"></a>**Sequential consistency** — The memory model (Lamport, 1979) in which every execution behaves as if all cores' operations occurred in one global order that respects each core's program order. *First defined in* [14-12](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-12-multicore-coherence-consistency.md). *See also:* [Memory consistency model](#memory-consistency-model).

<a id="serializer-and-deserializer"></a>**Serializer and deserializer** — The circuits (SerDes) that convert a parallel word into a fast serial bit stream for transmission and back again at the receiver, built around shift registers and a clock multiplied or recovered to the bit rate. *First defined in* [08-07](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md). *See also:* [Shift register](#shift-register).

<a id="series"></a>**Series** — An infinite sum Σ a_k, defined as the limit of its partial sums; it converges if that limit is finite. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="series-connection"></a>**Series connection** — Elements joined end to end with nothing else connected at the nodes between them, so they carry the same current; series resistances add. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md). *See also:* [Voltage divider](#voltage-divider).

<a id="series-termination"></a>**Series termination** — A resistor at a driver that brings its output resistance up to the line's Z₀, so that the reflection from an open receiver is absorbed at the source; the receiver sees one clean edge and no DC power is spent. *First defined in* [13-07](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-07-transmission-lines-time-domain.md). *See also:* [Parallel termination](#parallel-termination).

<a id="series-parallel-equivalent"></a>**Series–parallel equivalent** — The pair of two-element models (R_s + jX_s in series, or R_p ∥ jX_p) that have the same impedance at one frequency; R_p = R_s(1 + Q²) and X_p = X_s(1 + 1/Q²). LCR meters report capacitance and inductance in either model, and the two differ by the factor 1 + D². *First defined in* [07-05](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-05-sinusoidal-steady-state-and-impedance.md).

<a id="set-associative-cache"></a>**Set-associative cache** — A cache divided into sets of A lines (ways); a block may be placed in any way of the one set its index selects, and a replacement policy picks the victim within the set. *First defined in* [14-09](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md). *See also:* [Direct-mapped cache](#direct-mapped-cache), [Fully associative cache](#fully-associative-cache).

<a id="set-cover-problem"></a>**Set-cover problem** — Choosing the fewest (or cheapest) sets from a collection so that their union covers every element; it is NP-hard, which is why exact logic minimization does not scale and tools use heuristics. *First defined in* [08-03](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md).

<a id="setpoint-weighting"></a>**Setpoint weighting** — Applying a PID's proportional and derivative actions to b·r − y and c·r − y (with 0 ≤ b, c ≤ 1) instead of the full error; it softens the response to setpoint changes without changing stability, steady-state accuracy or disturbance rejection. *First defined in* [15-08](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-08-pid-control.md). *See also:* [PID controller](#pid-controller), [Derivative kick](#derivative-kick).

<a id="settling-time"></a>**Settling time** — The time a response takes to come and stay within a specified error band of its final value; τ·ln(1/ε) for a first-order system, and (N+1)·ln 2 · τ to reach ½ LSB of an N-bit converter. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="setup-time"></a>**Setup time** — The minimum time a flip-flop's data input must be stable before the active clock edge; together with clock-to-Q and logic delay it sets the minimum clock period, t_pcq + t_pd + t_setup ≤ T_c. *First defined in* [08-06](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md). *See also:* [Hold time](#hold-time), [Clock-to-Q delay](#clock-to-q-delay).

<a id="shannon-capacity"></a>**Shannon capacity** — The maximum error-free data rate of a channel with bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio SNR, C = B log2(1 + SNR). *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="shannon-expansion"></a>**Shannon expansion** — F = A'·F(A=0) + A·F(A=1), splitting a function on one variable into two cofactors; it is the logic of a 2:1 multiplexer and the basis of decision diagrams and lookup tables. *First defined in* [08-02](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md).

<a id="shared-memory-gpu"></a>**Shared memory (GPU)** — A software-managed on-chip scratchpad in each SM, shared by the threads of a block and divided into banks, used to stage data for reuse. *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [Bank conflict](#bank-conflict).

<a id="sheet-resistance"></a>**Sheet resistance** — The resistance of a square of a thin film, R_s = ρ/t (Ω/□); a trace's resistance is R_s times its number of squares, L/W. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="shielding-effectiveness"></a>**Shielding effectiveness** — The reduction, in dB, of a field by a barrier; for a solid conducting sheet roughly the absorption loss 8.686 t/δ plus the reflection loss 20 log₁₀(η₀/4|η_c|). Real enclosures are usually limited by seams and apertures instead. *First defined in* [13-06](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-06-reflection-and-transmission.md). *See also:* [Skin depth](#skin-depth).

<a id="shift-register"></a>**Shift register** — A chain of flip-flops in which each clock edge moves every bit one stage along; with parallel load and output it converts between parallel words and serial bit streams. *First defined in* [08-07](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md). *See also:* [Register](#register), [Serializer and deserializer](#serializer-and-deserializer).

<a id="shockley-read-hall-recombination"></a>**Shockley–Read–Hall recombination** — Two-step recombination through a trap level in the gap, at net rate (np − n_i²)/[τ_p0(n + n_1) + τ_n0(p + p_1)]; the dominant mechanism in moderately doped silicon, most effective for traps near mid-gap. *First defined in* [09-04](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-04-generation-recombination-continuity.md). *See also:* [Trap](#trap), [Capture cross section](#capture-cross-section).

<a id="short-circuit"></a>**Short circuit** — An element or connection with zero voltage across it whatever its current (R = 0); an ideal wire or a closed ideal switch. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Open circuit](#open-circuit).

<a id="short-diode"></a>**Short diode** — A diode whose neutral region is much shorter than a diffusion length, so the excess-carrier profile is a straight line, the diffusion length in I_s is replaced by the region width, and the stored charge is set by the transit time W²/2D rather than the lifetime. *First defined in* [09-06](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-06-pn-junction-iv-and-capacitance.md).

<a id="short-channel-effects"></a>**Short-channel effects** — The departures of a small MOSFET from long-channel behavior caused by velocity saturation and by the source and drain sharing control of the channel with the gate, chiefly threshold roll-off, DIBL, degraded swing and higher output conductance. *First defined in* [09-10](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-10-short-channel-effects-and-leakage.md).

<a id="short-circuit-current"></a>**Short-circuit current** — The current a source or network would deliver into a short circuit, I_sc = V_oc/R_int for a linear model; a model parameter, not a safe operating point. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="short-circuit-time-constants"></a>**Short-circuit time constants** — The time constants R_isC_i of coupling and bypass capacitors, each found with the other low-frequency capacitors shorted; the sum Σ 1/(R_isC_i) is a conservative estimate of the lower −3 dB frequency. *First defined in* [12-04](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-04-high-frequency-analysis-methods.md). *See also:* [Open-circuit time constants](#open-circuit-time-constants).

<a id="shot-noise"></a>**Shot noise** — Noise from the random, independent arrival of discrete charges across a barrier, with one-sided density 2qI; it follows from Poisson statistics. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="si-base-units"></a>**SI base units** — The seven base units of the International System of Units (kg, m, s, A, K, mol, cd), from which all others, including V, Ω, F and H, are derived. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="side-channel"></a>**Side channel** — An unintended leak of information through physical behavior such as timing, power consumption or electromagnetic emission, which can reveal secrets that the logical abstraction hides. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="sifting-property"></a>**Sifting property** — ∫ f(t) δ(t − t₀) dt = f(t₀) when t₀ lies inside the integration range (and 0 otherwise); in discrete time, Σ f[n] δ[n − n₀] = f[n₀]. It is the defining action of the impulse. *First defined in* [11-01](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-01-signals-classification-and-operations.md). *See also:* [Unit impulse](#unit-impulse).

<a id="sign-extension"></a>**Sign extension** — Widening a two's-complement value by copying its sign bit into the new high bits (8-bit 0xFB, −5, becomes 16-bit 0xFFFB); needed by hand for odd-width fields such as 12-bit sensor readings, e.g. (x XOR 2^(k−1)) − 2^(k−1). *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="signal-flow-graph"></a>**Signal-flow graph** — A graph whose nodes are signals and whose directed branches carry gains; each node equals the sum of its incoming branch gains times their source nodes. It is the input form for Mason's gain formula. *First defined in* [15-02](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-02-transfer-functions-and-block-diagrams.md). *See also:* [Mason's gain formula](#masons-gain-formula), [Block diagram](#block-diagram).

<a id="signal-to-noise-ratio"></a>**Signal-to-noise ratio** — The ratio of a signal's power to the noise power in the same bandwidth, usually in decibels, 10 log(P_s/P_n) = 20 log(V_s,rms/v_n,rms); a noise density alone does not fix it until the bandwidth is stated. *First defined in* [12-10](../courses/12-electronics-2/chapters/12-10-noise-in-circuits.md). *See also:* [Noise figure](#noise-figure), [Thermal noise](#thermal-noise).

<a id="silicon-on-insulator"></a>**Silicon-on-insulator** — A wafer with a thin crystalline silicon layer on a buried oxide over a silicon substrate (SOI), made for example by hydrogen implantation, bonding and splitting; it removes junction capacitance and enables thin-body transistors. *First defined in* [09-12](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-12-finfet-gaa-cfet-backside-power.md).

<a id="similarity-transformation"></a>**Similarity transformation** — A change of state coordinates x = T z, which turns (A, B, C) into (T⁻¹AT, T⁻¹B, CT); it preserves the eigenvalues and the transfer function, and is used to reach canonical (controllable or modal) forms. *First defined in* [15-10](../courses/15-control-systems/chapters/15-10-state-space-introduction.md). *See also:* [State-space model](#state-space-model).

<a id="simple-harmonic-oscillator"></a>**Simple harmonic oscillator** — A system whose restoring force is proportional to displacement, m ẍ = −k_s x, which oscillates sinusoidally at ω₀ = √(k_s/m) while energy sloshes between kinetic and potential stores. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md). *See also:* [Quality factor](#quality-factor), [Force–voltage analogy](#force-voltage-analogy).

<a id="simpsons-rule"></a>**Simpson's rule** — Numerical integration fitting parabolas through triples of samples, with weights h/3 × (1, 4, 2, 4, …, 4, 1); its error falls as h⁴. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="simt"></a>**SIMT** — Single instruction, multiple threads; the GPU execution model in which scalar per-thread programs are grouped into warps that share one instruction stream, with an active mask handling divergence. *First defined in* [14-13](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md). *See also:* [Warp](#warp), [Branch divergence](#branch-divergence).

<a id="sinc-function"></a>**Sinc function** — sin(x)/x (sometimes normalized as sin(πx)/(πx)); its removable discontinuity at 0 is filled with the limit 1. It appears throughout sampling and Fourier analysis. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="sinc-interpolation"></a>**Sinc interpolation** — Ideal reconstruction of a band-limited signal from its samples, x(t) = Σ x[n] sinc((t − nT)/T): each sample launches a sinc pulse that passes through its own sample and through zero at all the others. *First defined in* [11-10](../courses/11-signals-and-systems/chapters/11-10-sampling-aliasing-reconstruction.md). *See also:* [Sampling theorem](#sampling-theorem), [Zero-order hold](#zero-order-hold).

<a id="single-cycle-processor"></a>**Single-cycle processor** — A processor that completes every instruction in one clock cycle (CPI = 1), so its clock period is set by the slowest instruction, typically a load. *First defined in* [14-05](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-05-single-cycle-datapath.md). *See also:* [Multi-cycle processor](#multi-cycle-processor).

<a id="single-event-upset-seu"></a>**Single-event upset (SEU)** — A bit flipped in a storage element by the charge from a particle strike, without permanent damage; a concern for state registers in automotive, aerospace and large-fleet systems. *First defined in* [08-08](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-08-finite-state-machines.md). *See also:* [Illegal state](#illegal-state).

<a id="single-photon-avalanche-diode"></a>**Single-photon avalanche diode** — A junction biased above breakdown so that one photogenerated carrier triggers a self-sustaining avalanche (SPAD, Geiger mode), giving a digital pulse per detected photon, followed by quenching and a dead time. *First defined in* [09-14](../courses/09-semiconductor-devices/chapters/09-14-optoelectronic-devices.md). *See also:* [Avalanche photodiode](#avalanche-photodiode), [Photon detection efficiency](#photon-detection-efficiency).

<a id="single-stub-matching"></a>**Single-stub matching** — Matching with a length of line that brings the load's admittance onto the unit-conductance circle, followed by a shunt stub that cancels the remaining susceptance; there are two solutions per half wavelength. *First defined in* [13-09](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-09-smith-chart-and-matching.md). *See also:* [Stub](#stub), [Smith chart](#smith-chart).

<a id="singular-matrix"></a>**Singular matrix** — A square matrix whose columns are dependent, so Ax = b has no solution for most b and infinitely many for the rest; elimination on it cannot produce a full set of nonzero pivots. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="singular-value-decomposition"></a>**Singular value decomposition** — A = UΣVᵀ for any matrix, with orthogonal U and V and non-negative singular values on the diagonal of Σ; it maps the unit sphere to an ellipsoid with semi-axes σᵢ. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md). *See also:* [Low-rank approximation](#low-rank-approximation), [Condition number](#condition-number).

<a id="sinusoid"></a>**Sinusoid** — A signal of the form A cos(ωt + φ), with amplitude A, angular frequency ω and phase φ. This curriculum always uses the cosine as the reference form. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="sinusoidal-steady-state"></a>**Sinusoidal steady state** — The response of a stable linear system to a sinusoidal input after transients have died out, a sinusoid at the input frequency whose amplitude and phase follow from phasor analysis. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="skin-depth"></a>**Skin depth** — The depth δ = 1/√(πfµσ) at which a field entering a good conductor falls by a factor e; 2.1 µm in copper at 1 GHz. The current flows mostly within a few skin depths of the surface. *First defined in* [13-05](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-05-plane-waves.md). *See also:* [Skin effect](#skin-effect), [Surface resistance](#surface-resistance).

<a id="skin-effect"></a>**Skin effect** — The crowding of AC current toward a conductor's surface, within a skin depth δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)) (about 0.21 mm in copper at 100 kHz), which raises resistance at high frequency. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md).

<a id="slack"></a>**Slack** — The margin by which a timing path meets its constraint, the required time minus the arrival time; negative slack is a violation. *First defined in* [08-10](../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-10-timing-metastability-cdc.md). *See also:* [Static timing analysis (STA)](#static-timing-analysis-sta).

<a id="slew-rate"></a>**Slew rate** — The maximum rate of change dv/dt an amplifier's output can produce, usually in V/µs; it limits the full-power bandwidth to SR/(2πV_p). *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="small-signal-conductance"></a>**Small-signal conductance** — The slope dI/dV of a nonlinear device's I–V curve at its operating point; for a diode g_d ≈ I/V_T, so r_d = V_T/I ≈ 26 Ω at 1 mA. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="small-signal-model"></a>**Small-signal model** — A linear model of a nonlinear device valid for small deviations about a DC operating point, built from slopes such as g_d = dI/dV or a transistor's g_m. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="small-signal-resistance"></a>**Small-signal resistance** — The inverse slope of a diode's exponential characteristic at its bias point, r_d = nV_T/I_D (25.9 Ω at 1 mA for n = 1), valid for signals much smaller than 2nV_T. *First defined in* [10-01](../courses/10-electronics-1/chapters/10-01-diodes-and-diode-circuits.md). *See also:* [Small-signal model](#small-signal-model).

<a id="smith-chart"></a>**Smith chart** — The unit disc of the reflection coefficient Γ with circles of constant normalized resistance and reactance drawn on it, so that impedance transformations along lines and by series or shunt elements become rotations and moves along circles. *First defined in* [13-09](../courses/13-electromagnetics/chapters/13-09-smith-chart-and-matching.md). *See also:* [Reflection coefficient](#reflection-coefficient), [Normalized impedance](#normalized-impedance).

<a id="snells-law"></a>**Snell's law** — n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ for refraction at a boundary (angles from the normal), from requiring wavefronts to match along the surface. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="snooping"></a>**Snooping** — Cache coherence by broadcast, in which every cache observes all requests on a shared bus or broadcast network and updates or supplies its copies accordingly; simple and fast, but limited in scalability. *First defined in* [14-12](../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-12-multicore-coherence-consistency.md). *See also:* [Directory protocol](#directory-protocol).

<a id="snubber"></a>**Snubber** — A network, usually a resistor in series with a capacitor, placed across a ringing switch or tank to damp it; the rule of thumb is R ≈ √(L/C) of the parasitic tank and C several times its capacitance, at a cost of C·V²·f_sw in power. *First defined in* [07-03](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-03-second-order-rlc-transients.md).

<a id="soft-error"></a>**Soft error** — A non-destructive change of a stored bit caused by a particle strike (neutrons or alpha particles); it is corrected by rewriting, and its rate is quoted in FIT per megabit. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="solenoid"></a>**Solenoid** — A long helical coil whose interior field is nearly uniform, B = µ₀nI with n turns per meter, and whose exterior field is small. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="solid-angle"></a>**Solid angle** — The 3-D analogue of an angle, Ω = A/r², the area a cone cuts from a sphere over the radius squared, in steradians; a full sphere is 4π sr. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).
